Cleaned-up E-text + + + + + + + +
This commentary is being composed upon that *sādhana* of Mañjughoṣa, the *Samāja*,
which was compiled by Jñānapāda.

1.0 [1a5–2a2] Now, desiring to compose this treatise (*sādhana*), this Master—wishing for the increase of merit through the worship of his chosen deity and seeking his desired goal without obstacle—first performs that worship and then states the subject matter and other preliminary factors that cause the engagement of discerning persons, beginning with the words "The glorious ones" (*śrīmanti*).
"The glorious ones, free from all error and thus stainless; splendors adorned by the manifestations of infinite lineages..."
Having paid homage to that Mañjuśrī, whose limbs are radiant with the embrace of wisdom, for the sake of worshipping him:

[In this context, the worship of the Blessed One consists of praise and prostration. Therein, praise is the proclamation of actual qualities. And that is performed by means of the qualifications of his splendors, belonging as they do to the Blessed One himself; or rather, because in reality there is no distinction between the splendor and the one possessing the splendor, just as there is none between the moon and its light.]

1.2 In this context, *śrī* (glory) generally consists of the perfection of one's own welfare and the welfare of others. [The portion regarding] the desire for the welfare of others... [is as follows].

1.3 Alternatively, *śrī* is the equipment of merit and gnosis (*puṇyajñānasambhāra*). Those things in which this exists are "glorious" (*śrīmanti*). By this, the cause of the perfection of one's own welfare is stated, because the perfection of one's own welfare—characterized by the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)—has merit and gnosis as its cause.
1.4 And because those splendors belonging to the Blessed One are characterized by majesty, [it indicates] the determination of the state of the fruit... [text fragment].

1.5 Those [cognitions] by which all delusions characterized by ignorance have been cast aside and destroyed are "thus" (tathā). For this very reason, they are "spotless" (nirmala), meaning they are pure and devoid of the obscurations of all afflictions along with their latent tendencies (*vāsanā*). By means of this, the purity of these [cognitions] indicates the spotless knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); thus, the perfection of one's own welfare (*svārthasaṃpat*) is stated, as well as the superiority [of these cognitions] over those of the Śrāvakas and others. 1.6 Indicating [this further], he says: "infinite" (*ananta*).

1.7 [2b1-2] The "emanation" (*nirmiti*) of infinite [beings], such as those of a single family and so forth, is the "projection" (*āropaṇa*) [of them] into the mental continuums (*santāna*) of those to be trained (*vineya*). Those [emanations] for whom this is an ornament are "such" (*tathā*). By this, the perfection of the welfare of others (*parārthasaṃpat*) is stated, because of being a protector (*tāyitva*), or because the cognition of that form by those to be trained is established through its sovereignty. + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + 1.8 [2b2] (*Wisdom (*prajñā) has the characteristic of being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*); it is knowledge [*vidyā*].
1.9 The "limbs" (*aṅga*) of that wisdom are generosity (*dāna*) and the rest, which are pure and consist of the accumulations of merit (*puṇya*) and knowledge (*jñāna*). As it has been said:
Generosity and ethical discipline are the accumulation of merit; wisdom is the accumulation of knowledge.
Three others are for the sake of both; thus all five are the accumulation of knowledge.
Likewise: "For the Sage taught this entire preparation for the sake of wisdom. (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 18.39)

"Therefore, one should generate wisdom" (Bodhicaryāvatāra 9.1abc). Association with them is the cause for the accomplishment of one's own welfare, for it is from the accumulations that omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) arises. In this context, at the stage of the fruit, the limbs of the wisdom consisting of perfect enlightenment are the sixteen divisions of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

1.10 [2b2-3] Through *śleṣa* (union/adhesion), they are the limbs of one's own innate gnosis (*svābhavidyā*). Their "attachment" (*saṅga*) is their state of being of one flavor (*ekarasa*) with skillful means (*upāya*). The meaning is that it is a form that is profound and sublime, characterized by a continuous, effortless flow, and bringing benefit to the entire world without exception.

1.11 [2b3] By that [means], they are beautiful (*rucira*), radiant, and pervasive. Precisely because of this, his splendor (*śrī*) is tender and sweet, free from suffering and fear. They are beautiful through their attachment to the limbs of wisdom (*prajñā*).

Alternatively, by this [verse], the cause for the perfection of the welfare of others (*parārthasaṃpad*) has been stated, because it characterizes the great passion (*mahārāga*) which is the cause of the welfare of others. And from that, the distinction [of the author] from those who have fully awakened to the *Tattvasaṃgraha* and other [tantras] has been stated.
By the word "having prostrated" (*abhivandya*), the worship consisting of physical prostration and so forth is expressed.

Then, the connection is as follows: "Having prostrated to that Mañjuśrī whose splendors (*tejāṃsi*) shine and radiate in such a manner, I shall state the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) for his very worship" (cf. 2d).
2.0 [2b5] To demonstrate the excellence of this method, he says: "Śrīmatsamājanītyā," etc.
"One who has generated enthusiasm through the request of a virtuous friend according to the procedure of the *Śrīmad-samāja*."
I shall explain the ritual procedure which is the cause for the accomplishment of the welfare of the entire world.

(2.1) "Śrī" is the worldly and supramundane prosperity of the world. He who possesses that as his effect is "Śrīmān"; and he who is the *Samāja* (the Assembly) is likewise. The "method" (*nīti*) is the tradition (*āmnāya*), and by means of that.
2.2 [2b6–7] He states his own qualification: “sanmitra” and so forth. A “good friend” (sanmitra) is a teacher (guru).
2.3 For it is thus heard that the venerable Pālitapāda made a request to compose this treatise.
2.4 [3a2] “Encouraged by that [request], having generated effort, I shall speak. By this, he demonstrates his reliability through self-confidence.
2.5 Or rather, the Blessed One himself is the true friend. This treatise was composed with the zeal of seeking him out.

2.6 With the words beginning "sakala" (all), he qualifies the method (*vidhi*). "All" refers to the perfection of the welfare of the world—both mundane and supramundane—extending up to perfect enlightenment; it is the "cause" or "source" (*nidāna*) of that. By this, he has shown the purpose and other factors that serve as the basis for the engagement of a discerning person. For in this case, the perfection of the welfare of the world is the subject matter and the purpose of the treatise; the method, which is the source of that, is the subject matter (*abhidheya*).

The purpose of composing and studying this treatise (*prakaraṇa*) is its presentation in a manner that is not contrary to reality. Since this is accomplished by means of this very treatise, the relationship between the treatise and its purpose—characterized as that of the means (*upāya*) and the end (*upeya*)—is also effectively stated by implication.

Now, one might raise the objection: "Knowledge of the ritual procedure for the *sādhana* of Mañjuśrī may be obtained from the scriptures of the Blessed One or from the instructions of other masters; so what is the use of this? In response to such a doubt, he states the specific purpose of this *sādhana*, beginning with the words "the perfection of the moment" (*kṣaṇasaṃpad*).
This perfection of the moment is fickle...
Association with the virtuous is very difficult to find in this world;
it is that which makes this mind supremely inclined toward wisdom and skillful means.

3.1 [3a6–3b4] The perfection of the momentary personal existence (*kṣaṇa-ātmabhāva*) consists in being free from the eight inopportune states (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*). In this regard, these are the eight inopportune states: holding wrong views; rebirth in the hells; rebirth among the hungry ghosts (*preta*); rebirth among animals; not hearing the Buddha’s word; rebirth in the border regions; being mentally dull, mute, or speech-impaired; and rebirth among the long-lived gods. This perfection of the moment, characterized by liberation from these eight inopportune states that are so difficult to abandon, is fickle and perishable.

Furthermore, association with virtuous people who provide proper instruction in assemblies is very difficult for the world to obtain; this is because there is no distinction between the genitive and locative cases here [in the compound *loke lokasya*]. And it has been said:
"Does the appearance of those possessing all knowledge ever occur in the world, or not?
It may happen only once in a great while, like the flower of the *udumbara* tree."
Even more difficult to arise than that is indeed the practice of the way of mantra,
by which those who do not enter nirvana are able to accomplish incomparable benefit for sentient beings.
(Guhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi 203–204).
It is also stated in the *Samāja* by the Great Vajradhara:
"O Blessed Ones, sentient beings are unfit for the secret reality; therefore, it was not spoken at that time. (Guhyasamājatantra p. 109, ll. 6–7).
Thus, immediately following that, it was also said by the Tathāgatas:

"O sons of noble family, just as this general syllable has not been known or heard by you, so too has it not been [known or heard] by us, all the Tathāgatas, and by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas" (*Guhyasamājatantra*, p. 109, ll.
18–19), and so forth. By this, the difficulty of the arising of the Mantra system is shown, and thereby the difficulty of finding those who teach it is demonstrated.

3.2 [3b5-6] *Tat* means "therefore. *Adaḥ* refers to the mind of the world, which is included within the perfection of the characteristic of agility (*capala-lakṣaṇa-sampad*), and which is inclined toward wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya-pravaṇa*), having a profound and sublime form, and being under the sway of emptiness and compassion (*śūnyatā-karuṇā-paravaśa*). *Param* means "supreme," in the sense of having a non-dual nature (*advaita-rūpa*). This is connected precisely with the statement that he will explain the previously mentioned method (see 2d).

3.3 This is what is meant: Since this perfection of the moment is extremely difficult to find and is subject to destruction, and since association with the gurus is hard to obtain, I shall explain the procedure mentioned immediately below (see 2d) in order to prevent obstacles to listening to the detailed commentary on the text and so forth, and thereby to direct that mind toward the supreme application of wisdom and skillful means; the sense is that it will be done in brief.

4.0 [3b7–4a2] Now, since the perfections of the practitioner’s place and the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) are to be discussed, and because the practitioner himself is primary regarding the attainment of success (*siddhi*), there is first an instruction on him as one fit for success. Although the object of accomplishment is desired, it is taught later because it is produced subsequently, being preceded by its causes. Therefore, he explains how the practitioner becomes fit by means of two verses beginning with "therein" (*tatra*).
Therein, the mantra-practitioner, having generated the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) through the power of compassion...

"Adorned with virtues such as renunciation, and possessing conviction in the profound method. (4.1) Here, "therein" (*tatra*) serves as an introductory phrase. "Compassion" (*karuṇā*) is characterized by the desire to deliver [beings] from suffering or the causes of suffering; it has the nature of being rooted in the sorrow of the lineage (*gotra*). "By its power" (*tasyāḥ prabhāvāt*) refers to its connection with [other] qualities. The qualities such as the spirit of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) are implied by that [compassion]. One who has generated the mind directed toward enlightenment—that is, toward Buddhahood—is "one who has thus produced the mind" (*tathā... utpāditabodhimānasaḥ*). "The practitioner" (*mantrī*) refers to the yogi; the connection is that he should accomplish the one named Mañjughoṣa (see 6d).

4.2 Likewise, a compassionate person necessarily becomes intent on seeking the means [to achieve it] out of a desire to act for the welfare of beings. Thereupon, this one of supreme compassion, seeing that the welfare of the world cannot be accomplished in all its aspects due to a lack of omniscience, generates the mind directed toward the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). That too is impossible without a means; therefore, he practices that means. Then, having attained perfect awakening (*abhisambuddha*), he brings about the welfare of beings through the teaching of the Dharma and so forth—this is the sequence.
And as it was said by Prajñākaragupta:
That desire for others to be separated from suffering and from the causes of suffering is compassion; one who possesses it therefore directs the mind toward acquiring the means for that end.
(Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra 377).
For this very reason,
his status as a Tathāgata is merely incidental.

Thus it has been stated in various places. 4.3 [4a6-7] He states those very means in brief as qualifications of the practitioner—beginning with "renunciation" (*tyāga*). Renunciation and so forth refer to the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) and the others; they are called "qualities" (*guṇa*) because they are multiplied, that is, practiced repeatedly. The practitioner who possesses these as his ornament is described as such. One whose conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the profound system—the yoga of the mantra system in the form of selflessness—is an aspiration based on the ascertainment of reality, is likewise described. This is a compound meaning: one who is adorned with the qualities of renunciation and so forth, and who possesses conviction in the profound system.
5.0 He states the definition of the present subject:
"Endowed with the splendor of the ritual of the glorious *Samāja* maṇḍala and the perfection of consecration," and so forth.

The wise one, having duly obtained permission for the propitiation of his own mantra, and being illustrious through the intention of non-negligence regarding the afflictions, possesses the *Samāja* (Gathering). By its tradition, there are the mandala rituals; the consecrations performed by those means are "excellent consecrations. Their excellence is due to their having been received from true gurus according to the complete ritual procedure. This was stated for the sake of transforming the basis of the path through complete meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). He is "endowed with" or "possessed of" the perfection of these.

5.2 [4b1-2] “In accordance with the rule” (*vidhivat*) means that he has received permission from his gurus through the sequence beginning with the water-consecration and the crown-consecration; and having received that permission, he subsequently undertakes the observance of knowledge (*vidyāvrata*) and so forth, as well as all other permissions. Thus, he is one who has received permission in accordance with the rule. 5.3 [4b2-4] “One’s own mantra” (*nijamantra*) refers to one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), because there is no distinction between the mantra and the deity. Its “propitiation” (*ārādhana*) is the cultivation [of the deity] by means of service (*sevā*) and other methods. In this regard, the “wise one” (*dhīmān*) is one who possesses the realization of the non-differentiation of the limbs [of the ritual] through the pledges (*samaya*), vows (*saṃvara*), and so forth. And it was said by the Blessed One: “One should recite the mantra with undivided limbs.”
(Guhyasamājatantra 7.4c).

Alternatively, "one's own mantra" refers to the mantra of one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). Its "propitiation" is the sequence of meditative cultivation and so forth; in that regard, "the wise one" means one who possesses the cognition of non-duality regarding the mantra-deity and so forth, by way of its inconceivable nature and other qualities.

In this context, because renunciation and the rest function as qualifiers of the practitioner through the exclusion of their non-application, qualities such as being a knower of the secret, a yogin, and a knower of reality are also intended as qualifiers of the practitioner. As it was said by Bhadrapāda:

Even if one is endowed with yoga, fortitude, and so forth, if one lacks the aforementioned qualities, one is not fit for the welfare of sentient beings; for these qualities must be possessed by the virtuous.
(Guhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi 6).

6.0 [4b6-7]: "For the mind of one who is happy in a delightful place becomes concentrated; one whose mind is concentrated understands things as they truly are; and understanding things as they truly are, one is liberated. Having thus reflected in the mind, he states the qualification of the location—beginning with "in some place"—in order to characterize the practice of the objects that delight the mind.
On a certain mountain, whose slopes were resplendent with rows of excellent trees and an abundance of pure water,
[he saw] the Blessed One thus.
One should accomplish the one named Mañjughoṣa.

(6.1) "In some place" means in a location where no specific detail has been specified. "Whose vicinity is resplendent and beautified by both an abundance of pure water and rows of excellent trees"—that mountain (*bhūbhṛt*) is such a place; on that mountain.
(6.2) Alternatively, it is characterized as a site for the expansion of festivals. Its literal meaning, however, is that it "supports the pure knowledges of the earth."
6.3 Regarding the term "Bhagavant": *Bhaga* is said to mean "breaking," because of the breaking of the Māras of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth.
Since the afflictions are indeed to be slain by wisdom (*prajñā*), therefore wisdom is called *bhaga*.

Because of the statement [in the *Vajraśekhara*, 191b7], "bhaga" is that which possesses the breaking of the Māras of the afflictions, the aggregates, death, and the son of a god, and whose intrinsic nature is pure wisdom (*viśuddhaprajñā*). Alternatively:
"The totality of sovereignty, beauty, fame, and glory..."
Furthermore, the Vedic revelation states that "Bhaga" refers to knowledge and effort, as well as the six [faculties].

This is the definition. *Bhaga* consists of six meanings characterized by sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), form (*rūpa*), fame (*yaśas*), glory (*śrī*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and effort (*prayatna*). That which possesses these is [the Blessed One]. 6.4 [5a4-5] *Mañju* means sweet, because it removes all affliction; *ghoṣa* means speech. That which has this as its name—one should establish it here according to the sequence to be explained—meaning that one should cultivate it intensely at the four junctions of the day (*catuḥsandhya*).

6.5 This [practice] has been taught as the means for accomplishing Mañjuvajrayogin. However, for practitioners of other deities, the means for accomplishing their own respective deities should be understood in exactly this same way. The distinction is that, in place of the syllable *maṃ* and so forth belonging to Mañjuśrī, one inserts the seed-syllable and so forth of one’s own chosen deity. As he will state: “That would be his wheel, in whose center he himself should abide” (157cd).
7.0 Now, in order to explain that very meditation consisting of the three samādhis, he first speaks of the commencement of the *ādiyoga*, beginning with the words “firstly,” and so on.
First, the compassionate one, having placed the syllable *maṃ— known as the reality of shimmering, stainless rays— in the center of the moon within his heart at dawn;
One should perform the purification of the mouth and so forth.

(7.1) "First" refers to the commencement of the meditation (*bhāvanā*). "In the heart" means within the heart; the connection is that one should perform the purification of the mouth and so forth after having placed the syllable *maṃ* upon the lunar disc in the center of the moon.

(7.2) "In the morning" is a specific rule for the busy practitioner at the morning twilight (*prabhātasandhyā*). However, for the adept whose activity consists solely of meditation, all of this is to be visualized even during other twilights. But for him, it is specified as "in the morning," because at that time there is generally an absence of mental distraction.

7.3 [5a7–5b2] That *maṃ* syllable from which stainless rays radiate is itself called "Reality" (*tattva*), designated as the non-erroneous form, because it arises from the mantra-system whose essence is Great Passion (*mahārāga*). Thus, by the phrase "having placed the *maṃ* syllable—which is called Reality and possesses radiating stainless rays, which is the form of the lineage (*gotra*), and which has the nature of Great Compassion (*mahākṛpā*) and so forth, and which has the luster of fine saffron—red"—he states that this placement is the cause for the state of compassion. 7.4 By the term "compassionate" (*dayāvān*), he refers to the root of the tree of compassion born from the power of the seed-syllable (*bīja*). Since compassion is used here as an illustration, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the other [immeasurables] should also be understood to be present here.

7.5 This is what is meant: consequently, by virtue of one's spiritual lineage (*gotra*), through the vision of suffering and so forth, that which has the nature of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*)—consisting of great compassion and the like—is combined with the proximate causes of wisdom; it becomes dense, assumes the state of a seed endowed with the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata, and, through the impetus of the vows of Vajradhara and other factors, by the force of the power arising in the presence of a true guru, it generates great compassion in exactly that same manner.

In the same way, there is loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which serves as the means for the growth of the tree of compassion; it takes the form of knowledge (*jñāna*) in the perfect accomplishment of the true happiness of the Buddhas among sentient beings without regard for hardships, and it is like a consecration (*abhiṣeka*) because it nourishes that [compassion]. There is also sympathetic joy (*muditā*), arising from the production of delight with respect to the possibility [of enlightenment] when one reflects that purity is the bond [to liberation] and that the deity is specifically the means to that purity. Thus it is said: "Loving-kindness is the watering of compassion;
through the happiness felt in their suffering, there is vast nourishment; the clear growth of the branches..."
It should be known by way of the mental attention directed toward the source.
Through the relinquishing and taking up of leaves,
through the non-interruption of the continuum of vows,
and through the accomplishment of the two kinds of conditions.
From this, both the flower and the fruit are not in vain.

(*Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* 17.39–40). ... [omitted] ... by way of maturation. Because one obtains the very fruit that is the maturation of sentient beings, the fruit arises from this. Thus is the accomplishment of the tree of compassion. And here is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): if compassion were not the root...
There would be no endurance of difficult practices;
and an intelligent person, unable to bear suffering, would never contemplate the welfare of sentient beings.
One whose intellect is devoid of reflection would not form a resolve for future births in the realms of purity,
failing to pursue auspicious rebirths.
One would not ripen sentient beings at all.
(Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 17.37–38) Thus: ... and what [is it]?
Compassion, patience, and reflection.
The vow, birth, and the maturation of sentient beings;
these are the root, the trunk, the branches, the leaves, the flowers, and the fruit. (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 17.36ab)
This great tree of compassion has its roots at the beginning and its final fruit at the end.

(Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 17.36cd) For one who is engaged in the welfare of sentient beings out of compassion, even from suffering there arises happiness; thus, there is vast nourishment. This is the characteristic of patience (*kṣānti*). [The remainder of the verse] is a praise. This is understood from the song beginning with "if you so desire" and so forth (see 46d passim), because death is impossible for those who are non-existent [in the ultimate sense]. To distinguish the aggregates and so forth that possess the characteristic of patience, he says "the purification of the mouth and so forth."

7.5 [5b2-5] The "gate" (*mukha*) refers to the three gates of liberation (*trivimokṣamukha*), characterized by emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). These are the first among those [practices], such as the applications of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), etc. [The yogin should perform them]. Thus, immediately after the placement of the seed-syllables (*bījanyāsa*), purification (*viśuddhi*) was described. However, Bhadrapāda—having determined that there is no contradiction between the preceding and following states—in order to demonstrate its constant utility, stated regarding the complete purity of the gates of liberation: "In the heart-moon, the syllable *maṃ*, radiant with light" (*Guhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi* 9ab).
Thus, by this [verse], [the practice] prior to the placement of the seed-syllables (*bījanyāsa*) has been explained.

(8.0) Thereafter, one should perform the confession of misdeeds and so forth, preceded by worship, in the presence of the Guru, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas; thus he says: "With true sandalwood," and so on.
[The practitioner] is smeared with true sandalwood and other substances.
Seated upon a comfortable seat in a meditation chamber whose surroundings are strewn with fragrant flowers,
[he visualizes] the Buddhas residing in the three times.

8.1 Seated in that meditation-hall whose outer beauty is enhanced by being smeared with excellent sandalwood paste and the like, and strewn with fragrant flowers—this description should be understood as indicating, as far as possible, other conducive conditions for meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Thus seated, the wise one possesses a mind free from distinctions such as the teacher and the taught. 8.2 Or else, through the means of thorough knowledge, increase, and instruction, [he engages in] reflection and so forth...

8.3 [5b7–6a2] “Those who abide in the three times” refers to the Buddhas of the past, future, and present. Now, one might object: while the confession of misdeeds and so forth may appropriately take place in the presence of those of the past and the present, it is not tenable in the presence of the future ones, because they have not yet come into being. This is not so; for here, those who have mastery over perfect gnosis are designated as “future” because they possess the complete qualities of a Buddha within this very state, appearing in the form of the maṇḍala circle whose nature consists of all Buddhas made into one’s own self. Thus, the wise person, having first performed the emanation of clouds of various offerings and so forth, [should proceed].

One should perform that confession of sins and so forth for the sake of increasing virtue. (9.1) "Having taken as an object" means having reflected upon it with the mind (or this may be a qualification of the action).

9.2 + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + Because it is the cause of the activity of beginners, having considered that they might fall from the path due to delusion, [the author], wishing to make known the predominance of the auspicious (*śubha*), says: "Auspicious," and so forth. 9.3 [6a5-6] For what purpose should one perform [this]? For the sake of increasing the auspicious. That is, for the increase of merit (*puṇya*). For indeed, even karma such as the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*) is exhausted through the teaching. And it has been said: "Even most terrible sins have been committed..."
They become attenuated through self-reproach;
I declare that their complete uprooting comes from both revealing them and restraining them.
(*From an untraced source in the Locana*).

10.0 [6a6–6b1]: Thereafter, for one whose every stain has been removed, merit increases through the rejoicing in merit and other such acts. Just as a seed sown in a cultivated field sprouts, or as the dye of saffron becomes instantly vivid on a well-washed cloth, so too, for one who is sinless and accomplishes merit, auspiciousness increases without obstruction. For this very reason, he first states the confession of sins—(*"That which..."* etc.).
Whatever impurity has been accumulated through all my volitional constructions within this beginningless flood of existence,
that I confess according to the prescribed rite.
All that has been accumulated and acquired as defilement and sin, I confess all of that in the presence of the Greatly Compassionate Ones, the Buddhas.
"According to rule" means even that which is firmly conceptualized is [confessed] precisely as one's own conceptualization.
11.0 [6b4] Regarding the objects included by the word "and so forth" (ādya), he first speaks of rejoicing in merit— beginning with "By the Perfectly Awakened Ones," and so on:
whatever wholesome [deeds] have been performed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones, by the Bodhisattvas, by the Noble Ones, and by others;
Having rejoiced in that, I perfectly dedicate the remainder toward perfect enlightenment.

The *sambuddhas* are Vairocana and the others; the *bodhisattvas* are Kṣitigarbha and the others; and the *āryas* are Āryāmṛtakuṇḍali and the others. This is because in the tantra they are not designated by the terms "Buddha" or "bodhisattva," but are instead referred to by the term "ārya. And it is said: "The hero Āryāmṛtakuṇḍali" (see 89d). Others are Vajrahūṃkāra, Heruka, and so forth, who are not designated by any of these three [terms].
11.2 Here, even the distinction between the Buddha and the others is not real, because they possess the nature of Vajradhara. And as the Blessed One has said:

“That very Blessed One sat upon the crescent moon of the eastern half,” and so forth. [The distinction exists] merely as a conventional designation, because all conventional designations are established.

Alternatively, "the perfectly awakened ones" (*sambuddha*) are those who have attained complete enlightenment. "Bodhisattvas" are those who have entered the stages (*bhūmi*) beginning with the Joyful (*pramuditā*), and who seek complete enlightenment. "Noble ones" (*ārya*) are the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, such as those who have entered the stream (*srotāpanna*). "Others" are those who have deep faith in the Buddha and so forth, and who perform virtuous deeds.

11.4 Having rejoiced with supreme faith, thinking, "Whatever wholesome [deeds] have been performed by them, all that is perfect," there is the wholesome associated with rejoicing—that is to say, the wholesome produced by rejoicing. For one endowed with resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), merit is accumulated through the correct rejoicing in merit, because merit and demerit are primarily functions of the mind.

This wholesome associated with rejoicing, I dedicate toward complete enlightenment; the meaning is that I bring it to the state of being a cause for enlightenment characterized by accomplishment through the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*).

12.0 [7a4-5] By taking refuge in the distinguished Triple Gem, one accumulates the equipment of merit and becomes invincible to all; thus, he first speaks of taking refuge in the Buddha, beginning with "vilasat" and so forth:
"To those who possess infinite true compassion and skillful means, adorned by the stainless moon of a radiant mind..."
I go for refuge eternally to the Sugatas who abide within my own mind.

(12.1) "Radiantly shining" refers to the mind characterized by the wisdom (*prajñā*) of Samantabhadra in all its aspects. That very mind, because it removes the darkness of ignorance from the world, is like a stainless moon; thus it is called the "stainless moon," meaning that wisdom whose intrinsic nature is utterly pure. Because they are established as being conjoined with that [wisdom], they have an intrinsic nature inseparable from one's own mind—this is the meaning. "Eternally" means for as long as samsara is limitless, and not merely until the nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*) as is the case for those of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
13.0 [7b2] He speaks of going for refuge to the Dharma: "Free from all conceptual construction," and so forth.
It is that which is free from all conceptual construction and is the support for the excellence of all sentient beings without exception.
"I go for refuge to the Dharma, whose nature is the single flavor of all things.

(13.1) The connection is as follows: "I go for refuge to that Dharma by which all conceptual constructions characterized by the grasped and so forth are liberated and cast away. Of what kind is it? It is "that which is the basis," and so forth. "Sattvas" refers to Bodhisattvas; it is the basis—that is, the cause—of their entire prosperity, extending up to perfect enlightenment. For it is through the cultivation of the reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*) exactly as it is that all prosperities are obtained by Bodhisattvas.
13.2 And thus, for as long as Bodhisattvas cultivate the Dharma for the sake of purification, to that same extent there is the arising of the qualities of a Buddha.
13.3 "The nature of all things as having a single flavor" means that their essence is the equality of all phenomena, because they are not distinct from being merely one's own conceptual construction.
14.0 He speaks of going for refuge to the Saṅgha, beginning with the word "correctly" (samyak).
Whose bonds have been completely cast off, who possesses the glory bestowed by supreme compassion,
and who has entered the stages beginning with *muditā*.
I have gone for refuge to the host of lords of ascetics (yatīśagaṇa).

[He is so called] because he has, through the realization of the true nature of reality (*bhūtārtha*), cast away the bonds known as passion, hatred, and delusion—which are otherwise rendered beautiful by one’s own mere imagination; and because he has, through supreme compassion, bestowed and accomplished prosperity (*śrī*) and well-being for both himself and others; and because he has entered the nine stages (*bhūmi*), beginning with *muditā* and ending with *sādhumatī*.

Since a bodhisattva on the tenth stage is indeed a Buddha, and since that Perfectly Awakened One—who has attained the stages of a Perfectly Awakened One such as Samantaprabhā—is designated by the term "Former Sugata" (as seen in 12c), one abiding on the tenth stage is not to be included within the [ordinary] assembly. And it is said:
"On the tenth stage, a bodhisattva is indeed a Buddha, but not yet a Samyaksambuddha. (Pañcaviṃśatikā Prajñāpāramitā, p. xx)

Thus it is said. Regarding the phrase "that host of lords of ascetics" (*yatīśagaṇam*): "ascetics" (*yati*) refers to the *śrāvakas*, *pratyekabuddhas*, and so forth; their "lords" (*īśa*) are the *bodhisattvas*; and "host" (*gaṇa*) refers to that assembly. The grammatical connection is: "I have gone for refuge to that host. Alternatively, as before, although there is no actual difference between the Buddha and the others, going for refuge by distinguishing them as "Buddha" and so on is taught merely in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings.
Now, he speaks of the *bodhicitta* belonging to the stage of the equipment (*sambhāra-bhūmi*), beginning with the words "by the purity of intention" (*āśaya*).
By the purity of the maturation of one's intention...
I uproot all obscurations and habitual tendencies; I generate a mind adorned with resolute faith toward awakening. 15

15.1 Purity of intention (*āśaya*) is the resolve to uplift all sentient beings. Purity of maturation (*vipāka*) is the continuous succession of the results of stainless karma even in future lives. With reference to that purity of intention and maturation, which constitutes the abiding in the accumulations (*sambhāra*), it says: "In awakening" (*bodhau*). The connection is: "I generate the mind (*cetas*) directed toward awakening, that is, toward Buddhahood. Furthermore, "all obscurations" refers to the afflictions and other hindrances, as well as their latencies (*vāsanā*), characterized by the capacity to produce the modes of the afflictions and so forth; that is "thus" (*tathā*). The mind whose nature is to utterly eradicate those is "the mind that completely uproots all obscurations and their latencies."
15.2 *Adhimukti* is the conduct embraced within the system of mantra; it is the ornament of one who experiences it as an object.
Alternatively, 15.3 *adhimukti* is the aspiration for that [state] through the ascertainment of reality; it is precisely this which is the ornament of one [who possesses it].
15.4 [8a5–6] I shall generate such a mind. It is not something produced by chance or impaired by doubt and so forth, but rather it is adorned solely by *adhimukti*.
16.0 [8a6] He explains that very accumulation, which is the form of the path by which this aspiration is accomplished, beginning with the words "together with the sons":
"together with the sons, the single path of the Sugatas," which consists of the ten kinds of virtuous qualities such as generosity and so forth.
"I have now taken refuge in that which has as its nature the wisdom of the self-nature of all the Perfectly Awakened Ones.

(16.1) The Sugatas, together with their sons and accompanied by the Bodhisattvas—whatever single common path they possess, consisting of the tenfold practices beginning with generosity and culminating in the perfection of primordial wisdom (*jñānapāramitā*), which are themselves "white qualities" because they are free from the stain of objective apprehension (*upalambha*)—that path, whose form or intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is these very qualities, is what is meant. The meaning is: "I have taken refuge in that."

16.2 Anticipating the objection that this is irrelevant, he says: "By means of the awakened one" (*sambuddhena*) means by means of the intellect (*buddhyā*)—that is, by means of the cognition that identifies the form of the deity—which possesses the entire nature of the Awakened One (*sambuddhātmaka*) throughout both the states of cause and effect.

Alternatively, the Perfectly Awakened One, Vajradhara, whose nature is inconceivable—he is the very self of that mandala-circle which consists of the support and the supported, whose nature is the purification of the three worlds in the form of the primary elements and their derivatives, and who is the essence of all things and the self of all. By means of the realization that this very mandala-circle is the truth of the path, the meaning is: "I have taken recourse to the path through such certainty."

16.4 [8b2-4] Furthermore, since this mind that relies upon the path is in reality of the very nature of the bodhicitta of aspiration (*praṇidhi-bodhicitta*), the Master has indicated its inclusion by explaining the mind of the path between the two distinct types of mind—the mind of aspiration and the mind of engagement (*prasthāna-citta*).

Nevertheless, he intended that the mind of the path must necessarily be explained separately; for it was precisely to reveal this intention that Bhadrapāda, after stating the reliance upon the path, spoke of the general bodhicitta.

17.0 [8b4-5] Having made his vow and relying upon the path, the yogi sets out for the accomplishment of mantra. Thus, for the sake of the accumulation of gnosis (*jñāna-sambhāra*), he speaks of the bodhicitta of setting forth, beginning with "By compassion," etc.:
"Having taken hold of this entire world, which is ensnared by the net of views, through compassion..."
Having meditated upon the incomparable bodhicitta according to the ritual procedure, one becomes a mantra-practitioner (mantrin).

(17) In order to make it known that compassion alone is the primary factor in all circumstances, although compassion was already mentioned in the context of the "setting out" (*prasthāna*), it is stated once more: "having relied upon the world, which is ensnared by the net of views. Views refer to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth; their "net" is their collection, or they themselves are the net due to their similarity to one. It is "ensnared" by this, meaning it is bound. This means that the transmigrating being is bound merely by delusion.

"Enlightened mind" (*sambodhicitta*) refers to the *prasthāna-bodhicitta*, which is the nature of perfect enlightenment—that is, the knowledge of the selflessness of all phenomena. "Incomparable" means being devoid of scales because it has the nature of the *prasthāna*. "Thus" means that one should contemplate [it] as empty due to the absence of intrinsic nature, according to the method to be explained below (verse 18a), such as "Oṃ, emptiness," etc.; thus the practitioner (*mantrī*) should become one who utters the mantra beginning with "Oṃ, emptiness," etc.

Alternatively, the meaning is that immediately thereafter, one should worship the deity of the mantra according to the sequence to be explained below, beginning with "white as the autumn moon," etc. (verse 19a).
18.0 [9a2] Now, he explains the method for cultivating the bodhicitta of setting out (*prasthāna-bodhicitta*), beginning with "empty" and so forth:
"It is empty because it is devoid of intrinsic nature; likewise, it is signless because it is free from causes."
Due to the departure of conceptual construction (*ūha*), every object is free from volitional intent (*praṇidhāna*).

(18.1) That which is empty of its own-being (*svabhāva*)—whatever form is established for it—is devoid of defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) because such characteristics are inapplicable; therefore, there is separation from them.

18.2 Alternatively, because of the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—in the form of subject and object, unity and plurality, and so forth—all things are empty. Likewise, because of the lack of a cause that withstands analysis, they are signless (*animitta*). By the word "but" (*tu*), he shows that conventional causes are not at all negated. *Ūha* refers to discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) such as those regarding the destinies of gods and humans, or pleasure and so forth. Because of the departure from these, all things are free from aspiration (*praṇidhāna-nirmukta*).
The meaning is that they are free from that aspiration which takes the form of longing for specific destinies, enjoyments, sovereignty, and the like.

18.3 Furthermore, these three doors of liberation are established as empty in the ultimate sense of all categories, for the entire range of entities is devoid of the grasped, the grasper, and so forth. As he will state right here: "Free from the forms of form and so on" (110a), and by the words "And not one" (113a), he will demonstrate in this very context that everything is devoid of a nature such as being one or many. And it has been said by the author of the *Vārttika*:
"That form by which entities are conceptualized does not exist in reality."
Because neither a single nor a multiple form exists for them.
(Pramāṇavārttika Pramāṇasiddhi 360).
Therefore, because it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), it is empty (*śūnya*).

For this very reason, because it is unproduced from the outset due to the impossibility of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), it is signless (*animitta*). As it was stated in the *Pratyayaparīkṣā*:
A condition for an object that is neither non-existent nor existent is not tenable;
for what would a condition apply to if it were non-existent, and what need is there for a condition if it were already existent?
(Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 1.6).
It has also been stated by the master Dharmakīrti:
"Although an effect, being established, is not dependent on anything else, it is connected [to its cause] through conceptual construction."

And how can an existent that is entirely devoid of expectation depend upon anything?

(Sambandhaparīkṣā 3), and so forth. 18.5 [9b2-4]: For that very reason, there is no aspiration (*apraṇihita*). Indeed, an aspiration is not tenable with respect to that which lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and is incapable of the relation between cause and effect. For thus, a cause is not logical for what is non-existent, like the son of a barren woman; nor is it purposeful for what is existent. Furthermore, existence is not tenable for that which is devoid of a cause. Therefore, it is established that the entire collection of entities is like an illusion—without beginning or end, delightful only when not analyzed, and mere appearance (*pratibhāsamātra*); this is the reality (*tattva*).
We shall establish this through reasoning as the occasion arises.

Furthermore, since absolute emptiness is not something that provides assistance [in a conventional sense], the cultivation of emptiness—by means of its exclusion—is to be understood as occurring respectively through the characteristics of intrinsic nature (*svalakṣaṇa*), activity (*karmalakṣaṇa*), differentiation (*bhedalakṣaṇa*), and cause (*hetulakṣaṇa*), for the sake of pacifying conceptual construction, fear, indolence, and doubt.
For it is thus, by way of being the antidote to superimposition (*adhyāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*), that [emptiness] is established through its characteristic of intrinsic nature.
"For the non-existence of duality is the existence of that non-existence; this is the characteristic of emptiness" (Madhyāntavibhāga 1.13ab).
And thus, regarding this, the Bhāṣya states:

The non-existence of the duality of the grasped and the grasper, and the existence of that non-existence, is the characteristic of emptiness. Thus, the fact that emptiness has the characteristic of both non-existence and existence is fully elucidated. And that which is the intrinsic nature of that non-existence is neither existence nor non-existence. (Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya ad loc.; Madhyāntavibhāga 1.13c)

How is it not an existence? Because there is the non-existence of duality. How is it not a non-existence? Because there is the existence of the non-existence of duality. And this is the characteristic of emptiness. Therefore, unreal imagination does not have the characteristic of being either different or identical.

(Madhyāntavibhāga 1.13d) If there were separateness, it would not be logical for the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) to be other than the phenomena themselves, just as [it is not other than] impermanence or suffering. If there were identity, there would be no object of purification, nor would there be a universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). By this, the characteristic that is free from both identity and difference is illuminated. (Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya ad loc.
Thus, [the characteristic of reality is explained] by means of its function (*karman*), its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), its synonyms (*paryāya*), and their meanings (*tadartha*).
Suchness, the limit of reality, the signless, the ultimate truth, and the realm of phenomena—these, in brief, are synonyms for emptiness.
The meanings of the synonyms are, respectively: being non-other, non-erroneous, the cessation thereof, the sphere of the noble ones, and the cause of the noble dharmas.

(Madhyāntavibhāga 1.14–15). And likewise, the *Bhāṣya* on this very point states: "How is the meaning of the synonyms to be understood? It begins with 'not otherwise' (*ananyathā*) and so forth. It is *tathatā* (suchness) in the sense of being not otherwise, because it is eternally just so. It is the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality) in the sense of being non-erroneous, because error has no objective reality there. It is the *animitta* (signless) in the sense of the cessation of signs, because all signs are absent. It is the *paramārtha* (ultimate truth) because it is the domain of noble knowledge, since it is the object of supreme knowledge. It is the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm) because it is the cause of the noble dharmas, since the noble dharmas arise from having that as their objective support."
"For in this context, the meaning of 'element' (*dhātu*) is the meaning of 'cause' (*hetu*).
(Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya, ad loc.). By way of its characteristic of differentiation:
"It is both afflicted and purified; it is with stain and without stain."
Purity is held to be like the purity of the water element, gold, and space.
(Madhyāntavibhāga 1.16). Here, the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) states:

How is the differentiation of emptiness to be understood? Its differentiation is that it is both defiled and purified. In what state is it defiled? In what state is it purified? It is with stain and without stain. When it exists together with stain, it is defiled; when its stains have been abandoned, it is purified.

If it becomes stainless after having been stained, how is it not impermanent due to its nature of undergoing transformation? For it is said [in the *Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya*]: "Its purity is held to be like the purification of the water-element, gold, and space; because adventitious stains are removed, there is no alteration of its intrinsic nature. To eliminate doubt, [the Buddha] stated the characteristic of the cause: "If this [nature] were defiled, all embodied beings would never be liberated; if it were already pure, effort toward purification would be fruitless."
(Madhyāntavibhāga 1.21).
And likewise, the *Bhāṣya* on this very point states:

"How is the proof to be understood? It begins with the words 'defiled,' etc. If the emptiness of all phenomena were not defiled by adventitious secondary afflictions even when the antidote has not arisen, then all sentient beings would be liberated without effort due to the absence of defilement. On the other hand, if it were not purified even when the antidote has arisen, then the undertaking for the sake of liberation would be futile. Having established this, (the *Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya* at this point [continues]).
"It is neither afflicted nor unafflicted, and it is neither pure nor impure.
(Madhyāntavibhāga 1.22ab) How is it neither afflicted nor impure? By its very nature. (Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya ad loc.)
Because the mind is luminous (*prabhāsvara*),
how is it that it is neither afflicted nor pure? (Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya ad 1.22c)
Because affliction is adventitious.

(Madhyāntavibhāga 1.22d) Thus, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) consists in the grasping of existence, non-existence, both, and their separateness or inseparability. However, for those who lack conviction in grasping the characteristic of emptiness, there arises terror; and for the indolent who are satisfied with [merely] the characteristics of specific qualities (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the characteristics of activity (*karmalakṣaṇa*), there would be laziness (*kausīdya*).
Due to the difference in the basis (*ādhāra*), there is a difference in the afflictions and purification for embodied beings. (untraced)

Because of this statement, there may arise doubt as to how luminosity and adventitiousness [can coexist]. Thus, the cultivation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bhāvanā*) should be understood even through the methods described in the *Muktibindu*.

18.7 This is another classification: although its sole characteristic is the discernment (*viveka*) of persons and phenomena, emptiness is sixteenfold. For instance, there is the internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) of the internal [faculties] such as the eye and so forth. (Mahāyānalakṣaṇasamuccaya §7a, 298b4, 146b24)
This was stated by the Master:
"Internal emptiness is so called because it is the opposite of the inversion regarding the internal" (*Ātmasādhanāvatāra* 57b2).
The emptiness of the external (*bahirdhāśūnyatā*) arises from the departure from the perception of external objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
The emptiness of the internal and external (*adhyātmabahirdhāśūnyatā*) arises from the non-apprehension of the eye and so forth, of form and so forth, and of the cognitions thereof.
As it has been said:

"Internal and external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) has as its intrinsic nature the non-apprehension of the body that serves as the basis for those [internal and external phenomena]. (Ātmasādhanāvatāra 57b2–3).

"The great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*) is the great receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), distinguished by the various manifestations of parts such as the cardinal directions. (Mahāyānalakṣaṇasamuccaya §7d, 298b5, 146b26–27).

As it was stated by the Master Vasubandhu: "The basis of establishment is the receptacle world; because of its vastness, its emptiness is called 'great emptiness' (*mahāśūnyatā*). (Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya ad 1.17).

Because it is devoid of the grasped and so forth, just as they are imagined, emptiness itself is empty; this is the 'emptiness of emptiness' (*śūnyatāśūnyatā*). (Mahāyānalakṣaṇasamuccaya §7e, 298b5-6, 146b27-28)"
This has been stated in the *Ātmasādhanāvatāra*:
"Even regarding the knowledge of emptiness, because it is signless (*animitta*), there is the emptiness of emptiness" (*Ātmasādhanāvatāra* 57b5).

This is its meaning: by whatever knowledge the fourfold emptiness—beginning with internal emptiness—is known, because that [knowledge] is also signless and non-conceptual, the determination of emptiness is the emptiness of emptiness.
The master Vasubandhu also said:
"That internal sense-base and so forth by which it is seen to be empty— that is its emptiness, [seen] through the knowledge of emptiness" (*Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya* on verse 1.17).
There is also the emptiness of the ultimate regarding the ultimate itself.
As it has been said:
"And just as it is seen in the form of the ultimate, so too is its emptiness" (*Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya* ad 1.17).
Thus it has been said by the Master himself:
"Because there is no conceptualization (*aparāmarśa*) of the cause of the ultimate object, there is the emptiness of the ultimate (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*)" (Ātmasādhanāvatāra 57b5).

This is its meaning: that which has the supreme, unconditioned object as its referent is the "ultimate" (*paramārtha*), namely the *dharmadhātu* which is the perceived object. That very [dharmadhātu] is the cause of the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) directed toward it; because the self is in reality distinct from the nature of that which is to be determined and the act of determining, there is "conceptualization" (*parāmarśa*). Because it is empty even of such conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it is the "emptiness of the ultimate" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
The emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtaśūnyatā*) pertains even to the conditioned realization (*abhisamaya*) of generosity and so forth. As stated by the author of the *Bhāṣya*:

"And the emptiness of that for the sake of which the bodhisattva practices" (1.17d). For what purpose does he practice? "For the sake of attaining the two kinds of purity" (1.18a)—that is, for the sake of attaining the wholesome, both conditioned and unconditioned. (Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya ad 1.17–18)
Thus it is said. It is also stated in the *Ātmasādhanāvatāra*:

"Conditioned emptiness (*saṃskṛtaśūnyatā*) arises from not grasping at signs (*nimitta*) within the accumulation of conditioned merit (*puṇyasambhāra*). (Ātmasādhanāvatāra 57b5–6). This is the meaning: "conditioned" refers to the cultivation of the mind through acts such as generosity, by performing the welfare of all sentient beings without exception and by making offerings to all the Tathāgatas. "Merit" (*puṇya*) refers to the act of purification. "Accumulation" (*sambhāra*) is the gathering and repeated production of virtue that occurs through the process of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) over a continuous succession. As it has been said:

"That which is the nourishment for the cultivation of the virtuous again and again, having attained it through continuity— that is the equipment (*sambhāra*) for the steadfast one who accomplishes all goals" (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 18.40).

When the conditioned equipment of merit (*saṃskṛta-puṇya-sambhāra*) is being accomplished, there is the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), because the sign (*nimitta*), its formative conceptualization (*tatsaṃskāra-vikalpa*), and the self (*ātman*) are not grasped as distinct entities.
The emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛtaśūnyatā*) is that which brings about the effortless signlessness (*anābhogānimitta*) even of the unconditioned.
As it is said in the *Ātmasādhanāvatāra*:
"Because there is no grasping at signs even regarding the unconditioned equipment for awakening (*bodhisambhāra*), there is the emptiness of the unconditioned. (Ātmasādhanāvatāra 57b6)

Thus it is said: "Even regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)," because knowledge is pure by nature, and since the stains that obstruct it are merely adventitious, they are eliminated. Because knowledge is of the nature of direct experience (*saṃvedana*), the light of knowledge—which pervades all objects of cognition—proceeds like the mass of rays from the sun in a cloudless expanse of sky; this awakening (*bodhi*) is the thorough realization of all phenomena as they truly are. The equipment for that is the equipment of knowledge (*jñāna-sambhāra*). As it has been said:
"Nothing is to be removed from this, nor is anything at all to be added. Reality is to be seen as it truly is; he who sees reality is liberated."
(Abhisamayālaṃkāra 5.21).

In that regard, the conceptualization of the sign as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is removed by not grasping it—that is, by not apprehending it through differentiation—and thus the latent predisposition for the unconditioned is the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).
Because of non-attachment to the vow for the ultimate welfare of sentient beings, there is the emptiness of the ultimate (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). (Ātmasādhanāvatāra 58a1)

Thus it is said. This is the meaning: sentient beings have transcended the limit; their welfare culminates in perfect enlightenment (*sambodhi*). The vows directed toward that [welfare] are absolute emptiness (*atyantaśūnyatā*), because there is no attachment due to the absence of cognitive distortion (*aviparyāsa*) regarding them. As it has been said: "And always for the benefit of sentient beings" (Madhyāntavibhāga 1.18b).
Thus [it is said]. And the commentary on this point states:
"For the sake of the ultimate benefit of sentient beings" (*Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya* ad loc.).

"Because of not grasping at the vow, 'I must not abandon saṃsāra, which is without beginning or end,' there is the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*). (Ātmasādhanāvatāra 58a1-2). This is the meaning: that saṃsāra of which no "lower" (beginning) or "upper" (end) exists is so described. With respect to sentient beings, because of non-abiding nirvāṇa, it is not to be abandoned; thus, due to the non-grasping—that is, the non-adherence—to this vow, there is the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end. As it has been said: "And for the sake of not abandoning saṃsāra..."
Thus it is said in the *Madhyāntavibhāga* (1.18c). And regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* states:
"For one who does not perceive the emptiness of saṃsāra, which is without beginning or end, becomes despondent and might abandon saṃsāra" (*Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya*, ad loc.).

Thus, because there is no attachment to the thought, "I shall not scatter roots of virtue in the nirvana without remainder," there is the emptiness of non-dispersal (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*). (Ātmasādhanāvatāra 58a2–3)

This is its meaning: "upadhi" refers to the aggregates (*skandhas*) and the afflictions (*kleśas*); their residue is the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*). In that which is devoid of this—in the *tathāgata-dharmadhātu*, which is *nirvāṇa* because all conceptual constructions (*vikalpas*) have ceased therein—one should not scatter or distract from the wholesome (*kuśala*), which is so called because it moves away from or distances itself from base evil. Its characteristic is the generation of the thought of awakening by immeasurable beings, culminating in the attainment of perfect enlightenment. This is the emptiness of non-dispersal (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*) due to non-attachment. As it has been said: "And for the sake of the inexhaustibility of the wholesome."
And thus its commentary [states]:
"In the nirvana without remainder, that which one neither scatters nor abandons. (Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya, ad loc.)

Thus, because there is an absence of the aspiration, "I must purify the lineage (*gotra*) which has the characteristic of the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*)," there is the emptiness of the fundamental nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). This is the meaning: that which is connected to a succession of previous births, the present purity, the fundamental nature, the *dharmadhātu*, and its characteristic—the lineage of the Perfectly Awakened One (*sambuddha-gotra*) itself—is what is meant here, since nothing else is applicable in this context. The word "or" (*vā*) functions as a conjunction (*samuccaye*). Because that which is perfectly established (*pariniṣpanna*) cannot be purified, there is, in reality, an absence of the aspiration or vow, "I must purify it. As it has been said:
"And for the sake of purifying the lineage" (Madhyāntavibhāga 1.19a).
And it has been said by the author of the Commentary:
"For the lineage (*gotra*) is the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*), because it is innate," as stated in the *Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya*.

"Because there is no volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*) regarding the form-body (*rūpakāya*) consisting of the primary and secondary marks, there is the emptiness of marks (*lakṣaṇaśūnyatā*)," as stated in the *Ātmasādhanāvatāra* (58a5).

In the *sāmbhogika-kāya*, which consists of the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary signs (*vyañjana*), there is the emptiness of marks (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) because, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is devoid of volitional construction (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Furthermore, since the secondary signs are included as a derivative of the primary marks, it is said:
"For the attainment of the primary marks and secondary signs" (*Madhyāntavibhāga* 1.19b).
Thus [it is said]. And the Commentary states:
"For the attainment of the marks of a Great Man together with the secondary characteristics" (*Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya*, at this point).
The emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaśūnyatā*) arises from the non-conditioning of those dharmas whose intrinsic nature consists of the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, and so forth," this refers to the non-conditioning of everything from the applications of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. As it has been said: "The bodhisattva practices for the purification of the Buddha-dharmas."
Thus [it is said in] Madhyāntavibhāga 1.19cd. And the commentary states:
"of the powers, the intrepidities, and so forth. In this way, the systematic presentation of the fourteen types of emptiness should be understood. (Madhyāntavibhāga, at this point).
The non-existence of the person (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*) is its emptiness; this is the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāvaśūnyatā*).
As it is said in the *Ātmasādhanāvatāra*:
"Because there is no superimposition of a person or phenomena, there is the emptiness of non-existence. (Ātmasādhanāvatāra 58a6)

The *pudgala* is that which is imagined by the Vaibhāṣikas; by way of illustration, this includes the *ātman*, the *jīva*, and so forth. "Dharma" refers to form (*rūpa*) and the other aggregates. When there is the possibility of superimposition through the delusion of those who do not see reality—regarding these two, which are characterized like the hair of a tortoise—if one does not superimpose them by reversing that [delusion], that is the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāvaśūnyatā*).

Furthermore, this non-existence is not something other than the aggregates and so forth; rather, they themselves, characterized as manifestations of conceptual construction, are devoid of a grasper and the like. This is the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*). As it was said by the Master himself:

The emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*) results from neither repudiating the characteristics of emptiness as they have been explained, nor from performing any mental construction (*anabhisaṃskaraṇa*). (Ātmasādhanāvatāra 58a6–7) Regarding the phrase "as they have been explained": this refers to the emptinesses of the internal [faculties] and so forth. Their characteristic is the exclusion of superimposed phenomena (*samāropitadharmaviveka*). The intention is that if one were to repudiate even that [characteristic], then in the absence of the eye and so forth, their emptiness would likewise not exist; thus, by negating emptiness, there would follow the consequence of the existence of the person (*pudgala*) and other entities, as before. Furthermore, the actual existence of such a realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), which is of the nature of non-existence, is not an object for those of limited vision.

"This very nature of phenomena (dharmatā) remains constant," according to scripture. Because it is pure by nature and thus devoid of any need for further refinement, it is the emptiness whose intrinsic nature consists in the non-existence of that [nature].
But what, then, is emptiness in this context? (Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya, introduction to 1.20)
Thus, the compassionate Lord Maitreya, dispelling such doubt, taught the emptiness of non-existence. And in order to avoid the denial of that emptiness, he said:
"The actual existence of that non-existence within it—that is another emptiness."
(Madhyāntavibhāga 1.20cd).
By this, the emptiness of the nature of non-existence is indicated. And thus, the Commentary on this states:

The non-existence of the person (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*) is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and the existence of that non-existence within the aforementioned [categories] such as the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) and so forth is another emptiness. To explain the definition of emptiness, [the treatise] establishes two kinds of emptiness at the end: the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāva-śūnyatā*), respectively, in order to avoid the superimposition (*samāropa*) of a person and phenomena and the denial (*apavāda*) of their emptiness. Thus should the divisions of emptiness be understood. (Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya, ad loc.)

And this very [emptiness] has infinite modes due to its distinct manifestations in connection with form and so forth for the sake of abandoning their respective conceptual constructions; yet, within the aggregates and so on, it is non-dual, characterized solely by the discernment of the grasper and the grasped.
As it is said: "The emptiness of the enjoyer, the enjoyed, their body, and the locus of support."

Whatever is seen by whom, in what manner, and for what purpose—of that there is emptiness. This is for the sake of attaining the two kinds of purity, for the constant welfare of sentient beings, for not abandoning cyclic existence, and for the inexhaustibility of virtue.
For the sake of purifying the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), for the attainment of the primary and secondary marks,
and for the purification of the Buddha-qualities, the bodhisattva applies himself.
For here, emptiness is the non-existence of both the person and phenomena;
the actual existence of that non-existence within them is another kind of emptiness.

(Madhyāntavibhāga 1.17–20). In this context, the internal experiencers are the eyes and so forth; the objects of experience are the external forms and so forth. The basis for these two is the body, which pertains to both the internal and the external. The foundational entity is the great vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*). It is "seen" by means of the knowledge of emptiness; thus, it is emptiness. "In such a manner" refers to the mode of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). The final pair of emptinesses is for the purpose of negating the delusion regarding the characteristics of those [entities]. Likewise, the signless (*animitta*) consists of those very same emptinesses as they function as causes. And the wishless (*apraṇihita*) consists of those [emptinesses] as they function as results.

Furthermore, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is for the sake of abandoning the imagined (*parikalpita*) phenomena and the person (*pudgala*), as well as the adherence to them which consists of the dependent nature (*paratantra*). The wishless (*apraṇihita*) is for the sake of the direct realization of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*), while the signless (*animitta*) is for the sake of the non-interruption of the continuum of aspirations.
And in order to stabilize this bodhicitta—the undertaking that takes the reality of all things as its object—he speaks the empowerment of the mantra, beginning with *oṃ*:
*oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham* (Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness).

The syllable *oṃ* is the acceptance of the deity whose form is inconceivable. Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the nature of the selflessness of all phenomena; that itself is gnosis (*jñāna*), and because it is indivisible, it is the *vajra*. "I am of the nature of that"—thus it is said. And it was stated by the Blessed One: "Emptiness is not other than form; form is not other than emptiness" (*Prajñāpāramitāhṛdaya*, ed. p. 150, 145a).

And by means of this *rucijapa* mantra, taking the single phrase "consisting of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvātmaka*) as one unit, it should be understood that the sixfold *bodhicitta* mentioned in the *Bodhicittapaṭala* is expressed through its sixfold nature.
Now, he states the procedure for the accomplishment of the deity, beginning with "Thereafter" (*tadanu*): "Thereafter, [one should visualize her] white as the autumn moon... [9b6]
[She is] possessed of variegated light that revolves through the infinite directions of space;
she stands above, within a triangle, holding a vajra whose nature is the internal void. 19

19.1 Following that, immediately after the empowerment of the bodhicitta of application (*prasthānabodhicitta*), one should meditate upon the mudrā called Dharmodayā—this is the connection [of the verse]. "White as the autumn moon" means having a gentle, white form that gladdens the world. "Possessing variegated light pervading the circle of infinite directions" means she whose light is variegated—that is, of manifold forms—and which radiates throughout the circle, the collection, of infinite directions; she is thus described.

"Situated above" means having a form that has not fallen [downward]. Regarding "triangular," according to the tradition (*āmnāya*), two corners should be understood as being at the top. She is "one whose nature is the internal sky" (*antar-gagana-svarūpā*) and she "holds the vajras"—that is, the Tathāgatas in their radiant forms—thus she is the "Vajra-holder" (*vajradharā*); she is therefore the "Vajra-holder whose nature is the internal sky.
[She is] the mudrā called Dharmodayā, enriched by a lotus and a universal vajra situated in its center.
One should meditate upon her who arises from Samantabhadra on ground made of vajras by means of *HŪṂ*.

[Regarding the question of where one should meditate upon the mudrā of the qualities (*dharma*) such as the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), he says: "By means of *HŪṂ* and vajra," and so forth. On ground consisting of vajras, produced by the radiation of blazing vajras born from the syllable *HŪṂ* situated upon the sun.

20.2 [10b2–4] In this regard, the sequence for meditating on the protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*) is as follows: immediately after reciting the mantra beginning with "Oṃ śūnyatā... and having determined that the world—whose nature is merely body and so forth—is nothing but conceptual construction, the practitioner's *bodhicitta* (consisting of one's own body, speech, and mind) becomes dependent upon mere intention. This *bodhicitta* takes the form of the three syllables Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ, interspersed with two Hoḥ syllables. It is the seed of the transformation [of consciousness] at each junction (*pratisandhi*), and because it is the practice of non-attachment, it abides in space.

Having placed [the mantra] before the moon for the purpose of subduing the wheel of obstacles, one should meditate on the mudrā called Dharmodayā—possessing the aforementioned characteristics—which arises from the transformation of the Vajradhara seen as a manifestation free of obstacles, in the midst of the binding of the boundary, the binding of the directions, the vajra-fence, the vajra-canopy, and the ground made of vajra, all produced by the emanations of blazing vajras issuing from a blue *hūṃ* syllable situated upon the sun.

20.3 And this has been taught for one of weak mind. However, for one of superior mind, [the following] should be understood: the stages are made adamantine by them; the meaning is that when that wheel exists, it has been cultivated.

20.4 For thus, through the revolution [of the wheel], even the impressions (*vāsanā*) of the stages are severed. By means of the mirror-like [wisdom] and so forth, the four uncommon [qualities]—beginning with the support of equanimity (*samatādhṛtapādāna*) and ending with the limit—are purified through the transcendence of the triple world, and the stage of the Tathāgata is projected within the adamantine sphere of experience (*vajropamagocara*).

21.0 Then, when that [obstacle] has subsided and the nature of the obstacle has been understood, because of the absence of obstacles, one clearly realizes non-abiding nirvāṇa, which consists of the transformation of the threefold suchness. Having transformed the lotus and vajra—which have the nature of the purification of the conceptualizations of existence and peace—into the form of the purification of the factors of the path, he says "bhrūṃkāra...
and so forth, in order to describe the peaked pavilion born of Vairocana, which arises from the limbs of Vairocana together with his consort, produced from the wheel of the syllable *bhrūṃ*.
The entire circle of the directions is pervaded by the variegated rays of the assembly of radiant lords of sages.

Furthermore, these are the factors of the path: right view is mundane, consisting of the understanding of what has been seen as "thus" and "this is for me," and so forth; right mindfulness is [the mindfulness] free from faults such as lethargy; and right concentration is meditative absorption free from faults such as lethargy and excitement.
The Master, however, has said this:

for the sake of abandoning the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), there are eight limbs of the path manifested by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). They are as follows: right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is that subtle, non-erroneous wisdom (*prajñā*) regarding the equality characterized by the selflessness of all phenomena and regarding their differentiation, such as suffering and so forth. Right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*) is... [omitted] ...Right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*) is the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃmoṣadharmatā*) manifested by the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth, which follows the support of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so on, as well as one’s own vows.

And right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*) is the state of composure characterized by immeasurable first and subsequent meditations; it follows after the actions of body and so forth, serves as the basis for the production of distinguished qualities (*vaiśeṣikaguṇa*), and establishes non-conceptual knowledge (*avikalpajñāna*). (Mahāyānalakṣaṇasamuccaya §8g, 305a4–300b2, 146a26–147b10).

The syllable *Bhrūṃ* and the wheel produced from it; that from which the arising—that is, the origination—of the one accompanied by his consort (*svābhāprajñā*) occurs, is Vairocana. He is the limb (*aṅga*), and by him [the palace] is brought forth, i.e., accomplished. The connection is as follows: there, within the *dharmodayā*, upon the universal lotus and vajra, one should visualize the peaked palace (*kūṭāgāra*) distinguished by the aforementioned specific characteristics (cf. 28d). (See 28d).

The circle (maṇḍala) is the assembly of the radiant lords of sages; that by which the entire wheel (cakra)—the collection—of all directions is pervaded by their variegated (citra), that is, multicolored rays (aṃśu) or beams, is thus described.
Alternatively, the circles of the lords of sages are radiant... [of which] it is square (caturaśra) due to its lack of unevenness.

It is adorned on all sides with four gateways consisting of the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), and it is embellished by the altar of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) at the arches of the four dhyānas.

(22) Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of unevenness": because of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), there is equality among Buddhas, non-Buddhas, and so forth, and thus it is square. And it was said by Bhadrapāda:
It is square because of its lack of inequality, due to the equality of the awakened and the unawakened.
(Guhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi 327cd) Thus it is said.

22.2 For the sake of entering into the insight (*vipaśyanā*) that possesses fully developed aspects, directed toward the emptiness characterized as previously described— which has been unified by means of the perfections (*pāramitā*) projected through the cultivation of the protection wheel consisting of the ten spokes representing the purification of the ten stages beginning with the Joyous (*pramuditā*)— there are the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣikā dharmāḥ*).

22.3 “By means of the four supreme gateways of the faculty of mindfulness” means: mindfulness refers to the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) regarding the body and so forth. By these, the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa) and the four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) are characterized and should be understood. Within those [bases], the faculties are faith and the others; the meaning is that mindfulness and the others have mindfulness and the other objects as their domain. Furthermore, those here are established as the four untainted (anāsrava) gateways; by means of them, it is supreme—that is, most excellent.

22.4 This is the meaning: these [factors], consisting of body, feeling, mind, and phenomena (*kāyavedanācittadharma*), are called the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). For those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), they consist of the qualities (*dharma*) arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation; for those who follow by the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*), however, they are characterized by the absence of dogmatic grasping (*parāmṛṣabhāva*).
