Because they are not associated with diversity and so forth, wisdom (*prajñā*), once arisen, stands firm like a wedge through mindfulness (*smṛti*); or rather, mindfulness stands firm by means of this [wisdom]. 22.5 Thus it has been said:

For example, the application of mindfulness to the body is merely the arrangement of various parts; this body is characterized by being devoid of anything to be grasped and so forth. (Mahāyānalakṣaṇasamuccaya §8a', 299a5-6, 146c18-20) Thus it is said.

[Thus there are] the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*), the application of mindfulness to the mind (*citta-smṛtyupasthāna*), and the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*). Each of these is threefold, according to the distinctions of internal, external, and both [internal and external] bodies, and so forth. Because they are joined with vigor, concentration, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, and specifically because Bodhisattvas are joined with the mental attention toward the roots of virtue such as the thought of awakening and giving, they are called "applications of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*) due to the predominance of mindfulness, even though they consist of many factors. This should be understood in the same way for the others as well.
(Mahāyānalakṣaṇasamuccaya §8a’ cont’d, 299a6–7, 146c20–25)

Thus, because it is the precursor and the cause for entering into the Dharma, it is called "mere faith" (*śraddhāmātrakatā*). In that context, the gate at the front is that which is faith purified by that [realization]. And it was said by Bhadrapāda:
"Because of the impossibility of the body, sensation, mind, and phenomena being either different or identical..."
The mindfulness directed toward that, and the faith therein, are considered the gateway to awakening.
(Guhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi 328).

Thus, through the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), there is the realization of both the phenomena that constitute the adversaries and their remedies. For one who has faith, in order to destroy the perversion consisting of the nature of arisen adversaries, to prevent the arising of future perversions, to produce the true habitual tendencies (*tathyavāsanā*) in the form of unarisen remedies, and to establish non-existent true habitual tendencies, there arises—impelled by that—the fourfold vigor (*caturvīrya*) known as the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*). This takes the form of enthusiasm for the increase of the wholesome and the abandonment of the unwholesome, appearing in a non-dual aspect.
The southern gate has the nature of its purification. And it is said:
"Then, for the sake of abandoning and the non-arising of past and future errors, and furthermore, for the arising and stability of the reality that was previously unarisen."
"With the gate facing inward and possessing fourfold heroism" (Guhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi 329–330a).

22.8 Thus, having understood that when the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) are present, desire (*chanda*), vigor (*vīrya*), mind (*citta*), and investigation (*mīmāṃsā*) proceed with increased intensity toward perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), there arise for the practitioner of yoga (*yogācāra*) meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) based on desire and the other [factors], which are characterized by the attainment of encouragement regarding the acquisition of the signless fruit (*animittaphala*).

The four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*)—which, by relying on physical and mental seclusion, are based on the fading away of adverse factors and cessation, and culminate in effortless functioning—are cultivated through the eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*), namely: desire, vigor, faith, pliancy, mindfulness, clear comprehension, volition, and equanimity; these serve to eliminate the five defects of meditative concentration characterized by laziness, lack of instruction, forgetfulness, lethargy-and-excitement, and non-application as well as over-application, respectively. This is presented from the perspectives of both the conventional and the ultimate truths.

22.9 The "feet" (*pāda*) of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), characterized by traveling through space and so forth, are its members or causes. When these—desire (*chanda*) and the others—serve as the objects, mindfulness (*smṛti*), characterized by non-forgetfulness, attends upon one who has exerted vigor (*vīrya*). And the final gateway consists in the purification of that mindfulness which has been aroused by the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*). As it has been said: "Desire, enthusiasm, stability, and discernment; But the last are the bases of supernormal power; In this context, however, mindfulness is the gateway."
(Guhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi 330bcd).
22.10 And [the suffix *ka* is applied] after *chanda* and so forth.

The five faculties (*indriya*) are so called because faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom function with predominance toward the fruit known as the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). (Mahāyānalakṣaṇasamuccaya §8d-e, 299b3–4, 147a5–7)

It should be understood that these two stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are characterized by those [factors]: the stage of "Heat" (*ūṣmagata*) is primarily characterized by the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and the stage of "Summits" (*mūrdhan*) is primarily characterized by the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*). When these same factors—faith and so forth—have attained strength through the destruction of their respective opposites, they become the five powers (*bala*). Another two stages conducive to penetration are characterized by those [powers]: the stages of "Patience" (*kṣānti*) are primarily characterized by the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), and the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (*agradharma*) are primarily characterized by the faculties (*indriya*) and the powers (*bala*).
Thus it should be seen.

22.11 At that time, with respect to the phenomena previously mentioned in which all conceptual constructions have been destroyed, the mind—possessing an object of enthusiasm through serene confidence (*abhiprasanna*) and accompanied by mindfulness (*smṛti*)—brings forth the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*). By bringing an end to their opposites, such as lack of faith (*aśraddhā*), one becomes possessed of established mindfulness, and concentration (*samādhi*) characterized by one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) manifests. This is the subsequent door consisting of its purified form. And it has been said:
"Through the incomparable faculties and powers of faith, vigor, mindfulness, meditative absorption, and wisdom, concentration is thus the supreme.
(Guhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi 331abc)
Thus.

22.12 “The Gateway of the Four Dhyānas”: this refers to the four roots of merit conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*), characterized by the stages of Heat (*ūṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*agradharma*). These are manifested through the mastery and meditative concentration (*samādhāna*) over the previously mentioned four sets of emptiness (*śūnyatācatuṣka*) produced by non-attachment, and—just as before—they are primarily characterized by the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth. These are projected by the mantras, and from them arises the vast first dhyāna, characterized by seclusion from sensual desires and so forth.

Furthermore, that vastness is briefly of four kinds: (1) vastness of intention (*āśaya*), because it is characterized by the mind of complete enlightenment for the sake of all sentient beings; (2) vastness of application (*prayoga*), because it is perfected through applications such as signless giving and so forth; (3) vastness of penetration (*prativedha*), because it is conducive to the penetration of the all-pervading realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); and (4) vastness of dwelling (*vihāra*), because it is sustained as the basis for all qualities, such as meditative concentrations, until the limit of non-abiding nirvana.

This fourfold Vaipulya is manifold, arising from desire, from seclusion born of the wholesome, from joy and bliss, and from the concentration based upon them, as well as through the distinctions of the *pāramitās* and so forth.

And herein, within this meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), there is the divine eye. When, through the sequence of recollecting former abodes, one enters the signs of long-practiced awakening, and all internal and external phenomena have become stabilized, there arises the non-conceptual [wisdom] consisting in the non-apprehension of the aggregates and so forth in their imagined forms and other such natures; and there is the right resolve consisting of the vow for awakening for the sake of all sentient beings—this is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The first stage is the production of the thought of awakening (cittotpāda) which serves as the basis for the purification of the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).

The second stage is that which is free from the mental orientations of the śrāvakas and others, is the basis for the application of the ten paths of wholesome action for the sake of the complete enlightenment of all sentient beings, and is certain toward the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).

Then, for the sake of pacifying the defects of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), the second meditation (*dhyāna*)—which has as its basis the knowledge of equality regarding the fourfold range of emptiness, non-emptiness, and so forth—is placed before him. Its being placed before him is, as before, due to placing it before through the application of intention and practice (*āśaya-prayoga-pratiyoga*). As for the placing of the meditative concentration (*samādhi*): it is because the aforementioned concentration is placed before him by not ceasing day or night, serving as the antidote to all obscurations.

And there is the prioritization of insight (*vipaśyanā*)—because one prioritizes the aforementioned insight, which consists of the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) of contemplating the non-arising nature of the aggregates as previously described for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and which is accompanied by the equipment of learning, for the benefit of sentient beings. This is the third stage (*bhūmi*).

Through the application of extraordinary vigor, upon attaining the knowledge of equality regarding the four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), and through the application of the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣadharma*) whose sphere of activity includes emptiness and the non-emptiness of emptiness, and by relying on the second dhyāna, the fourth stage is attained.

Then, due to the softness of the mind resulting from joy (*prīti*) and because it lacks the quality of bringing forth superior wisdom (*prajñātiśaya*), there arises the third *dhyāna*, which is characterized by detachment from that [joy]. And that is fixed upon the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*). The immeasurables—characterized by loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—have all directions as their scope because they take all sentient beings as their object. This restriction [to the immeasurables] lasts until non-abiding *nirvāṇa* (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*), because the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is established through the previously mentioned vastness of intention (*āśaya*) and so forth, by virtue of unsurpassed knowledge. This is the fifth stage (*bhūmi*).

The determination of the immeasurable insight (vipaśyanā) manifested through the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*) is as follows: because among deluded beings, those with views conforming to other stages, those included among ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and śrāvakas, and among bodhisattvas who perceive objective referents (*aupalaṃbhika*), there is the determination that brings about the manifestation of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) by means of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). This wisdom—characterized by loving-kindness and so forth, having as its domain the various divisions of all emptiness, and primarily taking as its object the fourfold emptiness beginning with non-dispersal emptiness (*anavakāraśūnyatā*)—is what ensures this. For this very reason, this is the sixth bodhisattva stage.

Then, due to the absence of successive formative activities (*abhisaṃskāra*) arising from the experience of pleasure, and because it is conducive to the state of Samantabhadra, the fourth dhyāna is attained through the abandonment of that [pleasure]. And this is uncommon to the Śrāvakas and others. It is of eight kinds. The abandonment of pleasure is uncommon—because the abandonment of pleasure by worldly beings, Śrāvakas, and others is directed toward a nirvāṇa accompanied by ignorance (*sāvidya*), whereas the abandonment of pleasure by a Bodhisattva proceeds from the realization of the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*). For the sake of accomplishing the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), the Dūraṅgamā Bhūmi is characterized by the application of effortful signlessness (*sābhoga-nimitta-puruṣakāra-yoga*) and reliance upon various skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).

The abandonment of suffering is unique [to this path] because the abandonment of the suffering of other individuals is conducive to nirvana through renewed existence. However, the abandonment of suffering by a bodhisattva is for the sake of all sentient beings upon the attainment of perfect enlightenment, through the application of the methods described in the Vaipulya and other scriptures. The eighth stage is attained through the application of effortless, signless aspiration.

The abandonment of mental gladness is its uncommon [feature]; the abandonment of the others is as previously described. However, for the Bodhisattva, because of the empowerment of the power of practicing the signless (*animitta*), and because of the possession of the power that is beyond the reach of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas regarding their own equipment and entry into the stages, and because of the application of the abandonment of all doubts in all assemblies, there is the ninth stage.

The uncommon [cause] for the abandonment of mental distress is, as before, related to other persons. For the Bodhisattva, however, through the application of the aforementioned extensiveness (*vaipulya*) and so forth in all cases—and specifically in this state, when there is the synthesis of the emptiness of all phenomena—there is the tenth stage, which culminates in the stage of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) upon entering the stage of a Perfectly Awakened One (*sambuddha*). This stage is based on the empowerment by the rays of light of all Tathāgatas, by virtue of the ultimate commitment to the welfare of both oneself and others, and serves as the basis for the teaching of the Dharma of unsurpassed power.

Following that is the common [basis] of equanimity: its emptiness of absence, because it serves as the basis for the stabilization of the enjoyment of the knowledge of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitājñāna) for both oneself and others by way of correct practice.

And it is common to insight (*vipaśyanā*): because this insight has the nature of the knowledge that accomplishes the welfare of all sentient beings in all world-systems through its union with great loving-kindness and great compassion; and because it has the nature of the knowledge of the purity of the dharmadhātu regarding the aggregates and so forth, through the mastery over the mirrors and other [jewels] as described, and through the application of the unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*). By superimposing these [qualities], it possesses four archways; thus, it is "the fourfold meditation-archway."

22.13 [12b6-7] The meditative concentrations (*samādhi*)—which, for those practitioners engaged in the realization of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), are characterized by perfectly pure one-pointedness and possess immeasurable subdivisions according to their respective names—are to be understood here, by way of concise convention, as four: namely, those called Śūraṅgama, Gaganagañja, Nirmala, and Siṃhavikrīḍita. Adorned and embellished on all sides and everywhere by these, there is the gateway of the four dhyānas, which is further adorned by the altar of meditative concentration; this is a *karmadhāraya* compound. It rests upon that very altar.
Because it contains a multitude of *dhāraṇīs* occupied with the worship of the virtuous, and because it fulfills all the hopes of the world, adorned with every kind of ornament,
and since it fulfills the desire for all requisites and so forth, that gabled palace (*kūṭāgāra*) is therefore variegated with all ornaments in order to demonstrate its purity. (See 28d)
Therefore, that which pervades all the true Dharma of the ninefold teaching extracted from the Vinaya is like a row of banners raised by the wind.
His face in every direction resounds with the ringing of bells.

(24) Regarding the phrase "for the sake of discipline" (*vinaya*) and so forth: *Vinaya* means the disciplining of sentient beings. For that purpose, he has raised—that is, spread—the ninefold collection (*navāṅga*): *Sūtra*, because it strings together the meanings connected with the perfections (*pāramitā*) and so forth; *Geya*, because it is a recitation with poetic ornamentation, such as the *Bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna*; *Vyākaraṇa*, such as the *Maitreya-vyākaraṇa* and others; *Gāthā*, such as single verses and so forth; *Udāna*, such as: "O Desire, I know your root; you are born, they say, from conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa*)."

The *Mahāvastu* (III.190) and so forth are well-known from the Vinaya; the *avadānas* are such as the *Śūkarikāvadāna*; the *jātakas* are such as the *Vyāghrījātaka*; the *itivṛttakas* are compositions of narratives; and the *vaipulya-abhūtadharmas* are those that establish [doctrines] such as "disrespect toward the Buddha and the Dharma. The teaching (*pravacana*) consisting of these forms is itself the True Dharma (*saddharma*). It is so called because it goes toward, encompasses, and includes all of that.

And it was that whose faces in all directions were resonant and vocal with the sounds of the bells from the rows of banners—white, black, auspicious, smoky, crimson, variegated, yellow, and green—stretched across the directions starting from the east (Aindrī) and tossed by the wind; for since that gabled chamber (kūṭāgāra) [mentioned in verse 28d] pervades all things through the true Dharma of the ninefold scriptures shaken forth by discipline, it is therefore "possessing faces in all directions resonant with the sounds of the rows of banners tossed by the wind" due to its purity.
[It was also endowed] with the abundance of blossoming flowers of the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), which are ever stainless like the mirror of gnosis.
[He is] incomparable, adorned with necklaces, half-necklaces, mirrors, flower garlands, and various ornaments.

(25) Regarding the phrase "mirror of gnosis" (*jñānādarśa*) and so forth: "mirrors of gnosis" (*jñānādarśāḥ*) means that the gnoses themselves are the mirrors. By the word "gnosis," the five gnoses beginning with the mirror-gnosis are intended, because the word "mirror" is used as a figurative designation (*upalakṣaṇa*).

25.2 There are seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*). The factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness has the characteristic of not forgetting the hearing and realization of the vow for awakening for the sake of sentient beings. The factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) likewise primarily involves differentiation; it has the characteristic of discerning the selfless nature of phenomena by their very essence. The factor of enlightenment that is joy (*prīti*) is the cause for entering into the equality of the non-differentiation of qualities such as wisdom, its training, the sequence [of practice], and the perfections; it is manifested through future destinies.

And these, being included within the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), having the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) as their object, and serving as the antidotes to the obscurations of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*), are the limbs of perfect enlightenment (*sambodhyaṅga*); that is, they are the constituent parts of awakening. Thus they are called "limbs of enlightenment. (Mahāyānalakṣaṇasamuccaya §8f, 299b6–300a4, 147a14-26)

25.3 And there are the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), which are ever-pure and endowed with such qualifiers as "for the sake of sentient beings" and so forth. Because they bring about joy, they are like *āmodi* flowers. The compound [“jñānādarśa-sadāmalabodhyaṅgāmodipuṣpa”] means the mirrors of gnosis together with the ever-pure *āmodi* flowers of the factors of enlightenment. By reason of the perfection—the actual presence—of these, that gabled palace (referred to in verse 28d) is incomparable, peerless, and unequaled, being adorned with necklaces and other ornaments whose nature is their own purity. It is divine, being beautified by eight pillars that represent the purity of the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*).
Because it sets in motion the wheel of Dharma of the Vajra Way, it is joined with the vajra-thread.
26. Regarding "the eight liberations" and so forth:

The liberations (*vimokṣa*) are characterized by the aspect of non-attachment (*alobha*); they have as their primary aim the turning away from attachment toward all objects of perception; they are of the nature of the path of departure for the sake of accomplishing the appearance of whatever is intended. And these are eight: The first is: "Possessing form, one sees forms," being free from greed and having cast aside the perception of form. The second is: "Not having the internal perception of form, one sees external forms," because the perception of form has been transcended within. The third is: "Being intent upon the beautiful, one dwells without greed regarding forms and so forth. (Mahāyānalakṣaṇasamuccaya 301b1-4, 147c28–148a6)

When the mind has been brought to a state of being inclined toward the welfare of the world through the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), there occurs the attainment of all meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) by way of entering the immeasurables for the sake of realizing the nature of the immeasurable mind and for the joyful realization of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). Likewise, there is the attainment of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samāpatti*) with the thought, "There is nothing whatsoever," as well as the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samāpatti*).

And as for the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*): it is the cessation of mental formations preceded by the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), characterized by a profound internal restraint of one's own nature and by the obstruction of the hindrances to the peace of existence (*bhavaśama*). As it has been said: (Mahāyānalakṣaṇasamuccaya 301b4-5, ...

Possessing form, one sees form as empty. Being formless internally, one sees form externally as empty. One sees that which is produced by views of the beautiful and the ugly as empty. One sees the sphere of infinite space as empty. One sees the sphere of infinite consciousness as empty. One sees the sphere of nothingness as empty. One sees the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as empty. One sees the cessation of perception and feeling as empty.

26.3. Because it is characterized by turning away through the thought "it is empty" due to taking emptiness as its object, and because it thereby indicates the non-arising of afflictions, it should be understood as being included within the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśāyatana*). "Internally" refers to the second [sphere], because of the purification of passion (*rāga*). "Pure," and so forth, refers to the third, because even in the resolve for the beautiful (*śubhādhimukti*), there is an increase in non-attachment (*alobha*). The fourth is so called because it proceeds by means of mental attention (*manasikāra*) to the thoughts "space is infinite," "consciousness is infinite," or "there is nothing at all," and because these involve a mild perception (*mṛdu-saṃjñā*).

"Regarding 'the mass of perception' (*saṃjñāgaṇḍa*) and so forth: because delusion regarding the non-perceptual (*asaṃjñaka-saṃmoha*) is an engagement [of the mind], the cessation of the mental formations (*cittābhisaṃskāra*) and so forth preceded by that is the eighth [liberation].

(26.4) Thus, through the purification of these eight liberations, [the palace] is adorned and beautified by eight pillars. It is "divine" (*divya*) because it is comparable to heaven (*svarga*). The "Vajra Way" (*vajranaya*) is the Mantra Way (*mantranaya*). Because the Wheel of Dharma is turned by means of that, it is joined with a vajra-thread and a vajra-fence. This is due to the purification of the objects of the senses, such as form (*rūpa*), and so forth.
It possesses the unsurpassed and infinite fivefold qualities of sensual pleasure;
it is the outflow of the pure realm of the true Dharma, adorned with the five offerings. || 27 ||

27.1 [14a2-5] Regarding the phrase "form and so forth" (*rūpādi*): by the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), sound, smell, taste, and touch are understood. These very objects (*viṣaya*) are designated from the perspective of those with limited vision, since in reality their status as objects cannot be established. Their purification (*viśuddhi*) is the mind of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā-citta*), which is free from intrinsic nature; it is the outflow (*niḥsyanda*) of that, having the form of its fruit, and is characterized by the complete purity of all qualities such as the ten powers (*daśabala*).
It is the abode of the deities, presided over by the sun and moon, situated upon a lotus with a thousand petals.
One should visualize a gabled pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) constructed entirely of jewels there.

Regarding the phrase "the manifold" (*viśva*) and so forth: it means that one should visualize—that is, contemplate—a gabled pavilion fashioned from all (*niḥśeṣa*), that is, every kind of jewel such as sapphire (*indranīla*) and others, arranged according to its beauty; and wherein the nineteen locations of the deities are presided over (*sanātha*), that is, occupied, by the suns and moons situated appropriately upon a lotus with manifold-colored petals (*viśvadala*).
In the center of the central seat, according to the ritual rule, is the orb of the full moon, which arises from the collection of the sixteen digits.

One should meditate upon the mass of immeasurable light. (29) Regarding "sixteen," and so forth: the sixteen *kalās* are the phonemes beginning with *a*; the *kalāpas* are those beginning with *ka*. That full moon mandala whose origin or production (*prabhava*) is from those two is described as such. The singular number is used for the genus. The meaning is that there are two moons, which respectively indicate wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*). One should meditate upon these two moons, emitting a mass of immeasurable light, in the center of the central seat.

29.2 The meaning of "according to rule" (*vidhivat*) is as follows: the two moons—which have become one, which are established respectively below and above, and which consist of the nature of the bodhicitta of aspiration and application, and whose form is the purity of the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics—are thus produced.

29.3 These two moons, because they are clear due to being free from the impurity of resistance (*pratigha*), manifest the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). Their becoming one signifies "equality" (*samatā*). By this, two of the aspects of the fivefold awakening (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*) have been stated.
30.0 [14b7] He states another three aspects, beginning with "supreme primordial," and so forth:
"Herein, the vajra together with the lotus, which arises from the supreme primordial heart, resembles a ruby."

"Adorning the faces of infinite directions on all sides with the shimmering rays of Amitamuni"—this means, in this context, by the transformation of the two moons, or above them. And being one who has accomplished the supreme welfare of the world through infinite emanations (cf. 31b), and possessing that ego-sense (cf. 31b), he should behold the body of the Father of the Jinas (cf. 34d); such is the connection.

"Supreme" because it has the nature of the Tathāgata’s perfect awakening, and "primordial" because it serves as the cause for all; thus, "supreme-primordial" refers to Vajrasattva. His "heart" is the seed-syllable *hūṃ*, and that from which [the deity] originates or is born is so described. "Resembling a dawn-gem" means similar to a ruby (*padmarāga*). Having meditated on him—whose infinite directions are adorned on all sides by the rays of immeasurable, countless Munis—and who possesses the ego-identification with that [deity] at his heart, one [should emanate] through infinite transformations.

Having accomplished the supreme goal for the world, one should meditate upon that vajra—which is fashioned from the atoms of the best of sages—as being presided over by the seed-syllable of Vajrasattva, the first heart-mantra; that is to say, its central hub (*varaṭaka*) is empowered by the syllable *HŪṂ*. Having thus visualized such a vajra, the mantra-practitioner, possessing the ego-identification of that [vajra], is one who maintains the vajra-ego-identification, thinking "OṂ, I am of the nature of the vajra. By this, the stage of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇā*) is shown.

He is thus because he has accomplished for the sake of the worlds the supreme goal characterized by Buddhahood through infinite emanations that pervade the forms of Vairocana and the other [Tathāgatas]. Being such, he possesses the conceit "I am that," meaning he possesses the ego-identification: "Oṃ, as are all Tathāgatas, so am I. By this it is said: having made sentient beings into Tathāgatas by means of the Tathāgatas born from the syllable *Hūṃ* and having included them within himself, one performs the execution of duties while maintaining the ego-identification: "Oṃ, as are all Tathāgatas, so am I. And this is the meaning of the verse: "Having accomplished the purpose of the body of the Victorious One, he possesses the conceit 'I am that'" (*Guhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi* 25cd).
This has been made clear by this [statement], because there is no equality between those two due to their being composed of primary atoms (*paramāṇu*) of different types.
[She is] blue, red, and beautiful, with faces on the right and left that possess the white luster of the full moon.
She is embraced by his two arms, which bear radiant and variegated ornaments, and she is a true consort (*sadvidyā*).

This is a compound meaning that her right and left faces are blue and reddish, respectively, while she possesses a luster as white as the full moon. For the faces on the right and left of Vajrasattva are black and red, while his primary face and entire body are white; and she is embraced by those two arms adorned with radiant and variegated ornaments.
Adorned with a pair of remaining arms holding a vajra, sword, lotus, and jewel,
she is the ornament of the interior of the three worlds.
She from whom the lords of sages emerge from an array of various rays of light;

she who is enriched by her remaining pair of right and left arms holding a vajra, a sword, a lotus, and a jewel—meaning that her four remaining arms on the left and right are endowed with a red vajra, a sword, a jewel, and a lotus, respectively. She from whom the lords of sages emerge from those various arrays of rays which are the ornaments of the sky within the belly of the three worlds—meaning she possesses an emanation of a multitude of Victors pervading the expanse of space.
This is through the purity of the three gates of liberation.

One should perceive one's own body as the progenitor of the Victors, whose nature consists of wisdom and skillful means, who is supreme in compassion, and who is the single reality of the entire world. 34

34.1 [15b4-5] "The three gates of liberation" refers to the three forms of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). 34.2 These are indeed liberations because they are the causes for liberation from the web of conceptual construction (*vikalpajāla*); they are the very gates or doors for entering the Buddha-dharmadhātu. Thus it was said by the Master himself:

For the sake of accomplishing the perfection of the superknowledges (*abhijñāpāramitā*), there are three gateways to liberation (*vimokṣamukha*) characterized by the concise summary of all phenomena (*sarvadharmābhisaṃkṣepa*) as manifested through wisdom (*prajñā*): the gateway to liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatāvimokṣamukha*), and [the others]. Furthermore, that [emptiness] has the characteristic of discerning (*viveka*) the aggregates and so forth by means of the distinction between phenomena and persons (*dharmapudgala*). Consequently, because of the absence of the signs of conceptual construction (*parikalpanimitta*) such as "beautiful" or "ugly" regarding the aggregates and so forth, and because of the discernment of signs such as the "grasper" even within emptiness, there is the gateway to liberation of signlessness (*animittavimokṣamukha*), which serves as the antidote to non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) internally.

The door of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*) is that which serves as the antidote to external afflicted ignorance regarding the aggregates and so forth when they have been rendered signless (*animittīkṛta*), and is characterized by non-attachment. (Mahāyānalakṣaṇasamuccaya §15, 302a1–3, 148a20–b1).

34.3 By means of such purity acting as a cause, one should perceive—that is, meditate upon—the body of the progenitor of the Jinas, namely Śrī Vajrasattva. This body is essentially composed of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*); although its actual nature is wisdom, it is characterized primarily by skillful means. It is the "single reality of the entire world," meaning that because the whole world is non-different from one's own manifestation, it is of a single reality in the form of non-duality (*advaita*). It is the cause for the arising of the entire circle of deities whose essence is the Buddha. "One's own" (*nijām*) means having a form non-different from the manifestation of the yogi. By this, the gnosis of the perfectly pure realm of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*) is demonstrated.

35.0 [15b7–16a1] Having explained the fivefold awakening (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*) of Vajrasattva, [the text] speaks with the words beginning "firstly, the supreme" (*tāvat parametyādi*), in order to bestow empowerment for the sake of purifying the sentient beings to be converted (*vineya-sattva*), for the purpose of arranging the mandala within the lotus, and because the process of disciplining those to be disciplined through passion proceeds by way of that very [lotus]; thus, it is by means of that alone that there is the satisfaction of wisdom and method.
"Relying upon the world as a whole, which is to be disciplined through the perfection of supreme passion..."
One should cause the entire assembly of Jinas to enter within by means of the sound of the illusion of passion (*ratimāyādhvani*).

Having perceived the world of beings to be converted by relying on the perfection of supreme passion, which is great bliss (*mahāsukha*), and having seen that it is fashioned through the illusion of the appearance of passion, there the very sound of the illusionist—the resonance produced by the striking together of the lotus and the vajra—is the sound; by that sound, one should cause the entire assembly of Jinas to enter within the body through the pores of the skin. By this, the pleasing of the Wisdom Consort (*prajñā*) is described.

36.0 [16a2-3] Now, by the words "atha tat" and so forth, the second propitiation is established; for, through the method of the emergence of Jina in the form of the Goddesses, there is a specific injunction for the purpose of propitiating the Means (upāya).
Thus, having emitted all the Vidyās in the form of the totality of objects such as the forms of Locanā and the other [Goddesses], one should abandon all [ordinary] Vidyās.

One should cause them to enter into one’s own vidyā. (36) Regarding "the vidyās beginning with Locanā": there are four goddesses who are the vidyās beginning with Locanā; and there are five, such as Rūpavajrā, who are all objects of the senses—form and so forth—through the purification of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. By means of their being—that is, by taking on their form—one should cause that host of Jinas to emerge from the pores of the skin. These very vidyās, whose nature consists of the host of Jinas emerging in the form of Locanā and the others, are the ninefold goddesses; one should cause them to enter into one’s own vidyā, that is, into the body of the young woman held by one’s own pair of arms.
One should cause [them] to enter. By this, the pleasing of the Means (upāya) is stated. And so it is said in the *Samāja*:

"Then all those Tathāgatas, for the sake of pleasing the Blessed One, the Lord of the Vajra Body, Speech, and Mind of all Tathāgatas, having emanated their own forms as female forms... (*Guhyasamājatantra*, p. 5, ll. 2–3), and so forth.
Furthermore, in that very same place, it is stated in order to show the radiation of the goddesses precisely through the transformation of the respective Tathāgatas of their own families:
In that regard, some [say] "in the form of Buddhalocanā" (*Guhyasamājatantra* p.
5, l. 4). The Buddhas are Vairocanas; [it means] in the form of Locanā produced from them. Likewise—"in the form of Samayatārā" (*Guhyasamājatantra* p. 5, l. 5).

Thus, the *samayas* are *Amoghas* by virtue of their manifestation in the form of Tārā. In this way, for the others as well, the transformation into their respective families should be understood as being for the sake of illustration. As for Dharmadhātuvajrā, her radiation is not mentioned because the *dharmadhātu* is omnipresent, or because she is embraced by Vajradhara; or else, it is for the purpose of making known the primacy of the great bliss born of touch (*sparśaja*) at the time of awakening, or because in the *Nidānapaṭala*, the emergence and entry of the nine goddesses ending with Sparśavajrā are demonstrated.
Therefore—
Having withdrawn all the wheel-bearers by means of the method of great passion alone,
and having emanated the goddesses ninefold, one should place them within the body of the sādhya.
Thus it is also stated in the eighteenth [chapter]:
"Therefore, here too, all the vidyās should be understood as the goddesses in exactly nine forms."

36.4 And the reason for the Victors assuming the form of women is solely their intentional resolve (*abhisandhi*) to discipline those beings who are to be guided by such forms. As it is said in the *Guhyatilaka*:

"Aho! How great is the desire for the welfare of all beings inherent in the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), that these heroes assume even the form of women out of consideration for those to be disciplined. (= *Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha* 1,217,322)
Thus,
within the pericarp of that lotus is a mandala produced from the rays of the stainless moon.
Having meditated with the intellect upon the entire [assembly], one should cause the multitude of people to enter therein.

Regarding the phrase "that lotus," and so forth: within the interior of the pericarp (varaṭaka) of the lotus belonging to that one's own *vidyā*, one should meditate on the mandala consisting of the stainless moon—the *bodhicitta*—which, due to its being the destroyer of the darkness of all ignorance, is like a ray of light; this mandala is accompanied by Vajrasattva, the sovereign of all Buddhas and others. Having meditated thus, one should cause the entire multitude of people to enter that mandala by means of the intellect.

38.0 [16b4-5] Then he says, "One should consecrate him," beginning with *sadguhya* and so forth: having placed the assembly of Victors, Vairocana and the others, within the center of the lotus of the six secret places, in the form of the fluid of the moon—
One should sprinkle him with that [fluid].

38.1 [16b5]: Having caused the multitude of Jinas, drawn in by the rays from the heart and entered through the mouth, to settle within the center of the excellent secret lotus, one should sprinkle that assembly of people (janakāya)—the meaning is that they are sprinkled—by means of that multitude of Jinas which has manifested in the form of lunar fluid and is transformed into the nature of bodhicitta.

39.0 [16b5-7] Then, at the conclusion of the consecration, in order to show that the beings— having obtained the bliss and mental satisfaction of all the Tathāgatas, having become purified according to their respective inclinations through the sequence of their own seed-syllables and signs empowered by the transformation of the seed-syllables *caṃ*, *dravībhāva*, *kṣiṃ*, and so forth, and having become pure in the form of Kṣitigarbha and others who are the purification of the eye and other faculties— emerge, he speaks the five Āryā verses beginning with "Kṣitigarbha": "Kṣitigarbha, Vajrapāṇi, Khagarbha, Lokeśvara, and Viṣkambhin."
And the illustrious Samantabhadra—these are reckoned as the eye and so forth. (39)

39.1 Following that—that is, immediately after the consecration (*abhiṣeka*)—one should emit the six [bodhisattvas], Kṣitigarbha and the others, who are reckoned as the eye and so forth; that is, in due order, as the forms of the purification of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. By means of the "seeds"—that is, by the six seed-syllables beginning with *kṣiṃ*, which belong to the eye and the other [senses]—they are produced according to the ritual rule.

One should "emit" them—that is, one should mentally bring them forth from the peaked pavilion within the lotus of the consort who is one's own radiance, because they have been introduced by the intellect alone.

39.2 These seed-syllables beginning with *kṣīṃ* were taught by the Master for the purpose of accomplishment (*niṣpatti*), and not for the purpose of emission (*utsarga*), as others believe; for that [emission] is established by the mind alone, just like entry. Otherwise, an infinity of seed-syllables for accomplishment would result.
[The objects are: form, sound, smell, taste, the tangible, and the vajra of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
And those known as Locanā and the others have earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness as their intrinsic natures.

Thus, one should emit the six [goddesses], Rūpavajrā and the rest, according to their respective order, as having the nature of the purification of form, sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). By means of the six seed-syllables—*jaḥ* and so forth—which belong to Rūpavajrā and the others, they are produced according to the ritual rule and should be emitted as before.

Likewise, the four goddesses named Locanā and the others, who respectively possess the nature of earth, water, fire, and wind, should be emitted just as before— having been produced according to the ritual by means of their seed-syllables, *lāṃ*, *māṃ*, *pāṃ*, and *tāṃ* (as seen in 43a)— by means of the seed-syllables (as seen in 41d). They are described as being of the same nature as the mental formations (*saṃskāra*) that serve as the causes for the experience of form (*rūpa*).
"Then one should emit the Sugatas, Vairocana and the rest, by means of their seed-syllables.

(41) This means that one should subsequently emit the five Sugatas, Vairocana and the others—who are described as having the nature of the five aggregates known as form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—in due order, by means of the seed-syllables *vuṃ* and so forth belonging to Śāśvata and the others. These have been explained as being produced according to the ritual procedure through the signs of experiencing the five forms (*pañca-rūpa-anubhava-nimitta*) and likewise through the mental formations (*saṃskāra-mānasa*). "By means of the seed-syllables" refers to the five seed-syllables beginning with *vuṃ* belonging to Śāśvata and the others; the connection is that one should emit them as previously described once they have been thus completed. Śāśvata is Vairocana.
The phrase "in due order" (yathākramam)— as seen in verse 43d— is to be connected with everything that precedes it.
These syllables— *kṣiṃ*, *jraṃ*, *khaṃ*, *gaṃ*, *ṣkaṃ*, *saṃ*— are said to belong to the eye and the other [senses].
Jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ khaṃ raṃ are said to belong to Rūpavajrā and the others;
likewise, lāṃ māṃ pāṃ tāṃ.
Likewise, the seed-syllables of Locanā and the others have been declared.
For Śāśvata and the others, they are, in due order: *vuṃ*, *āṃ*, *jrīṃ*, *khaṃ*, and *hūṃ*.
[43–44] Regarding the entry of the three syllables for the purpose of the arising of Mañjuvajra, he says: *oṃ* and so forth.

One should visualize the mind as the syllables Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ, radiant and containing the syllable Bhrūṃ within them; according to the ritual procedure, one should behold this incomparable [mind] situated in the center of a lotus, liquefied by the passion of wisdom (prajñārāga). 44

44.1 “Mind” refers to the intermediate state consciousness previously mentioned, which has as its object the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and contains within it the radiant syllable *BHOḤ*. By means of the two radiating rays, the three syllables are placed in the center by the parents, Vajradhara and his consort, through the red syllables *HOḤ*. Having entered according to the ritual rule via the mouth and passed through the path of the vajra, they are established within the interior of the lotus of one’s own consort; thus, abiding in the lotus’s interior and being devoid of the forms of body and so forth, those three incomparable syllables are [united] with the passion of wisdom (*prajñārāga*).
One should behold [the moon] liquefied by the churning of the lotus with the supreme bliss of one's own innate wisdom (*svābhavidyā*).
Having seen both [the sun and moon] likewise liquefied by the power of its radiance— thus [says] the goddess Locanā and the others.

One should meditate upon the impulsion of the sound of song. Regarding the passage beginning with "of that" (*tasya*): "of that" refers to the mind in the form of the syllable just mentioned, which has become liquefied. By the power of its red-colored light, one should see both the Vidyā and Vajrasattva as liquefied like the moon and transformed into the state of the *kalala*.

For it should be understood that the specific states of mind such as compassion, produced by the Blessed One through his physical teaching, sequentially attain the nature of Locanā and the others—[who are] the rays of the moon-like liquid—and, appearing in the forms of the lords of their respective families, they praise and impel Vajradhara.

46.0 [17b5-6] Here, although it was stated as "Locanā and the others" in accordance with the noble *Mātr̥kā*, in this tantra, however, in order to demonstrate the primacy of the mind (*citta*), the exhortation to Māmakī alone is stated first. Thus, he shows her at the very beginning with the words:

"O Vajracitta, Lord of the World, protect me, O realm of beings, through your delightful passion and great purpose! Love me, O progenitor of beings, O supreme kinsman, if you desire my life, O Protector! (46)

In this regard, it should be understood that Māmakī, who is the embodiment of the purification of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables], praises and exhorts Vajradhara in the form of Cittavajra, the lord of her own family.

46.2 Vajracitta is Cittavajra, Vajrasattva, because his nature consists of the perfectly pure wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*. He is the Lord (*īśvara*) of the wheel (*cakra*) in the world (*bhuvana*). He is the element (*dhātu*) of sentient beings (*sattva*) because he effects their welfare. "Being" (*sat*) is existence; its state is "sentience" (*sattva*), which is Buddhahood; he is the progenitor of that, thus "progenitor-sentient-being" (*janakasattva*). Alternatively, he is the progenitor-sentient-being because he is the cause for the arising of Mañjuvajra and the others. For this very reason, he is the "Great Supreme Kinsman" (*mahāgrabandhu*). Having thus awakened [the assembly] with praise, he said to Vajradhara: "Protect me! (*trāyasva mām*); that is, "save me. How? This is the intended meaning.

47.0 [18a3] Now Locanā, whose form is the purification of compassion and the other [perfections], praises and exhorts the Blessed One by means of the form of Kāyavajra, the lord of her own family, beginning with the words “You are the Vajra-body,” and so forth:
“You are the Vajra-body, the wheel of commands beloved by many beings; you who perceive the welfare of the ultimate meaning of awakening and the purpose of the Buddhas.”
O Lord, if you desire to live by me, then through passion, enjoy my passion. (Guhyasamājatantra 17.73)

47.1 Because he has the nature of the Vajra Body, which is the form of the Mirror-like Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), he is the Vajra Body; the Blessed One himself is the Vajra Body because his form is inconceivable. Because he loves many beings, he is "Beloved by Many Beings" (*bahusattvapriya*). Because he turns the wheel of command, he is the "Wheel of Command" (*ājñācakra*). Because he demonstrates the welfare of beings—the purpose and objective of the Buddhas—by means of skillful methods, leading to the culmination of supreme enlightenment, he is the "One who Demonstrates the Welfare of the Supreme Meaning of Enlightenment and the Purpose of the Buddhas" (*buddhārthabodhiparamārthahitānudarśin*).

Having thus addressed Vajradhara, she said: "By passion" means by great bliss (*mahāsukha*). Passion is the desire to uplift the world; she whose commitment (*samaya*) is that very passion—meaning she whose nature is compassion—is the one called "Rāgasamayā. "Lust after me" means this. The rest is as before. Then Pāṇḍarā, who is the embodiment of the purification of joy and the other [joyful states], praises and exhorts Vajrasattva in the form of her own lord, Vāgvajra, saying: "O Vajra Speech," and so forth. "O Vajra Speech, you who are compassionate for the welfare of all..."
Always engaged in performing deeds for the benefit of the world,
O Samantabhadra, fulfill my desire through the practice of sexual union, if you wish for me to live, O Lord! 48
(Guhyasamājatantra 17.74) 48.1 [18a7–18b3] This is as before.

49.0 [18b3] Now, Tārā, whose nature is the purification of equanimity (*upekṣā*) and so forth, praises and exhorts the Blessed One in the form of Amoghasiddhi, who is her own presiding deity, with the words beginning "You are Vajrakāma," and so on.

O Vajra-Lover, supreme of commitments, you who act for the great benefit of others, the ornament of the lineage of the Perfectly Awakened Ones, and compassionate with equanimity; desire me, the treasury of virtues who am like a multitude of jewels, if you wish for my life, O Lord! 49

(Vajraśekhara Tantra 17.75) 49.1 [18b3–6] He is Vajrakāma because his desires—such as form and so forth—are characterized by the deity whose nature is the supreme primordial wisdom of the vajra-form. He is Samayāgra because he is the unfailing pledge (*samaya*) and is supreme precisely because he acts for the benefit of sentient beings through the nature of the performance of activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna*). He is Mahāhitārtha because great benefit (*mahāhita*), which is the welfare conducive to the future path, arises from him for those to be trained (*vineya*). He is Sambodhivaṃśatilaka because he is the most excellent ornament within the lineage (*vaṃśa*) or family (*gotra*) of perfect enlightenment. He is Samatānukampī because he shows compassion through equality, that is, through emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

He spoke thus to such a Vajrasattva: "Desire me. This means: "Since I am a treasury of qualities by virtue of being the support of the Victors (*jinādhāra*), desire me who am like a multitude of jewels; for through service to me in this way, the accomplishment of all the aims of oneself and others occurs. The meaning is: "Leaving aside the state of misfortune, favor me by resorting to my form, which is inseparable from the nature of Samantabhadra. The remainder is to be explained as before.
[50.0] Now, he describes the arising of Mañjuvajra by means of the sequence of seed-syllables and signs, beginning with the words "Thus, the song," and so forth.
Thus, in accordance with the requirements of the song (*gītikā*)...
Through the realization that all things are like an illusion,
may one become oneself the embodiment of one's own mantra, consisting of a radiant circle of light rays. 50

50.1 The practitioner, who has realized that all things are like an illusion, should himself become the form of the syllable *maṃ*, with a sword born from the fluid-like radiant *maṃ* held in his fist, and a circle of radiating rays situated upon a moon within it.
Having mentally placed all the Lords of Sages, emanated in the forms of his own deity, inside him by means of their rays of light—

"Śrīmān" refers to Mañjughoṣa. [51] By means of the radiance of that syllable *maṃ*, one should dissolve all the Lords of Sages (*munīndra*), who are emanations of one's own deity Mañjuśrī in that very form, into that same syllable *maṃ*. Then, with the mind, one should become Mañjughoṣa, characterized by the attributes to be described as "Śrīmān. This means that one should perceive oneself as Mañjuvajra.
[52.0] He states the attributes indicated by the word "iti" in two verses beginning with "satkuṅkuma... and so forth.
Having the reddish luster of excellent saffron, with the right and left faces of blue and white color respectively,
and adorned with various ornaments—
His two arms are embraced by true wisdom;
he possesses a radiant sword and arrow,
holds a bow of blue lotuses, and has infinite luster.
The Protector, by whom the entire expanse of the sky is adorned with all the radiant families beginning with the Tathāgata family.

(53) [Commentary: He is such because the entire mandala of the sky is adorned by all the radiant families, beginning with that of the Tathāgatas. *Tāya* is the teaching of the path as it has been seen by oneself; he who possesses this is a *tāyin*. Alternatively, a *tāyin* is one whose nature is to ferry the world across [to liberation].

53.2 Therefore, by this, the *samayasattva* (pledge-being) should be understood as being fully accomplished (*niṣpanna*). 54.0 Since the described form possesses the logic of the pledge (*samaya*), its primary status is untenable; thus, it is merely an indicative illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). To this effect, he says: "The object of apprehension," and so forth.
54.1 Others, however, explain it differently. Here—
From attachment to existence, existence becomes endless; attachment to peace brings about misfortune.
One who practices cultivation through illusion shall become identical with the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).

(Guhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi 48) Thinking thus, in order to demonstrate that this Blessed One has the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, he says: "Because of being devoid of the grasped and the grasper," and so forth.
Having realized that all things lack intrinsic nature, one should take as one's basis the fact that attachment to purification is a flaw. 54

54.2 In ultimate reality, because of the absence of the grasped and the grasper, all things are devoid of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatā*), since intrinsic nature consists in the form of the grasped and the grasper. As it has been said:
"The external characteristic does not exist in the form of the grasped and the grasper;
therefore, because they are empty of characteristics, they are revealed to be without intrinsic nature."
(Pramāṇavārttika Pramāṇasiddhi 215).

Therefore, having realized that lack of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatā*), and for the sake of the destruction—meaning the exhaustion—of both purification (*vyavadāna*) which is *nirvāṇa*, and attachment (*abhiniveśa*) which is *saṃsāra*, one should perform the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) thinking: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.

54'.1 By forming two phrases from "consisting of the nature [of the letters] beginning with Oṃ" and so forth, there is an exhortation regarding the sixfold reality of body and so on by means of six phrases. It is the *dhātu* (element) of the phenomena (*dharma*)—namely, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and so on—because it is their basis (*ādhāra*), as it is that which accomplishes them.

54'.2 For it is thus: since the aspect (*ākāra*) is characterized by tranquility and so forth through the conceptualization of distinctions such as color according to the inclinations of sentient beings, its purpose is fulfilled in that very [basis].

Others, however, explain it differently: having understood the absence of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatā*), for the sake of destroying—that is, for the sake of exhausting—the attachment to purification (*vyavadāna*) and to *nirvāṇa*, one should perform the empowerment of the mantra, thinking: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*. The meaning is: "I am of the nature of the *dharmadhātu* which does not abide in either cyclic existence (*bhava*) or *nirvāṇa*."

For when there is knowledge of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) in all things collectively, attachment to existence (*bhava-abhiniveśa*) is indeed exhausted. There would then be non-attachment even toward *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, for the sake of abandoning that [non-attachment] as well, one must take the true nature of the *dharmadhātu* as one's basis; for even attachment to *nirvāṇa* is a cause for the destruction of the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*). As it was said in the *Bandhamokṣaparīkṣā*: "I shall attain *nirvāṇa* without grasping; *nirvāṇa* will be mine"—for those who have such a fixation, their grasping is a great grasping (*mahāgraha*).
There is no superimposition upon nirvāṇa, nor any removal of saṃsāra. Where [these do not exist], what is saṃsāra there, or what nirvāṇa is conceptualized?
(Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 16.9–10). It is also stated in the Examination of Nirvāṇa:
"The limit of nirvāṇa is the same as the limit of saṃsāra."
Not even the slightest subtle interval exists between those two.
Thus [it is said in] the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (25.20).
Furthermore, it is stated in the *Ratnāvalī*:
Nor is nirvāṇa even a non-existence; how much less could it be an existence?
The exhaustion of the grasping after existence and non-existence is called nirvāṇa.
(Ratnāvalī 1.42). Thus it was also said by the Blessed One:
"Indeed, non-nirvāṇa is taught as nirvāṇa by the Lord of the World."
A knot tied by space is released by space alone.
Thus,
by this, it is stated that the first limb, called "service" (*sevā*), which consists of the deity resembling the cause, is the fruit of the soft outflow (*mṛdu-niḥsyanda-phala*).
55.0 [19b5] He states the second limb:
"Thereafter, having filled the eyes and so forth with the radiance of their respective seed-syllables..."
"By Kṣitigarbha and the others, in the stainless moon-disk within one's own heart, situated inside the hub of the vajra... (55).

"Thereafter" means immediately following the service (*sevā*). "By the radiance of their own seed-syllables" means by the seed-syllables of the six [bodhisattvas], Kṣitigarbha and the rest—namely, the syllable *kṣiṃ* and so forth—which reside respectively in the locations of the eyes and other sense organs within the hubs of their respective emblems; and by the radiance of those very [seeds], that is, by those same individual rays of light, it refers to the Tathāgatas who have been brought forth and transformed into the forms of Kṣitigarbha and the others.

Thus, having filled the eyes and other sense organs with those six [bodhisattvas], Kṣitigarbha and the rest, who have been produced by their own seed-syllables as causes, one should meditate (see 56c). This means that one should contemplate Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin, who has a black face and white and red faces on his right and left respectively; and above the navel, one should contemplate Samantabhadra, born from a white *saṃvajra*, who has a black face and red and white faces on his right and left respectively.

55.2 These [deities], beginning with Kṣitigarbha, have bodies whose root color, faces, and hand-symbols correspond to their respective seed-syllables. Viṣkambhin holds a sword in his right hand and a wheel; [the others] hold a jewel and a lotus in their left hands. Lokeśvara has a wheel and a conch-shell; Khagarbha has a wheel and a lotus. They should be visualized as seated upon moon-maṇḍalas, in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, adorned with all ornaments and jeweled crowns, and embracing their respective wisdom-consorts (vidyā).

55.3 By this, the subsidiary practice (*upasādhana*) limb, characterized by omniscience and having the fruit of a mild maturation, has been explained; for the eyes and other faculties take on the forms of deities such as Kṣitigarbha, and because each possesses all the sense-faculties—such as the ear and so forth—it is possible to fully know all objects, such as sounds and so forth, and because one fully knows the specific qualities of objects, such as their subtlety and so on.

55.4 He states the third limb, beginning with "in the stainless" (*amale*), etc. "In the stainless moon of one's own heart, situated within the hub of the vajra" means that the *Cittavajra* (the syllable *HŪṂ*) is situated in the center of the hub of the vajra produced from the black syllable *HŪṂ*.
And at the navel of the lotus-circle of the face and head,
one should meditate upon Vāgvajra and Kāyavajra by means of the syllables ĀḤ and OṂ. 56

56.1 “*Hūṃkāracittavajra*” means that one should meditate on the Mind-Vajra, resembling Vajrapāṇi, by transforming the black *hūṃ* syllable from which the vajra arises, as well as the *hūṃ* syllable situated in its center. In this way, the accomplishment through the transformation of the seed-syllable and the emblem should be understood for both the Speech-Vajra and the Body-Vajra. Furthermore, regarding the lotus of the mouth, the head, and the navel of the wheel: [the lotus is] at the root of the tongue in the center of a red *āḥ* syllable; [the wheel is] at the head in the center of a white *oṃ* syllable.

The connection is as follows: with the syllable *āḥ* and the *praṇava* (*oṃ*), one should meditate on Vāgvajra, resembling Lokeśvara, by means of the syllable *rakta* (*ra*), and on Kāyavajra, similar to Kṣitigarbha, by means of the white syllable *oṃ*.
[One should meditate on them] surrounded by streams of light from their hearts, shining through union with true wisdom (*satprajñā*).
Having worshipped the Lords of Jinas, one should consecrate one’s own *cittavajra* and so forth with those [mantras].

(57) Regarding "their hearts" (*taddhṛdayāni*): this refers to the hearts of those [deities], such as *Cittavajra* and the others. "By the multitudes of their rays" means by the rays of the white syllable *HŪṂ*, the syllable *OṂ*, and the syllable *ĀḤ*, which reside upon the moon-seats within the vajra, lotus, and wheel located inside the moon-discs at the hearts of *Cittavajra* and the others. This is the meaning.

He qualifies [the deities] by way of their nature: "shining through union with true wisdom. Having worshipped, according to the ritual, the Cittavajra and others residing in the hearts of the lords of sages situated in the ten directions all around—by means of the forms of the offering goddesses such as Rūpavajrā and the rest, which have emerged from the tips of the rays—one should then consecrate one's own Cittavajra and the others in the sequence beginning with: "The glorious Cittavajradhara, meditated upon as the indivisibility of the three vajras" (58a). "The glorious Cittavajradhara, meditated upon as the indivisibility of the three vajras; [He is] the lord of the Tathāgatas, the supreme sovereign of the three realms. Then, having worshipped those very Jinas—the Cittavajra and others—who shine through union with true wisdom, one should subsequently [consecrate]. Thus, the glorious Cittavajradhara... [and so forth]. One should consecrate one's own Cittavajra and the others in this order.
"The glorious Cittavajradhara, meditated upon as the indivisibility of the three vajras; [He is] the lord of the Tathāgatas, the supreme sovereign of the three realms."
"May the Lord of the Mind-Vajra bestow upon me today the state of empowerment.

(Guhyasamājatantra 12.74) Regarding the phrase "cultivated as the indivisible three vajras": the meaning is that one has cultivated the non-duality of the Body-Vajra and the others; thus, it refers to having realized their intrinsic nature.
May the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, who have cultivated the indivisibility of the three vajras,
grant me today the state of empowerment, O Vajra-mind ones!
(Guhyasamājatantra 12.75)
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra-mind of all Tathāgatas.
The glorious Dharma, the path of speech, which is cultivated as the indivisibility of the three vajras—
may it today grant me the state of empowerment as the Vajra of Speech.
(Guhyasamājatantra 12.72)
60.1 [20b3-4] "The path of speech" (vākpatha) is that which is produced at the root of the tongue; the rest is well known.
May the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, who have cultivated the indivisibility of the three vajras, grant me today the state of empowerment as the Vajra of Speech. (61)
(Guhyasamājatantra 12.73) Oṃ, I am of the nature of the speech-vajra of all Tathāgatas.
The glorious holder of the body-vajra, who is cultivated as the indivisibility of the three vajras,
may today grant me the state of empowerment of the Body-Vajra-holder.
(Guhyasamājatantra 12.70)
May the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, who have cultivated the indivisibility of the three vajras,
grant me today the state of empowerment, O Vajra-Body holders!
(Guhyasamājatantra 12.71)
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra body of all Tathāgatas.

64.0 [20b4] Then, in order to demonstrate the inconceivability of the Three Vajras— which have entered through the supplication in verse and are empowered by the mantra beginning with "Oṃ"— he says: "Having taken as the object the Three Vajras, whose nature is like space and which are devoid of characteristics," and so forth.

Having exhorted the multitude of sages dwelling within the circle of all directions with the splendors of his heart, the meaning is that [the deity] has a nature like space because he is devoid of the characteristics of differentiation, and thus his form is inconceivable. Having taken as an object this suchness, which consists of the three vajras, one should have a crown resplendent with the Lord of one's own family; this is the connection with what follows.

64.2 By this, the limb of the means (*sādhana*)—which consists of the three bodies characterized as the Dharma, Enjoyment, and Emanation, and is termed the Vajras of Mind, Speech, and Body—is said to be the fruit of the "mild" human effort (*puruṣakāra*). As it has been said: "The state of benefiting the world is carried forth by the Dharma, Enjoyment, and Emanation [bodies]; therefore, for the sake of accomplishment, there should be the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the secrets of the mind and so forth."
(Guhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi 51).

This is the meaning: therein, the *dharmakāya* is twofold—conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Among these, the conditioned is that which has the nature of effecting perfect buddhahood, is untainted (*anāsrava*), and has attained manifest enlightenment in the pure abode of Akaniṣṭha, as follows:
The factors conducive to enlightenment, the immeasurables, the liberations in their successive order,
the ninefold meditative attainments, and the tenfold totalities.
The bases of mastery are of eight kinds according to their classification;
[as well as] the absence of strife, the knowledge resulting from prayer, the superknowledges, and the analytical knowledges.

The body of dharma (*dharmakāya*) is said to consist of: all the aspects [of knowledge], the four purities, the ten masteries, the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the absence of hesitation, the threefold application of mindfulness, the threefold quality of non-forgetfulness, the total eradication of habitual tendencies, great compassion for living beings, the eighteen qualities unique to the Sage, and omniscience.

The individual characteristics (*pratilakṣaṇa*) of those phenomena are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Although it is not separate from them, it is as if separate; it is attained through the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*) but is not produced. Because it is uncreated, it is the essential nature (*svābhāvika*). As it has been said: "Those untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena which have attained purity in all its aspects—the body of the Sage (*muni*) in its essential nature (*svābhāvika-kāya*) is their characteristic of primordial nature (*prakṛti-lakṣaṇa*)."
(Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.1).

This body, characterized by the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) and consisting of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), is the *dharmakāya*. It is conjoined with the *sāmbhogikakāya*, equal for all Tathāgatas, and subtle; it serves as the cause for manifesting the *saṃbhoga* [body] at will and for the state of the *saṃbhoga* mind. Thus it is said:
"The essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*) is considered equal, subtle, and conjoined with that [the *sāmbhogika*]."
It is the cause for the mastery of enjoyment, in that it displays enjoyments according to one's wish.
(Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 9.62).

This twofold [body], consisting of purified mind and mental factors, has the nature of the cultivated *cittavajra*; therein, the specific excellence of attaining the variegated nature of vision is to be understood through its direct manifestation regarding all objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) in all their aspects. However, that body by which he teaches the Dharma to the Bodhisattvas who have entered the stages is the Enjoyment Body (*sāmbhogika*), characterized by the primary marks and so forth; it is differentiated by the assemblies of disciples, the Buddha-fields, names, physical forms, enjoyments, and activities. As it has been said:
In all realms, the Enjoyment Body (sāmbhogya-kāya) is differentiated by its assemblies of followers, fields, names, bodies, and its activities for the enjoyment of the Dharma.
(Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 9.61).

And that [body] is preceded by non-concentrated wisdom (*asamāhitaprajñā*) and is characterized by the cultivated Vajra of Speech (*vāgvajra*). In this regard, the excellence of attaining mastery over teaching (*deśanāvibhutva*) is to be understood from its immeasurable teachings through various, manifold, and inconceivable gateways that are profound, sublime, and diverse. Furthermore, the body by which one effects the discipline (*vinayana*) of other sentient beings is the emanation body (*nairmāṇika*); it is uninterrupted as long as cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) lasts, because it performs the welfare of various worlds. As it is said: "By means of which it equally performs diverse benefits for the world..."
Until the end of existence, that emanation-body of the Sage remains uninterrupted.
(Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.33). And again:
"Always [manifesting] through the display of arts, great enlightenment, birth, and nirvāṇa..."
This emanation body of the Buddha is a great means for liberation.
(Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 9.64).

Because it is the great means (*mahopāya*), the fulfillment of the welfare of others (*parārthasampatti*) alone is primary. And since that [fulfillment] consists of the nature of the cultivated Vajra-body (*bhāvitakāyavajrātmaka*), the specific attainment of mastery (*vibhutva*) therein should be understood as the basis for the performance of activities for the sake of sentient beings, by virtue of being the support for immeasurable and unimpeded qualities of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*). Furthermore, the fulfillment of the welfare of both self and others in all its aspects is established in these two bodies—the Enjoyment Body (*sāmbhogika*) and the Emanation Body (*nairmāṇika*). As it has been said: "In the two [bodies], the fulfillment of the two purposes is established in all its aspects."

(Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 9.63cd). However, when the essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*) is intended as distinct [from the wisdom body], then its nature as knowledge—which is both secluded and non-differentiated—is difficult to comprehend. Therefore, in order to indicate that it is clear yet appears unclear even though it is clear, the Jñānasattva, whose nature is the essential body, should be understood separately according to the sequence to be explained. For the Tathāgata’s body is not something else that falls within the domain of another, nor is it accessible through the supramundane path in any other way.

64.4 Therefore, by this, the four seals (*mudrā*) should be understood as explained: therein, the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) has the nature of the Mind-Vajra; the Pledge Seal (*samayamudrā*) has the nature of the Wisdom-Being (*jñānasattva*); the Dharma Seal (*dharmamudrā*) has the form of the Speech-Vajra; and the Action Seal (*karmamudrā*) has the nature of the Body-Vajra.

64.5 With the words beginning "having exhorted" (*saṃcodya*), he states the fourth limb. Just as before, one should understand that the gnosis-being (*jñānasattva*) who is seen is, alternatively, at the very moment of the emergence of Cittavajra and the others, seated upon the moon situated in the center of a fist with a sword-blade [held] like a hare-marked [moon], located between Vāgvajra and Cittavajra, resembling the pledge-being (*samayasattva*). By means of the light rays from his heart, he exhorts the multitude of sages abiding within the circle of all directions; then, by means of vases raised by the hands of the hosts of vidyās issued from the rays of the Supreme Sage (*munivara*), [he performs the consecration].
"Consecrated with the water of gnosis, he shall have a crown shining with the Lord of his own family.

(65) From the rays of those very same eminent Sages who were thus impelled, there emerge the hosts of Vidyās, Locanā and the others. With their hands, they lift up vases filled with the water of gnosis; being consecrated by that water of gnosis, the yogin Mañjuvajra shall have a crown shining with the Lord of his own family—that is, his diadem shall be illuminated by Akṣobhya.

The meaning is that immediately after the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), Akṣobhya—perfected by the waters of knowledge (*jñānāmbu*) from the worship of the consecration goddesses—is to be visualized upon the crown of Mañjuvajra.

By this, the limb of the Great Accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*) has been described as having the fruit of great purity in the form of consecration, because purity is produced through the consecration with the water of knowledge. Thus, these four limbs beginning with "service" (*sevā*) have been explained as being "superior" insofar as they relate to the sovereign (*adhipati*); yet, because they are not capable of exhausting all adverse factors (*vipakṣa*) and are therefore not fully potent, they are designated by the term "mild" and are said to have the fruit of a mild outflow (*mṛduniḥsyanda*).

66.0 [21a5-6] Now, in order to state another fourfold limb of service, together with its results such as the outflow (*niḥsyanda*), which purifies wisdom and is characterized by the term "middling" because it occupies the middle position between the weak and the intense [limbs], he says: "In that same way...
"In that same way, having beheld with one's own heart the Vidyā emanated, possessing the radiance of one's own deity,"

[The practitioner], whose body is radiant with the arrangement of the three syllables and who possesses eyes and other features that are fully perfected, should—having visualized the Vidyā through the sequence of service (*sevā*) and so forth, like Mañjuvajra—the mantra-knower who knows reality, with the conviction (*adhimokṣa*) "I delight the Sugatas," begin the pleasure (*rati*) together with her. This is the connection [of the verse]. Demonstrating that very sequence of service and so forth, he qualifies the Vidyā [with the words]: "from his own heart" (*svahṛd*).

This is its meaning: in the same manner, by means of a ritual that lacks the empowerment of beings for the mutual satisfaction—consisting in the inclusion of other Tathāgatas in the form of one’s own reflection (pratibhāsa) impelled by the moon situated before one who has come from Kākandī—one produces (*nirmitā*) or brings to completion (*niṣpāditā*) the radiance of one’s own deity, namely, the form of Mañjuvajra, by means of the seed-syllable of Vajradhara-drava-Ja-Mañjuvajra at one’s own heart. By this, it is indicated that the service (*sevā*) of this [deity] has the intermediate outflow (*madhyaniḥsyanda*) as its fruit.

66.3 “With the eyes and so forth fully perfected” means, as before, the sixfold set of the eyes and so forth, which have been brought to completion through their respective seeds and are presided over by Kṣitigarbha and the others. By this, the *upasādhana* (near-accomplishment), which is the intermediate fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*), is indicated.

66.4 “The three syllables” refers to the three syllables *HŪṂ*, *ĀḤ*, and *OṂ*. As previously stated, their meditation and placement consist of visualizing them in the forms of Cittavajra and the others in the aforementioned locations. By this, the *sādhana* (accomplishment), which is the intermediate fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*), is indicated.

66.5. Then, as before, through the consecration with the water of gnosis (*jñānāmbu*) and so forth, she possesses a radiant and stainless body; thus she is "she whose body is radiant through the arrangement of the three syllables. By this, the Great Accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*), which has the fruit of intermediate purity, is indicated.
67.0. Distinguishing her specifically as the one who gathers the five families (*pañcakulakalāpinī*), he says: "On the head," and so forth. [The knower of reality] on the head and the heart...
At the navel, the secret place, and likewise at the pair of thighs and so forth,
[one should recite] "Oṃ Hūṃ Svā Āḥ Hā," together with the primary families of the Body, Mind, and Vajra. 67

67.1 On the head, heart, navel, secret place, and the pair of thighs—and by the inclusion of "and so forth," on the atoms of their respective parts—she is empowered by the five syllables known as Oṃ, Hūṃ, Svā, Āḥ, and Hā, which are the nature of the five families of Body, Mind, and Vajra, beginning with the Body-vajra.
