Because there is no distinction between the mantra and the deity, she is empowered by these five syllables alone, whose forms are those of the deities;
she is encircled by a true radiance that pervades the three worlds.
[She is seated upon] an eight-petaled lotus emanated from the syllable *HŪṂ*, which has a multicolored pericarp formed by the syllable *ĀḤ*.

Her limbs are empowered by the five [families]. Among them, that which is called the Body-Vajra family is the Delusion family; the Mind-Vajra family is the Hatred family; and by the inclusion of the first [term], the Jewel family is likewise [included].

69.0 [22a2-3] Having thus observed that very [nature], which has reached five stages through instruction and the stimulation of the seed-rays, and which is internalized, he asks: "In what state should one initiate delight? To this, he says: "The existent," and so forth.
"[One whose] own body is of the nature of the outflow of true wisdom and consists of skillful means..."
"The mantra practitioner should begin the rati [sexual union], thinking: 'I am pleasing the Sugatas.

(69) And she is "Satī" because, through her intention of great compassion (*mahākṛpābhisandhi*), she possesses all aspects; and she is "Wisdom" (*prajñā*) because she is the nature of unsurpassed liberation, and thus there is no further excellence beyond her. Alternatively, she is Satī by virtue of having the form of the nine goddesses which symbolize the ninefold maturation. For this very reason, she is the female principle endowed with means (*upāya*).

69.2 And that true wisdom is the *vidyā* of the causal Vajrasattva; the practitioner (*mantrin*) whose own body is of the nature of its outflow (*niḥsyanda*) and serves as the means (*upāya*) is "such" (*tathā*).
69.3 It is through such a practice of profound and vast forms—which serves as the basis for the complete accomplishment of the welfare of both oneself and others—that all the Tathāgatas are pleased.
69'.0 Regarding that, he states the mantra which is the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the yoga of pleasing them, beginning with *oṃ*.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra that impassions all Tathāgatas.
By this much of the text, the first meditative absorption (samādhi) called the Initial Yoga has been explained. Now,

in order to explain another fourfold set of limbs of service (*sevā*) along with their results— such as the natural outflow (*niḥsyanda*)— which are common to all deities yet distinguished by a superior degree through the power of specific knowledge, he describes the Meditative Absorption of the Supreme King of Mandalas according to the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), beginning with "In the moon at the heart," etc., [referring to] "by the rays of the mantra in the moon at the heart."
Having caused the entire assembly of Buddhas to enter,
[he visualizes] the stainless form of the Excellent Mind, emerging from the *hūṃ*-vajra and abiding within the lotus. (70)

70.1 [22a6-7] The "moon-mantra of the heart" refers to the syllable *maṃ* situated upon a moon disk located in the center of the symbol (the *viśvavajra*) which rests upon the moon in the heart of the Jñānasattva. Having caused the entire assembly of Buddhas to enter into oneself by means of its radiance through the mouth, and having meditated on [them] as being born from one's own heart in the form of all the members of one's own maṇḍala—for the sake of the welfare of the world—one should, with a steady mind, emit [them]. This is the connection [of the sentence]. By means of the syllable *hūṃ*, the vajra is the "Hūṃ-vajra."

Having emerged through that path, it is stainless and takes the form of the excellent mind; this is the bodhicitta born from the transformation of the assembly of Buddhas who have been caused to enter. "Residing within the lotus" means residing within the interior of the goddess’s lotus. Having meditated [on it] as having issued from one's own heart in the form of all one's own maṇḍala deities...
"Thus, with a steady mind, one should emit [the bodhicitta] for the sake of the welfare of the world.

(71) Having meditated on that very bodhicitta as having arisen in the form of all the members of one's own mandala through the process of transformation from the syllable *maṃ*—which is the aforementioned "own heart"—one should emit it according to the method to be described. The meaning is that one should cause it to issue forth from the mandala within the womb of the goddess’s lotus in order to place it within the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*).
72.0 [22b2] He states that very procedure for the relinquishment, beginning with "having exhorted," etc.:
"Having exhorted Cittavajra as 'Vajradhrk'— the one who accomplishes the supreme welfare of the worlds."
[He is] white on the left and red on the other [side], [with the color of a sapphire].

(72) Cittavajra Akṣobhya, endowed with the aforementioned specific attributes, like the Primordial One, is possessed of arms holding the vajra and other implements (as in 73a). Having been exhorted by the mantra "Vajradhrk" and awakened in its true sense, one should dissolve him and establish him within oneself (as in 73c–d).
The meaning, however, is this: the mind that does not take an object and which abides in its own nature is called Vajradhṛk. As it has been said:
"The five *hetis* and the *vetis* are designated as 'vajra';
'dhṛk' is known as 'holding'; thus the mind is Vajradhṛk, the holder of the vajra of consciousness."
(Guhyasamājatantra 18.40).

And its meaning is as follows: because the five causes—consisting of transformation (*pariṇāma*), intention (*abhisaṃdhi*), and so forth—are applied as the respective causes for the establishment of the afflicted (*sāṃkleśika*) and purified (*vaiyavadānika*) states, and because the conceptualization of the five states beginning with form (*rūpa*) occurs through the conventional designation of phenomena (*dharmasaṃketaka*), they are called the "five causes. In relation to those, because they are applied as the nature of the results, the five results are designated by the names "mirror" (*ādarśa*) and so forth.

And all this culminates in the nature of gnosis; thus, because it possesses the common characteristic of being unimpeded due to its luminous essence, consciousness (*vijñāna*)—which appears as the perceived object and so forth—is "indestructible" (*vajra*). And by virtue of sustaining that [gnosis], it is "that which sustains" (*taddhṛk*). The mind (*manas*) is, in reality, the resonance of that [consciousness], a cognition established in its own intrinsic nature.

72.3 Alternatively, "heti" means cause (*hetu*), as before; "veti" means fruit (*phala*). The five prongs of the vajra consist of the five Buddhas. These very [prongs], through their upper and lower arrangement, are the forms of the purity of cause and fruit. One who holds that vajra is Vajradhṛk, whose nature is the purity of the dharmadhātu, and he is precisely the mind.
... [Endowed with arms] like those of Paramādya...
the wise one, having withdrawn [them] into himself...
"One should cause [him] to enter with one's entire being" (sarvabhāvena).

"Having withdrawn" (*saṃhṛtya*) means that the wise one, possessing the intention to fulfill the [meditative] forms, should—by withdrawing the manner of the previously manifested radiation—bring [the deity] back and cause him to enter into oneself in the form of Mañjuśrī. Alternatively, it means being free from the grasping of the entered and the enterer.
"Jinajig" refers to Kāyavajra.

Having exhorted him... one should likewise meditate upon Kāyavajra-Vairocana, characterized as previously described, marked with the signs of the wheel and so forth—that is, distinguished by the wheel, sword, lotus, and jewel. "Likewise" means that, having exhorted him with the general mantra *Cittavajra-jinajig*, one should meditate upon him in the center of the moon within the previously mentioned lotus.

74.2 Here too, *saṃcodana* (incitement) is, in fact, *sambodhana* (awakening). The meaning, moreover, is this: in reality, the mind (*manas*) is called *jig* because it has transcended the grasped object and so forth; and it is called *jina* because it is inconceivable due to being free from the four extremes, such as existence and non-existence. As it has been said: "The body of all sentient beings is beyond existence, non-existence, and the middle; it arises from the primary elements and their derivatives. It is *jig* because it is the victor over all, and *jina* because it is the progenitor."

(Guhyasamājatantra 18.41) Existence (*sat*) is being (*bhāva*); non-existence (*asat*) is the absence of that. The middle between those two—existence and non-existence—is beyond them because it is inconceivable. What is that? It is that which, by way of having the form of the appropriated primary elements and their derivatives, is reckoned as a sentient being (*sattva*); which, due to its predominance, takes on the form of a specific [object]; and which, due to being moistened by delusion, has an insentient nature. Furthermore, that which is not appropriated—such as walls and the like—is "possibility" (*sambhava*), because it exists in that form; it is what is denoted by the word "body" (*vigraha*). In reality, the mind is indeed without an object (*anālambana*); because it conquers the graspable and so forth, it is "conqueror" (*jina*), and because it is inconceivable, it is the "Victorious One" (*jina*).

74.3 Alternatively, [the body] is that which transcends existence, non-existence, and the middle, being free from conceptual constructions such as "existence" and so forth; its nature is the purity of the mirror-like form of the primary elements and their derivatives. That very thing is the "body" (*vigraha*), namely the *ālayavijñāna* of all sentient beings. This is called *jinajik*. He states the meaning of the word *jina* itself: "generation is *jina*. By the word *jina*, birth is expressed. Because it conquers (*jayati*) that [birth], it is *jinajik*. The meaning is that it does not arise with an imagined nature. To the right is Ratneśa, who holds jewels and has the appearance of a youth through his faces.
The six beautiful hands [are adorned] with emerald jewels and other ornaments resembling molten gold. || 75 ||

75.1 “With faces like those of a youth” means that with his right, left, and middle faces—which are blue, white, and yellow—he is equal to Mañjuśrī. “With six hands as beautiful as refined gold, emeralds, jewels, and so forth” means that his face resembles pure gold and his six hands are adorned by an emerald, a sword, a lotus, a wheel, and the embrace of Prajñā. Having exhorted [the practitioner] with the mantra “Ratneśa, Ratnasambhava, Ratnadhṛk,” one should meditate on him to the right of Mañjuvajra; this is the connection.

75.2 Here too, the invocation is exactly the same. As for the meaning, that very non-conceptual mind (*manas*), when characterized by the qualifiers to be mentioned, is called Ratnadhṛk. As it has been said:
"The mind is renowned as 'jewel' because it arises from all objects; the object of cognition, which is to be known without a knower, is sensation—the jewel-bearing mind. (Guhyasamājatantra 18.42)

Thus, that mind which arises in all forms of objects—all of that is simply mind, as previously stated; it alone is the "jewel" (*ratna*) because of its preeminence and its priceless nature. Anticipating the doubt that there might be another [entity] distinct from it that perceives the self and so forth, he says: "without a perceiver. For this very reason, the jewel is merely sensation (*vedanā-mātra*). And because it maintains that state through inconceivable means (*upāya*), it is "that-bearer" (*tad-dhṛk*). In another sense, the mind itself is established in its own essential nature.

Alternatively, "with all objects" (*sarvārthaiḥ*) refers to that equanimity which arises from all objects; the very mind produced by that is the jewel. And because it cannot otherwise be established, it is to be known by the experiencer through self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*); thus, the mind purified of sensation is called the "bearer of the jewel.
"*Ārolig*" means that his two faces are like a lotus, reddened by passion (*rāga*).
To the west, one should meditate on Amitābha of blazing radiance, whose hands bear the marks of the lotus and so forth—[verse 76].

"Red like the color of a lotus" means as crimson as rubies (*padmarāga*). "His two faces are likewise" means that his right and left faces are blue and white, respectively, just like those of the Youth (*Kumāra*). "Hands bearing the marks of the lotus and so forth" means his hands are distinguished by a red lotus, a sword, a wheel, and a jewel. Having exhorted him with the mantra "Amitābha Ujjvalaprabha Āroliṅ," one should meditate [him] to the west of Mañjuvajra; this is the meaning.

76.2 The exhortation here is as before. The meaning, however, is this: that very non-conceptual mind (*manas*), when endowed with the qualifiers to be mentioned, is called *ārolig*. And it has been said:

"In all respects, through every means, and in every way, the state of being characterized by the relationship between the object of definition (*lakṣya*) and the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)—that delight is the defining characteristic, and it is called *ārolig*."

(Guhyasamājatantra 18.43) Likewise, the "object" (*lakṣya*) is the domain of conceptual adherence (*abhiniveśa*); its "sign" (*cihna*) is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). By means of those states—that is, by way of that very nature—the particle *tu* has the sense of "consequently. Every entity exists in every manner, everywhere, and at all times, including the past and so forth; therefore, both the object being characterized and the characteristic itself [are established] solely through conceptual adherence. Or, by way of the form of the object, the mind itself, appearing in that form due to the initial state, is called *Ārolika*.

Alternatively, regarding the phrase "by way of the relationship between the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*"): the "characterized" refers to blue, yellow, and so forth; the "characteristic" is the determination thereof; and "state" (*bhāva*) is the mind in its sixth form of conceptualization. Therefore, in every respect, that delight which is the discernment of the welfare of sentient beings is indeed pure. That characteristic and the characterized mentioned immediately above is called *Ārolig*.
It has the luster of an emerald and is endowed with the excellence of the face and other features as previously described.
To the north, one should meditate on the one named Amoghasiddhi, who "holds wisdom" (*prajñādhṛk*) by means of a sword and other implements.

(77) "Having the luster of an emerald" means having a color similar to a green gem. "Endowed with the perfection of faces and so forth as before" means being possessed, as previously described, of the perfection of blue, white, right, and left faces, along with the emanation of various kinds of light rays. "By means of a sword and other implements" means being endowed with a sword, a wheel, a lotus, and a jewel. Having exhorted Amoghasiddhi as "holding wisdom," one should meditate on him to the north of Mañjughoṣa (cf. 74d).

77.2 The exhortation here is likewise the same. That very mind is called "possessing wisdom" (*prajñādhṛk*) by way of another classification. As it has been said: "That consciousness which is produced through excellence is called 'wisdom' (*prajñā*);
that which is sustained by volitional formations and intention is termed 'possessing wisdom' (*prajñādhṛk*)."

Because it is a mere appearance and lacks the characteristics of external objects, the second and subsequent consciousnesses, in relation to the first arising, are said to be "supreme" due to their excellence. Therefore, that very same consciousness, when maintained by the volition of formative impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced from such a continuous stream, is called "the holder of wisdom" (*prajñādhṛk*).

Alternatively, "cognition produced by excellence" refers to that cognition in the form of the performance of duties (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna*) which is produced through the excellence of the practice of loving-kindness, compassion, and so forth; this is called *prajñā*. That which sustains it—the mind purified of mental formations and volitions—is called *prajñādhṛk* (the sustainer of wisdom).
These Buddhas are to be understood as having these pure qualities.
Regarding all of them, he states the common qualifiers beginning with "delightful" (*rucirā*), and so on.
Adorned with excellent crests of beautiful matted hair and ornaments blazing with the luster of various jewels,
their bodies are presided over by the Vidyās.
All [deities] are to be meditated upon as seated upon sun-maṇḍalas.

They are described as such because they possess beautiful matted-hair crowns (*jaṭāmukuṭa*) and are radiant with ornaments shining with the light of various supreme jewels. Regarding the phrase "their bodies are accompanied by the Vidyā," this means those whose bodies are "accompanied" (*sanātha*), that is, favored, by their own Wisdom (*prajñā*) embraced by the Vidyā. The word "all" implies that even those whose seats have not been explicitly mentioned are to be meditated upon as seated on sun-maṇḍalas. However, since for Vairocana a moon-seat has been specifically prescribed, there is no possibility of him being seated on a sun-maṇḍala.
And thus is the convention of those who know the science of grammar: "Rules prescribed in a general manner are superseded by rules prescribed in a specific manner.
[In this case,] the goddess Locanā is to be situated in the region of the southeast, [as it is said: "One should be deluded at Moharati."
Residing upon the orb of the full moon, she is the supreme Śṛṅgārakāyavajrābhā (Radiant with the Body-Vajra of Passion).

(79) "Supreme" means she is preeminent by virtue of having the nature of the stages of *kṛpā* (compassion), *kṣiti* (morality), *upāya* (skillful means), and *dūraṅgamā* (the Far-Reaching). "Radiant with the Body-Vajra of Passion" means she is adorned with the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of passion; through her face and other features, she resembles Vairocana. Residing upon the full moon, the goddess Locanā—being the delight of delusion (*moharati*)—should be situated in the region of the southeast due to being impelled by the mantra.

79.2 The exhortation here is also as before. Delusion (*moha*) is the ego-conception regarding cognition (*jñāna-ahaṃkāra*), arising from the union with cognitions whose forms appear as duality and so forth. As it has been said: "Ego-conception regarding the phenomena of non-dual gnosis is called delusion" (*Guhyasamājatantra* 18.50ab).
Thus [it is said].

79.3 Alternatively, the egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) that consists in the conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding one's own nature within those things whose form is non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*) by virtue of their true nature (*dharmatā*), is called delusion (*moha*) because it has a limited form.

79.4 Since there is no possibility of differentiation even in terms of the forms of delusion and so forth within delusion and the rest, there is delight (*rati*) which is of a unitary form and has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). And it is said:

"Rati is ultimate enjoyment" (Guhyasamājatantra 18.51c). It is "ultimate" because it attains the nature of the desired compassion and so forth; it is "enjoyment" (*bhoga*) because it is correct (*samyak*), being free from error.
In the southwest corner is Lāsyā, like Citteśvara... Māmakī, who is intensely eager for the great passion known as "delight in hatred," is to be meditated upon.

(80) The meaning is that she is so called because she is supremely eager for the great passion (*mahārata*) which is the attachment to the welfare of sentient beings; Māmakī, whose nature is the mountain-like water of the vow of loving-kindness (*maitrīpraṇidhi*), is exhorted as "Delight in Hatred" and is to be meditated upon in the southwest corner.
80.2 The exhortation is as before. Hatred (*dveṣa*) is indeed the aversion toward the apprehended object and the apprehending subject. As it has been said:
"The mutual friction therein is designated as hatred" (*Guhyasamājatantra* 18.50cd).

And this is the reasoning regarding the non-application of gnosis (*jñāna*), because when there is friction or shattering of the duality, hatred exists in mutual dependence. For instance, the negation of the apprehended object depends upon consciousness, and the negation of consciousness depends upon the absence of that [object].
80.3 Alternatively, that which is the mutual friction of the non-dual form is itself hatred (*dveṣa*).
80.4 And passion (*rati*) is as before.
[She is] Vāgīśā of pure body.
"Delight in passion" is in the direction of the wind;
there, the atom known as Pāṇḍarā [is to be meditated upon as possessing immeasurable jewels of qualities]. 81

81.1 She whose body is stainless like that of Vāgīśa is "thus" (tathā). This means she possesses a pure body of red color and so forth. The term *paramān* refers to the one named Pāṇḍarā, who is supreme because she is the nature of the purity of joy (*muditā*), splendor, power, and goodness; having the form described above, she is called "one who delights in passion" (*rāgarati*) and, being thus exhorted, is to be meditated upon in the direction of the wind.
81.2 Here too, the exhortation is as before. Passion (*rāga*) is the mode of intense attachment. As it has been said: "The characteristic of passion is attachment."
(Guhyasamājatantra 18.51a).
Thus, "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to passion (*rāga*) in the form of attachment (*abhiniveśa*). Another synonym for this very [passion] is "clinging" (*āsakti*).
Alternatively, that which is the characteristic whose nature is clinging, having the aspect of non-duality (*advaya*), that alone is passion.
81.4 Here too, the passion (*rati*) is as before. Tārā, whose essential nature is like that of Ratneśa, is exhorted as Vajrarati.
In the northeastern direction...
she is to be visualized. 82.

82.1 [23a6-7]: "Having the nature of Ratneśa" means that she is equal to Ratnasambhava in terms of color and other attributes; Tārā, whose form is the purity of the perfection of equanimity, the wind-element, and the Dharma-megha stage, and who is characterized by the aforementioned qualities, is exhorted as Vajrarati and is to be visualized in the northeastern direction.
82.2 The exhortation is as before. Knowledge devoid of the specific afflictions such as delusion (*moha*) and so forth is called "vajra" because of its non-obstruction.
82.3 Alternatively, that very knowledge of an indivisible nature which was just mentioned is called "vajra.
82.4 Regarding the explanation of the second [category] beginning with delusion, there are these four [types of] delusion and so forth.
"Rati" refers to ultimate enjoyment;
it should be understood as occurring in one place.
82.5 Here too, the delight is as before.
83.0 He states their primary signs, beginning with "saccakra" and so forth: *saccakra... [red lotus].
The mudras are a lotus, a yellow water-lily, and the remaining ones are taught to be like their respective lords. 83

83.1 “The remaining” means that for Locanā, the remaining emblems are the sword, the lotus, and the jewel; likewise for Māmakī. For Pāṇḍarā, however, they are the sword, the wheel, and the jewel; and for Tārā, they are the sword, the lotus, and the jewel—this is the meaning.
They should be placed in the four corners of the maṇḍala and on both sides of the main entrance.
"The Vajra goddesses of form and so forth are like the body and so forth by way of the three principles.
Regarding the words "maṇḍala" and so forth: those six goddesses, Form and the rest, are respectively like Body-Vajrā and the others.

84.2 “By means of the three *tattvas*”—the meaning is that, having offered with the mantra *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*, one should meditate upon them according to the ritual procedure as possessing their primary symbols, such as the mirror and so forth, which will be described below.

84.3 In this context, Kāyeśa is Vairocana; Rūpavajrā, who is similar to him, has the mirror as her symbol, along with the remaining symbols of the sword, lotus, and jewel. She is the nature of the purity of the sense-field of form (*rūpāyatana*), the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), and the [Bhūmi] Pramuditā. Śabdavajrā likewise possesses the symbol of the sense-field of sound (*śabdāyatana*) and the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
84.4 All these goddesses are to be understood as being of the nature of purity (*viśuddhisvabhāva*).

85.0 Now, for the yogin who possesses faith—characterized by the desire for grace through the conditions of action, which have as their causes existence, possession of qualities, and capability—there occurs, by means of wisdom relying on reasoning and scripture, the planting of the roots of merit conducive to liberation, such as faith and so forth. This is for the purpose of entering into the knowledge that is entirely secluded from the manifold world; it pertains to the objects of the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) regarding the body and so forth, and becomes increasingly firm through practice, being free from the four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).

He describes the four gatekeepers, such as Yamārya, who perform acts of protection, summoning, and so forth through meanings corresponding to the welfare of sentient beings— such as being the remover of the obstructions of the outflows consisting of lack of faith, laziness, forgetfulness, distraction, faulty wisdom, and wrong views, and having the nature of great delusion and the like— with the words beginning with "In the east," etc.: "In the eastern gate is known [Yamārya],
who has the terrifying appearance of infinite [beings] turning away from all hopes."
"In the radiant one, Yamāntaka has a shadow like that of a mass of fierce clouds at the time of destruction.

(85) This means that his infinite, terrifying radiations revolve in all directions; thus it is so. Furthermore, it means that he possesses a shadow identical to that of the orb—the collection—of the fierce clouds belonging to the "destruction," which is the time of universal dissolution (*pralaya*); thus it is so.
By means of the manifold fierce family-radiations issuing from the body of the Equal One, the Sovereign King of Mind,
he is the destroyer of Yama, the son of Vivasvat.

The glorious one, whose body ornaments consist of fierce serpents, is the Sovereign of Mind, Akṣobhya. His body, which is identical to that of Yamāntaka in its faces and other features, is characterized by the radiance of numerous fierce families of deities who have issued forth from it. He is so described because fierce and wrathful serpents serve as his bodily ornaments; he is "glorious" (*śrīmān*) because he attains all goals. Being such, he is the "Ender of Yama, the Son of Vivasvat"; thus exhorted as "Yamāntakṛt," the meaning is that he is to be meditated upon at the eastern gate.

86.2 The exhortation here is also as before. Yama is of the nature of skillful means (*upāya*) because he is fixed upon the welfare of sentient beings; and he is of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*) because he brings about an end by destroying the afflictions (*kleśa*). Thus it has been said:
"Phenomena are of an indestructible nature by virtue of their unborn essence;
he is the *samaya* (commitment) of all things, and for that very reason, he is Yama, the bringer of the end."

(Guhyasamājatantra 18.53). This is the meaning: for one possessed of faith, through the clear comprehension (*samprajanya*) arising from the commitment (*samaya*) of practicing the performance of the welfare of others, there occurs a gradual realization of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) as they become condensed into their objective spheres and take on a purified form. Because phenomena are unarisen due to their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), the knowledge of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatājñāna*) is, in reality, of the nature of non-knowledge; thus it consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*). It is wrathful because it serves as the antidote to grasping.

The form of the deity arises from the consolidation and firmness of the state of being well-disposed toward the welfare of sentient beings. He is *Yama* because he restrains the welfare of sentient beings; and he is the "End-maker" (*antakṛt*) because he destroys the afflictions.
Alternatively, he is the "End-maker of Yama"—that is, of the nature of necessity—because his illusory form brings an end to that necessity.

Or else, *Yamāntakṛt* refers to the purification of the fetter of hatred and its hater. Adorned with the eight nāgas beginning with Ananta, which represent the purification of the nature of the fetter of ignorance and delusion, he is the primary wrathful being whose essence is the purification of delusion itself. As the very antidote, he is the "End-maker" of ordinary delusion. Thus it has been said:

Delusion, through the enjoyment of delusion, becomes the exhaustion of delusion; he who has brought an end to Yama becomes the end-maker of the body, and by that very means, he becomes the end-maker of all objects of knowledge.

(Guhyasamājatantra 18.58). This is the meaning: because there is no object of knowledge through investigation, it is non-knowledge; yet, since it takes the form of the knowledge of reality, it is "delusion" (*moha*) due to its association with the characteristic of delusion. And because it is the antidote to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in this way, it has the form of "wrath" (*krodha*). The others as well have delusion as their root.

Delusion consists of the eight fetters (*saṃyojana*). They are called "fetters" because they bind one to various forms of suffering. They are as follows: the fetter of aversion (*pratigha*), the fetter of attachment (*anunaya*), the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā*), the fetter of pride (*māna*), the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā*), the fetter of avarice (*mātsarya*), the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi*), the fetter of grasping (*parāmarṣa*), and the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā*).

Regarding these, the fetter of aversion: it is "aversion" (*pratigha*) because one is struck or repelled by it; that very thing is the "fetter," thus forming a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). This same analysis of the compound should be understood for the fetter of attachment and the others as well.

The fetter of attachment (*anunayasaṃyojana*): "attachment" (*anunaya*) is that by which one is attached; it is passion (*rāga*) characterized by clinging to the three realms. The fetter of ignorance (*avidyāsaṃyojana*): ignorance (*avidyā*) is lack of knowledge; its synonyms are darkness, stupor, and delusion (*moha*). As it has been said:

"Ignorance is non-comprehension regarding the [four] truths, the [three] jewels, actions, and their fruits; it is the perception of a self in the aggregates and so forth, which are not-self; and it consists of passion and the other [afflictions]. (Mahāyānalakṣaṇasamuccaya §4a, 297b2, 146a4-6)

Thus [it is said]. The fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*): that by which one thinks is "pride" (*māna*). It is of seven kinds, namely: pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*), the pride of "I am" (*asmimāna*), overweening pride (*abhimāna*), the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*), and false pride (*mithyāmāna*). In this context, pride is that which, regarding those who are inferior in qualities such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, thinks "I am superior," or regarding those who are equal, thinks "I am not equal"—that pride which, having taken those causes imagined through qualities as its basis, is the conceit, the act of conceiving, and the state of being puffed up. This sevenfold pride is called the "fetter of pride."
The fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) is mental resentment; it is a distress of mind preceded by an inability to endure the prosperity of others.
The fetter of avarice (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*) is the grasping of the mind. As it has been said:
"Avarice (*matsara*) is the thought, 'May this object not go from me to another'; the state of such a person is avarice (*mātsarya*). (untraced)

The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭisaṃyojana*) consists of three views: namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Regarding these, the "receptivity based upon [them]" and so forth is as explained previously. False view refers to one who denies either the truth of origination, the truth of suffering, the truth of the path, or nirvāṇa; the "receptivity based upon that" and so forth is as explained previously. Thus, these three views constitute the fetter of views.

The fetter of clinging (*parāmarṣa-saṃyojana*) consists of two types of clinging: namely, clinging to views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*) and clinging to rules and observances (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*). Therein, "clinging to views" means that one clings to [wrong] views. It is, as before, the acceptance (*kṣānti*) and so forth based on regarding the five aggregates of grasping (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) as foremost, supreme, distinguished, and preeminent. "Clinging to rules and observances" means that one clings to moral conduct and ascetic vows.

For one who perceives the five aggregates of clinging as pure, as liberation, and as leading to transcendence, there arises—based on that—the patience [of certainty], and so forth, as previously described.

Regarding the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*): doubting is doubt, which is indecision regarding the [Four] Truths. As it has been said: "Hostility, attachment, ignorance, pride, envy, and avarice..."
Wrong view, adherence to views, and doubt—these are the nine [unwholesome roots].
Thus [it is said].

And regarding these fetters (*saṃyojana*), their enjoyment consists in the observation of their intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) through investigation, because they are not joined [to reality] when analyzed; it consists in the movement toward objects as being for the sake of another, because they are joined [to the self] through the pursuit of worldly aims.

As for the transference of the object: because sentient beings are infinite, through the power of great compassion and wisdom over infinite time, there is an infinity of hatred arising from the faults of perversion, such as the afflictions and cognitive obstructions of all infinite sentient beings, and from the superimposition of infinite qualities and cognitions. For this very reason, it is black.

Great passion, characterized by attachment to the welfare of the entire world without exception, is *anunaya* (affectionate attachment); that itself is Takṣaka; therefore, he is red. Ignorance (*avidyā*) is at the end, as before, being Yamāntaka in the form of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*); and that has already been explained. However, he is black by way of his intolerance for perversions.

Egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and pride (*māna*) are the elevation toward all sentient beings through [the realization of] equality. That very [pride], by virtue of being the seed of stainless gnosis and through great wisdom (*mahāprajñā*), is the white *Mahāpadma*. Envy (*īrṣyā*) is the green *Kārkoṭaka*, because it is profound in its activity; it consists in the application of attributing the qualities of unsurpassed gnosis—which are not shared with others—to the world through intolerance of worldly qualities that are contrary to the supramundane.

*Matsara*: "May all defects—which are imagined by others as belonging to oneself—depart from me, the source of non-delusion (*mā-viparyāsa*). Thus, because he brings about the prosperity of the universe (*viśva*) within all lineages (*viśvakuleṣu*), the Kulika is one whose color is the universe (*viśvavarṇa*).

The view that there exists a self which is the immediate cause for the welfare of others within this *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* is the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). The two extremes are existence and non-existence; by refuting them through inconceivable means, one causes sentient beings to grasp at the perfection of bliss—this is [the function of the view]. Alternatively, because it acts as a destroyer regarding the two extremes, it is like a "grasping" (*graha*); a view consisting of this nature is the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). The view whose aspect is that "there is no self, sentient being, and so forth," or "there is no grasped object, grasper, arising, and so forth," is the false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

And these three views are the yellow Śaṅkhapāla, because they are gladdened by great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) through the removal of the stains of the self, cause of suffering, and so forth, and by the accomplishment of the nourishment of the qualities of gnosis (*jñāna*).

For those who desire purity by any means whatsoever, there is the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), because—by means of the three vehicles corresponding to their spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and through the conventional reality of yogins (*yogisaṃvṛtti*) which is bound to the cultivation within one's own continuum—they are constantly joined to the welfare of the world with the joy of the enjoyment of stainless bliss that is awakening. And these two fetters (*saṃyojana*) are the white Vāsuki.

Because he cuts through the doubts of those who are uncertain due to a lack of correct understanding regarding the jewels of the Truths and other matters, and because he administers the medicinal treatment of the nectar-like medicine of knowledge—which is the antidote to the various diseases of the afflictions by distinguishing them from resentment and other faults—he is Vicikitsā-sita-padma (the White Lotus of Doubt).
For this very reason, he has cruel serpents as his ornaments.

Furthermore, he states "Kṣayamoha" (Destruction of Delusion) to show that the destruction of ordinary delusion occurs in this manner. Thus, when the causes for the influx of similar births—which consist of ordinary delusion—are removed through discernment, its destruction is the state [of liberation].

"Ending the body" (*kāyāntakṛt*) refers to the "body" (*kāya*) as the accumulation of the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); this is indicated by the term's figurative sense. Furthermore, because it consists in the vision of selflessness through investigation in the form of an antidote to the Māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*), it is called "ending.

It is also "ending" because it brings an end to the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the [obscurations] of application, etc., since it takes the form of a deity and serves as the basis for purity and so forth.
What is that obscuration? What are purity and the rest? (From the *Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya*, ad loc.)
Lack of application, that which is directed toward what is not a proper sphere or not according to the method, non-arising, lack of mental attention, and the incompleteness of the accumulations.
Lack of a spiritual friend and lineage, weariness of the mind,
lack of application in practice, and dwelling among base and wicked people.

One's own functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*) and the state of being incomplete with respect to the three [trainings] constitute the immaturity of wisdom; furthermore, there is inherent functional rigidity, indolence, and negligence.
Attachment to existence and to enjoyments, as well as a mind that is despondent,
lack of faith, lack of resolute conviction, and investigating according to the literal meaning.
Lack of respect for the true Dharma, excessive concern for gain, likewise meanness, loss of what has been heard, meager learning, and lack of cultivation through meditative concentration.
This is the obscuration. What are "the auspicious" and so forth? The auspicious, awakening, formal undertaking, intelligence, non-delusion, and non-obstruction. (Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya ad loc.)
In this regard, there is no envy on their part, and they possess mastery as well as virtue and the other qualities.

Regarding these [qualities] such as the wholesome and so forth, it is asked: which ones are to be known as the obscurations of which? It is said: "Indeed, three and three are to be known as the obscurations of these. (Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya ad loc.)

(Madhyāntavibhāga 2.10ab) There are three obstacles to the harvest of the wholesome: lack of confidence in the person, lack of resolute belief in the Dharma, and investigating the meaning according to the literal expression. There are three obstacles to non-stinginess: lack of respect for the true Dharma, respect for gain, honor, and worship, and a lack of compassion for sentient beings. There are three obstacles to mastery—by which one does not attain sovereignty: the ruin of what has been heard due to the performance of karma that leads to the ruin of the Dharma, having little learning, and the lack of cultivation of meditative concentration.

Furthermore, regarding this obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) with respect to the wholesome and so forth, there are ten types of causes for an object (*artha*), as follows: (1) the cause of transformation (*pariṇatikāraṇa*), such as goldsmiths and others in the transformation of gold and other materials into the form of bracelets and so forth; (2) the cause of conviction (*sampratyayakāraṇa*), such as smoke and so forth for fire and so forth; (3) the cause of communication (*sampratyāyanakāraṇa*), such as a logical reason (*hetu*) for a thesis (*pratijñā*); (4) the cause of attainment (*prāptikāraṇa*), such as the path and so forth for nirvāṇa and so forth.

Thus, the cause of arising (*utpatti-kāraṇa*) is to be seen in relation to the wholesome (*śubha*), because it is that which is to be produced. The cause of duration (*sthiti-kāraṇa*) is in relation to awakening (*bodhi*), because it is unshakable. The cause of support (*dhṛti-kāraṇa*) is in relation to formal undertaking (*samādāna*), because it serves as the basis for the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*). The cause of manifestation (*prakāśana-kāraṇa*) is in relation to sovereignty (*tva*), because its characteristic is the attainment of mastery (*vibhutva*). The causes are tenfold with respect to arising, duration, support, manifestation, transformation, separation, alteration, cognition, effort, and attainment. The eye, food, the earth, a lamp, fire, and so forth, are cited as examples thereof.
The sickle, knowledge of craftsmanship, smoke, the cause, the path, and so forth are other [examples].

One who desires to attain awakening must first of all generate roots of virtue. Then, through the empowerment of the strength of those roots of virtue, awakening is to be attained. Furthermore, the foundation for that generation of virtue is the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*). With regard to that thought of awakening, one should—possessing a mind free from fear and perceiving the qualities in phenomena—extensively proclaim those phenomena to others.

Then that Bodhisattva, having thus attained the acquisition of the power of various virtues, quickly realized unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and attained mastery over all phenomena. This is the sequence of the [perfections] beginning with virtue. (Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya, ad loc.)

The deity’s status as the locus of auspiciousness and so forth should be understood through the nature of the firmness of this superimposition (*āropa*). First, the purification of this cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is explained; for, through its purification, there is the abandonment of the cognitive obscuration preceded by the abandonment of the afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and likewise, there is the abandonment of the obscuration of birth preceded by the abandonment of the obscuration of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*), according to the principle that "birth [results] from karma. Regarding the term *bhāsvatī* (as seen in 85c), she is said to be—meaning she is declared—to be situated at the eastern gate within the solar mandala (as seen in 85a). The meaning is that she is to be visualized there.
The one who stands at the gate of the southern direction is Prajñāntakṛt, the unsurpassed light,
possessing arms and other features like those of Kāyeśa.
*[Ugra, Aparājita, Prasabha] || 87.1 “Dakṣiṇā” and so forth. 87.2 Because he dispels the darkness of delusion in the world, he is the unsurpassed light.
87.3 Like that, Kāyeśa is Vairocana; he is fierce by virtue of his arms, faces, and colors.
87.4 Because he cannot be overcome by the Māras of the afflictions (kleśamāra), he is Aparājita. "Prasabha" means one whose form is exceedingly violent.

87.5 This is the meaning: [he is] with a frowning face, a mouth formidable with fangs, and a face smiling like an opened lotus; with a large, hard, and fleshy belly, thighs, and chest; with a lolling tongue and short, stout limbs and members; with flaming tawny beard and hair standing erect; and with moving, round eyes that have the brilliance of the sun with its blazing rays. And this qualification, as an indication of fierce wrath, should also be applied to Yamāntaka and the others.
87.6 Being thus exhorted as "the Maker of the End of Wisdom" (*Prajñāntakṛt*), he is to be visualized at the radiant southern gate.

87.7 The exhortation here is also as before. The meaning, however, is explained: *prajñā* (wisdom) is so called because its nature is supreme knowledge (*prakṛṣṭajñāna*), and it is the "end-maker" (*antakṛt*) because it brings an end to the crop of afflictions (*saṃkleśa*). Thus it has been said:

"Phenomena whose nature is non-cognition are, by virtue of their purity as the supreme syllable, the commitment (*samaya*) of all minds; therefore, the Victor is the 'Wisdom-End-Maker' (*prajñāntakṛt*)."
(Guhyasamājatantra 18.54). Thus:

that which is projected by faith (*śraddhā*)—in the form of conviction (*sampratyaya*) regarding signs such as existence—and which has the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) as its object, is the "factor conducive to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*). As it becomes increasingly firm, it takes on the nature of door and doorkeeper through the relationship of object and subject (*ālambya-ālambaka*). Through constant and devoted application, it is called "the wealth of becoming," and so forth. The remainder is as before. Furthermore, wisdom (*prajñā*) brings an end to the ultimate limit, and he is the "Victorious One" (*jina*) because all adversaries of affliction have been conquered. Therefore, he is called "Unconquered" (*aparājita*).

Alternatively, because he is the embodiment of the purification of hatred, he is called the "End-maker of Passion" (*kāmāsravāntakṛt*) and the "End-maker of Wisdom" (*prajñāntakṛt*). This is due to his wearing the ornaments of the *nāgas* as before to represent the purification of ordinary hatred, and because he serves as the antidote to the other fetters (*saṃyojana*), as well as the afflictions of the outflows of passion (*kāma-āsrava*), the views of grasping at extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), and the other defilements. As it has been said:

"The fault [of hatred] is destroyed by the experience of that very fault; thus, one whose faults are exhausted is the 'End-maker of Wisdom. By that means, one becomes the 'End-maker of Mind,' and likewise the 'End-maker of Afflictions.'"

(Guhyasamājatantra 18.59). This is the meaning: because there is no desire for knowledge and the object of knowledge, lack of joy is a fault due to its incompatibility with analytical investigation. Or, regarding the afflictions (*kleśa*) which harm sentient beings, that very same fault is anger (*krodha*), as previously stated; furthermore, other [faults] characterized by that, such as those which corrupt the body and so forth, are faults—namely, the eight fetters (*saṃyojana*) beginning with delusion (*moha*). The enjoyment of these occurs through analytical investigation, and so forth, as before. Among those, the outflow of desire (*kāmāsrava*) has the nature of attachment (*saṅga*); it is "mind" (*citta*) because it is of the nature of consciousness.

That hatred (*dveṣa*) is pleasant, and through its enjoyment it becomes Akṣobhya, whose nature is great hatred. The meaning is that through the practice of perfectly pure non-hatred, one becomes Vajrāyate. Regarding "the fault of destruction" (*kṣayadoṣa*): he who brings about the destruction of the possibility of that very Akṣobhya entering into outward-directed hatred is called the Door-Overseer, Prajñāntakṛt. And for this reason, he is the "End-maker of the Mind" (*cittāntakṛt*): "mind" (*citta*) refers to that which perceives, consisting of the subject and so forth; he is the end-maker of that. Precisely because of this, he is the "End-maker" (*antakṛt*); since the afflictions have the subject as their cause, and Aparājita is the opposite of that.
*Hayakandharaḥ ... at the western gate ... [is] Padmāntakṛt ...
|| 88 || 88.1 Regarding "Hayakandhara" and so forth: "Like Vāgvajra as to arms and so on" (referring to 89a) means that he resembles Amitābha in terms of his arms, faces, and colors.

88.2 The summary meaning is as follows: Hayagrīva, possessing the aforementioned further qualifications, being thus exhorted as "the destroyer of the lotus," is to be meditated upon when the sun is situated at the western gate.

88.3 Here too, the exhortation is as before. The meaning, however, is this: mindfulness directed toward zeal and so forth, which has arisen from the realization of the nature of reality (*vastudharma*), is the "lotus" because it indicates purity. Just as this red lotus is not defiled by the stains of passion (*rāga*), so too is this mindfulness.
Thus, the pure triple world is [afflicted] by various defects of dwelling.
(Sarvabuddhasamāyogaḍākinījālaśaṃvara 5.66) Thus, because he brings an end to the afflictions and so forth, he is the "End-maker" (*antakṛt*). As it has been said:
"The phenomena are of an ineffable nature; they are the cognition of non-existence, namelessness, and formlessness."
He is the commitment (samaya) of all phenomena; therefore, the all-pervading Lord is Padmāntakṛt.

(Guhyasamājatantra 18.55). As before, faith draws forth vigor, which in turn draws forth mindfulness whose domain is the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). And that [mindfulness], becoming firm, serves as the door for the binding of the yogi’s mind to awakening by virtue of its nature as a gateway. This restraint through mindfulness is the *samaya*. Moreover, since this is the knowledge of others' minds according to the yogi’s conventional truth (*yogisamvṛtti*), how could there be any room for faults in oneself or others in reality (*tattvataḥ*)? In this way, there would be a binding of the mind to awakening. This too is a *samaya* because it operates everywhere.

Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is, in reality, non-knowledge because of the equality of conceptual afflictions (*vikalpakleśa*) occurring within one's own and others' continuums, and so forth, as previously explained. Likewise, this analytical observation is a "lotus" (*padma*) because it indicates purity; and it is "the end-maker" (*antakṛt*) because it brings an end to the afflictions and so forth. He is "all-pervading" (*vibhu*) because he has attained sovereignty through his mastery in dispelling distraction by means of the formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*).

Alternatively, since he brings an end to the extremes of substantiality, non-substantiality, and so forth—being of an ineffable nature—the Blessed One is designated as "the Lotus-End-Maker" (*Padmāntakṛt*).

Alternatively, because he is the nature of great passion (*mahārāga*) in the form of wrath, he brings an end—just as before—to ordinary passion and, by extension, to the other fetters (*saṃyojana*), such as the outflow of views (*dṛṣṭyāsrava*), death, and the conceptualization of objects; thus he is called Padmāntakṛt, the "End-maker of Passion. As it has been said:
"Passion, through the enjoyment of passion, becomes the destruction of passion; [therefore] he is Padmāntakṛt. By that means, he is Vāgāntakṛt, and likewise Samāpattyantakṛt."
(Guhyasamājatantra 18.60). "Attainment" (*samāpatti*) means consensus characterized by the relationship between object and subject; the meaning is "one who destroys that.
[He is] like Vāgvajra with respect to his arms and so forth.
[The two-faced Bhairava with a terrifying countenance,] [who causes the mountains to tremble with his roaring laughter,] [and the Lords of Sages. 89
90.0 He states the dismissal of Vighnāntaka: "Like Akṣobhya," and so forth.
[Vighnāntaka is] at the door, possessing a face and other features like those of Akṣobhya.
The heroic Āryāmṛtakuṇḍalin is fierce like the fire at the end of an eon;
he resembles Akṣobhya in his face, arms, and color.
90.2 Fierce like the fire at the time of universal dissolution.

90.3 The Noble Amṛtakuṇḍalin is "Noble" (*ārya*) because he has gone far away from, indeed at a great distance from, evil states. This qualification should also be understood as applying to Yamāntaka and the others, by way of illustration, for the purpose of dispelling the notion that their hostility is merely superimposed upon them as a form of anger.

90.4 Because he destroys all obstacles, he is a "Hero" (*vīra*). Being thus exhorted as the "End-maker of Obstacles," he is to be meditated upon in the radiant [deity] stationed at the northern gate; this is the meaning.

90.5 The exhortation here is also as before. The meaning, however, is this: he is the "End-maker" (*antakṛt*) because he brings an end to obstacles such as conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). As it has been said:
"Phenomena are non-conceptual by nature, for their state is inherently peaceful; therefore, he is the Lord who brings an end to obstacles, the pledge (*samaya*) of all vajras."
(Guhyasamājatantra 18.56).

Thus, the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) characterized by the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), which has the sense faculties and their objects as its domain, is projected by the previously mentioned mindfulness; becoming dense, when the form of the deity who is the adversary of distraction becomes manifest, there is no opportunity for the obstacle of distraction. And through the pacification of the obstacle of distraction, the pliancy (*prasrabdhi*) of the body and so forth arises, whereby the true bliss of the meditative absorption of wisdom and method is born; thus, this is "satisfying" (*toṣakara*). It is also the "pledge" (*samaya*) of all Vajras because it operates everywhere within meditative absorption.
And it is said: "Pure intellect, resembling the moon, is designated as the 'Vajra'."

Thus it is said [in an untraced classical source]: "For in this way, a property (*dharma*) to be grasped (*grāhya*) as the cause of differentiation is not tenable; because that [property] does not exist, the grasper (*grāhaka*) is also not [tenable], since [the mind] is the knowledge of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*). As long as there is no appearance of duality, there is no duality characterized by the grasped and the grasper other than the mind, due to its being devoid of unity and plurality, like a lotus in the sky. Likewise, because of the appearance of afflictions such as passion (*rāga*) or the appearance of wholesome qualities such as faith (*śraddhā*), there exists no afflicted passion or wholesome quality such as faith as a phenomenon distinct from the mind. Thus it has been said: 'The mind appears as a duality...'"

Just as it is accepted that there is an appearance of passion and so forth, or an appearance of faith and so forth, yet no afflicted or wholesome phenomenon exists [as a separate entity], [so too is the case for the mind]. (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 11.34)

For thus, because it lacks the characteristics of duality and is distinct from the appearance of duality, that mind does not attain the nature of volition (*cetanā*). Having understood through wisdom that there is no objective support (*ālambana*) other than the mind, one realizes the non-existence of even that "mind-only," since in the absence of an object to be grasped (*grāhya*), there is no grasper (*grāhaka*). Having realized the non-existence of this duality characterized by knowledge and the knowable, one abides in the *dharmadhātu* which is devoid of duality. As it has been said:
"Having realized through the intellect that there is nothing beyond the mind, one arrives at the non-existence of the mind itself."
Having realized the non-existence of the duality, the wise one abides in the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) which is free from that [duality].
(Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 6.8).

Because he has performed his duty in both the mastery of dispelling the adverse factors through the nature of stability and in their actual dispelling through the nature of movement, he is the "Lord" (*prabhu*). Therefore, it is said that he is "heroic" (*vīra*).

Alternatively, because the earrings (*kuṇḍala*) perform all functions, they represent—just as before—the purity of any one of the [four] measures (*māna*) and so forth; thus, the ordinary measure and the rest are represented by the serpent ornaments (*nāgābharaṇa*). Furthermore, because they take the form of the deities who are the antidotes to the other fetters (*saṃyojana*), they are called "the end-maker of obstacles" (*vighnāntakṛt*), as they bring an end to the outflow of desire (*kāmāsrava*), the obscurations of karma and rebirth, the latent tendencies of the mundane (*prākṛtavāsanā*), the outflow of ignorance (*avidyāsrava*), the son-of-the-gods Māra (*devaputramāra*), and every obstacle. As it has been said:
"That which is the destruction of all afflictions (*kleśa*) is likewise the destruction of all karma."
The knowledge that exhausts all obscurations is known as the "End-maker of Obstacles."
(Guhyasamājatantra 18.61).

Regarding the phrase "of all afflictions" (*sarvakleśasya*), according to the sequence just mentioned, it refers to the exhaustion of the outflows of desire (*kāmāsrava*) and so forth, as well as the exhaustion of karma. Regarding "all obscurations" (*sarvāvaraṇa*), it refers to the obscurations of karma and birth; their exhaustion occurs in this very manner. Furthermore, this should be applied by following the sequence beginning with experience (*upabhoga*). Precisely because of this application of the destruction of all obstacles (*vighna*), he is called the "End-maker of Obstacles" (*Vighnāntakṛt*). This is what is meant: knowledge, which is the nature of the antidote to the afflictions and so forth, and which consists of the purification of the results of purified karma, is the "End-maker of Obstacles."

Alternatively, the meaning of the passage beginning with "all afflictions" (*sarvakleśa*) is as follows: it is the very knowledge capable of effecting the destruction of the obscurations of karma and afflictions without remainder that is designated as the "performer of all activities" (*sarvavyāpārakāraka*) and the "end-maker of obstacles" (*vighnāntakṛt*).
Vairocana, Maunīndra, Amitābha, and Citteśvara are [the deities] on the crown, in sequence.

*...the hammer, staff, lotus, vajra, and so forth in the hand.* (91) Regarding "Vairocana" and so forth: in the consecration to be described, one should visualize that upon the crowns of these very deities—Yamāri and the others—the lords of their respective families, Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi, appear in sequence. Furthermore, the four primary insignia, beginning with the hammer, should be meditated upon in the hand in their proper order. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it is meant that other implements such as the sword and so on should also be applied according to the appropriate circumstances.

And when they take on the form of wrath, the sole purpose of those possessed of compassion is the disciplining of sentient beings. Thus it is said in the *Mahāsamayatattva*: "Aho! How truly firm is the vajra-activity of all the Buddhas, in that those who are peaceful become fierce for the sake of benefiting the fierce!"
...thus it is said. Likewise, in the *Guhyatilaka*:
"Oh, how wonderful is the knowledge of mastery belonging to the Buddhas who perceive reality!"
For in that state, even the pure means of discipline turn into the nature of anger.
Thus [it is said].
Thus it is completely accomplished.
Beholding the maṇḍala with one's whole being,
one should visualize the Sugatas summoned by the hooks of light rays from the heart-mantra. 92

92.1 [24b2-5] "Thus, all around," and so forth. In the manner just described, having visualized with every aspect of one's being the mandala that has been completed on all sides, one should meditate upon the Sugatas who have been summoned and drawn in—appearing in the form of the wheel of the Lord Mañjuvajra—seated upon the universal lotus situated before the pledge-mandala (*samayacakra*). This is accomplished by means of the hooks that are the very rays of light from the mantra at the heart of the Jñānasattva; through their impelling, Yamāntaka utters the syllable *jaḥ*, and the wrathful deities issuing from his heart establish protection through various apertures. By this, the summoning of the wisdom-wheel (*jñānacakra*) is explained.
One should meditate on the wheel of Antaka, which is filled with true bliss born from the stainless samādhi consisting of wisdom and means.
"By the crushing [of the enemies] and so forth, protection is established.

(93) Regarding "wisdom" (*prajñā*) and so forth: that stainless meditative absorption (*samādhi*) which consists of wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya*) and has the nature of the Knowledge-Person (*vidyāpuruṣa*), and the excellent bliss produced from it—that wheel (*cakra*) is filled by that. "By the crushing of the End-Maker (*Antaka*) and so forth" means: by Yamāntaka and the others, protection is established and provided for the Wheel of Gnosis (*jñānacakra*), characterized by the removal of obstacles and characterized by the re-establishment of the boundaries that were disrupted upon entering that wheel. A yogin who is thus constituted should meditate. "The water-offering (*argha*) consecrated by one's own heart-mantra..."
Having offered [the vessel] rich with excellent sandalwood, flowers, and so forth— as if it were his own consecration— [the practitioner], being purified, should worship it thus. 94.

94.1 Having offered—that is, having presented—to that maṇḍala-circle the *argha* (water for honor), which has been consecrated by one's own heart-mantra and infused with the essence of the three syllables, and which is enriched and augmented by *ācamana* (water for rinsing) and so forth, as well as by excellent sandalwood, flowers, and the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) prepared according to the procedure to be described; having thus offered that *argha*, one should, being diligent, worship—that is, honor—that maṇḍala-circle with the "consecration" (*abhiṣeka*) according to the procedure to be described, by means of the impulsion of light rays from one's own heart.

94.2 Here, however, the fourfold set of limbs beginning with service (*sevā*) and their resulting fruits, such as the outflow (*niḥsyanda*), are characterized by the qualification "intense" (*adhimātra*) because they possess the capacity to exhaust the opposing factors due to their having become fully potent; they are also "general" because they pertain to all deities.
94.3 As for the near-attainment (*upasādhana*) and so forth, they are exactly as before; however, one should understand that the distinction here is produced by resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).

94.4 Immediately following the empowerment, Akṣobhya is to be visualized upon the crowns of the Buddhas and of Māmakī, Śabdavajrā, and Dharmadhātuvajrā. Likewise, Vairocana is for Locanā and Rūpavajrā; Amitābha is for Pāṇḍarā and Rasavajrā; Amoghasiddhi is for Tārā and Sparśavajrā; and Ratnasambhava is for Gandhavajrā.
94.5 For Yamāri and the others, the presiding lords have already been stated.

95.0 Thus, he explains with six Āryā verses, beginning with "In the center of the lotus" (*kamalodare*) and ending with the worship mantra, the procedure by which the wheel for which the consecration has been performed is to be worshipped:
"Having drawn in all forms and so forth by means of the radiance of one's own seed-syllable in the center of the lotus..."
One should meditate on a circle of light rays whose nature is the mind of awakening (*sambodhicitta*).

(95) By means of the radiance from the seed-syllable in the heart of the Jñānasattva, one should draw in all forms and so forth, cause them to enter one’s own body, and having caused them to emerge through the path of the vajra, one should meditate on that circle of light rays— which is the very essence of the mind of awakening— within the lotus of one’s own consort (*vidyā*).
A magnificent array of various kinds of light rays arising from every pore of wisdom,
pervading the expanse of space.
The wise one should emit that [light] everywhere.

(96) Having meditated in this way—starting from "that" (referring to 95d)—the wise one, being free from the perception of distinctions such as emission and so forth, should emit in every direction, in all respects, that array of an expansion of various kinds of light-rays which has pervaded the entire expanse of space; [this light] arises from every pore of Prajñā, having been nourished by the entry of his own goddesses drawn in by the rays of their respective [seed-syllables] located upon that moon.
[It is] stainless, having emerged from the mouths of the light-rays...
[With goddesses whose limbs are well-adorned with all ornaments, and with mirrors, lutes, pure nectar, garments, the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*), and so forth.

97. From the mouths of the rays, there emerge the goddesses of form and the other sense objects, their limbs well-adorned with all stainless ornaments; they proceed in sequence—according to the order—with the six primary symbols beginning with the mirror, and with the others such as the sword as previously described.
With signs appearing in succession,
[he whose hands shine with playful grace—
] fashioned by radiant rays of light.

By means of those [deities] whose splendor and radiance shine forth with playful, sprout-like hands, and by means of those emanations of various clouds of offerings— extensive arrays of clouds consisting of forms and other objects created by their brilliant rays—
which are like illusions and so forth...
[They are] skilled in the analytical knowledges and free from worldly views;
[they are] those for whom conceptual constructions have been utterly destroyed, and who have become the cause for the arising of supreme bliss. 99

99.1 By means of the goddesses of form and so forth—who are skilled in those two, namely the cognition of things as having a nature like an illusion and the view that conforms to worldly beings attached to their respective objects; who are adept at performing them; and who are the cause for the arising of true bliss through the destruction of all conceptual constructions—and likewise by means of all external perfumes and so forth: *The Tibetan text corresponding to this section is:* *sgyu ma lta bu la sogs pa’i rang bzhin gyis dngos po rnams kyi yang dag par rig pa gang yin pa dang / gang yang de dang de’i yul la rjes su chags pa’i ’jig rten dang mthun pa’i lta ba ste / de gnyis legs par byed pa la mkhas shing de dag sgrub pa la spobs pa dang ldan pa / rtog pa ma lus pa bcom nas bde ba dam pa skye ba’i rgyur gyur pa’i gzugs la sogs pa’i lha mo rnams dang / de bzhin du phyi rol gyi dri la sogs pa thams cad kyis so //*
One should worship the Lords of Jinas, free from conceptual constructions regarding their distinctions.

(100) Thus, with such goddesses as Rūpavajrā and others, and likewise with external offerings such as all perfumes and so forth, the practitioner of mantra (*mantrin*), being free from conceptual constructions regarding the distinction between the object of worship and the act of worship, should worship the Lords of Jinas who are contained within the mandala-circle by means of the empowerment of the mantra: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the worship of all Tathāgatas. Thus he should worship.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the worship of all Tathāgatas.
101.0 [25b6] Now he states the offering of praise, beginning with "pratiśabda" and so forth:
"Having examined the entire collection of sounds as being like echoes, and thereafter..."

One should meditate thus: "The dharmas that are vocalized as praise for one’s own mind, which is the presiding deity (*adhidaivata*). (101) Regarding this: "Thereafter" means immediately following the ritual of worship. Examining—that is, reflecting upon—the entire collection of sounds in the form of praise, like an echo, one should cultivate through the verses beginning with "Akṣobhyavajra" (102a) those dharmas appearing before the mind that are vocalized as praise for one’s own mind, which is the presiding deity, one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). These dharmas are those that have ascended to the level of mental manifestation (*pratibhāsa*).
Akṣobhyavajra, great wisdom, Vajradhātu, great enlightened one, triple mandala, supreme among the three vajras, O Sound-Vajra, homage be to you!
(Guhyasamājatantra 17.1)

102.1 [26a1-7] He is called Akṣobhya because he does not waver, due to his nature of perfectly established conduct (*suvṛtti*), which is unimpeded and indivisible. Thus, the purity of the gnosis that accomplishes what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) has been described. Having addressed Akṣobhya, who is of such a nature, at every step with the words "Homage be to you" (*namo 'stu te*)—meaning "Homage be to you"—and having thus paid homage, the Dharmas, whose mouths are ready for praise, say: "Proclaim! This physical homage preceded by a hymn of praise should be understood as implying mental homage as well, by the force of the context. Vairocana, Greatly Pure One; Vajra Peaceful One, Great Joy!
O you who are the supreme among the supreme, naturally luminous, O Teacher, O Vajra—homage be to you!

(Guhyasamājatantra 17.2) Thus, through the purity of the selflessness of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, Vairocana is [so named] because he shines forth (*virocana*); his utter purity has been explained. "Greatly pure" means that, by virtue of having the nature of the bodhicitta which is the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) and so forth, he is the most excellent even among the most excellent; thus he is "naturally luminous, the supreme among the supreme. This refers to the purity of activity (*kṛtyaviśuddhi*). Having thus addressed him, they say as before: "O Teacher, O Vajra—homage be to you!"
O King of Jewels, most profound, as stainless as the vajra of space;
naturally pure and untainted—homage be to you, Vajra Body!
(Guhyasamājatantra 17.3)

104.1 The bodhicitta, which is the intrinsic nature of things as they are (*yathābhāvasvabhāva*), is a jewel because of its excellence and because it is the cause of delight; thus, it shines, and is therefore called the "King of Jewels" (*ratnarāja*). Its utter purity has been described. It is profoundly deep because, while devoid of defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it takes the form of conduct that manifests the world as a reflection of the secret. It is the purity of the mirror. It is the stainlessness of the space-vajra, being as stainless as space due to the greatness of the indivisibility of selflessness (*nairātmya*) and phenomena that are equal to space. This is the qualification by way of equality.

Because it indicates being unstained and indivisible through the purity of the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-dharmatā*) by virtue of momentariness, it is "pure by nature and unstained" (*svabhāva-śuddha-nirlepa*). This is the purity of discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣā-śuddhatva*). Because it is an accumulation of indivisible phenomena in the form of the essence of awakening (*bodhicitta*) by way of the method of awakening (*bodhi-naya*), it is the "Vajra Body" (*kāya-vajra*) as a unity. This is the purity of enlightened activity (*kṛtya-viśuddhatā*). Having thus awakened [the disciple], they spoke as before:
"O Vajra Amita, Great King, holder of the non-conceptual space-vajra;
you who have attained the perfection of passion (*rāga-pāramitā*), speak! O Vajra, homage be to you! (105)
Because the nature of the mind is unarisen and because it is beyond the scope of measurement, he is the Vajra-Infinite. He is utter purity. As before, they said:

"O Amoghavajra, Perfectly Awakened One, fulfiller of all hopes!"* (*The text contains a corrupt reading: *bhāvābhiniveśarahitarāśyā*. The phrase in parentheses, *pūrvavad āhuḥ*, indicates that the following is a quotation from a previous section.)
"O Vajrasattva, born from the pure intrinsic nature, homage be to you!

(Guhyasamājatantra 17.5) [27a4-7] Because he is of the nature of the Tathāgatas—body and so forth—which are indivisible due to their natural purity (*prakṛtipariśuddhi*), and because he is never disconnected from the fruitfulness of the welfare of sentient beings and so on, he is the "Infallible Vajra" (*amoghavajra*). Thus, his utter purity is shown. Because he is primordially pure (*ādiśuddha*) and has wisdom as his essence, being of the nature of stainless Buddha-gnosis, he is the "Perfectly Awakened One" (*sambuddha*). This is an exposition of the mirror-like [wisdom]. Because he fulfills all hopes through the supreme Dharma for all by means of teaching the practice whose essence is equal to space, he is the "Fulfiller of All Hopes. This is an expression of the wisdom of equality (*samatā*).

Because he has arisen through the nature of the bodhicitta that is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), he is "born from a pure nature. The purity of discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣā*) has thus been described. Because his mental nature is indivisible due to its form being the way of emptiness (*śūnyatānaya*), he is "Vajrasattva. Having thus awakened him, they said as before, "Homage be to you! (107.0).
Having uttered this hymn of praise, he now describes the tasting of the nectar (*amṛtāsvāda*), beginning with the words "delightful" (*rucira*) and so forth:
"consecrated by the delightful *praṇava*."

Having ignited the Radiant One (Arciṣmat), who resides within the mandalas of wind and fire, as well as the Lord of Sages (the Buddha) who is immeasurable and empowered by the three seed-syllables of the five nectars; 107.

From the syllable *yaṃ* arises a wind mandala, smoke-colored and marked with a banner; therein is a triangular fire mandala arising from the syllable *raṃ*, which is fire; therein is a vessel supported by the syllable *āḥ*. Within that reside the five substances, empowered by their respective seed-syllables. By means of the rays of light from the internal seed-syllables, the infinite Lords of Sages are drawn forth. Through the blazing, heating, and melting of the *hūṃ*-syllable into vajra, those [substances] situated upon the lotus are duly transformed into the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), empowered by the throbbing syllable *oṃ*, and ignited.
Having ignited it instantly with the word "dhag," then afterwards, as much as desired, one should recite the three-syllable mantra;
[the practitioner], whose tongue is a vajra placed upon the syllable HŪṂ, [partakes of] that which has the nature of the nectar of gnosis.
One should satisfy the entire circle of Victors (*jinacakra*) residing within the moon at one’s heart by means of that [nectar].

(108) Having meditated on its nature as the nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*) because it removes the sufferings of death and so forth, and having visualized one’s own tongue as consisting of a three-pronged vajra produced from a white syllable *HŪṂ*, one should satisfy the entire circle of Victors without attachment—residing in the center of the moon at the heart and present in each hand—by means of that nectar through the stimulation of the rays of light from one’s own seed-syllable. This is the meaning. Furthermore, in this context, the conceptualization of pure and impure should be abandoned, because the universe is pure by its very nature.
108.2 By this much, the second samādhi, named Maṇḍalarājāgra, has been explained.
109.0 Now, with the passage beginning with "on all sides" (*paritaḥ*) and ending with "filling the universe" (*viśvam āpūrayan*), he describes the yoga of the drop (*binduyoga*).
On all sides, free from delusion...

Having internalized the entire world— which has been transformed into the state of perfect awakening by the lords of sages emanated from the light rays of his infinite heart— within his own mantra. 109

109.1 [27b5-7] There are infinite Lords of Sages (*munīndra*) emanated by the light-rays from the heart of the Knowledge Being (*jñānasattva*); by them, the entire world has been made fully awakened, and for that very reason, all delusion has been cast out from every side. Having thus reflected on the meaning—that one’s own mind, having internalized the entire world within its own mantra, namely the mantra of the Knowledge Being’s heart, is freed from forms and so forth (as seen in 110a)—one should contemplate one’s own mind as the form of the drop (*bindu*) of the excellent mantra (as seen in 127c). This is the connection (as seen in 127d).

110.0 [27b7–28a2] One might object: "If external objects truly exist, how can the meditation on the entire universe as being contained within the seed-syllable situated upon the sword in the heart of the sentient-being of consciousness (*jñānasattva*), and the visualization of the maṇḍala-wheel whose nature is the universe within that drop (*bindu*), be logically consistent? Thinking thus, [the author] first states the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the existence of external objects, beginning with the words "devoid of the forms of color and so forth" (*rūpādyākṛti*).
"That which is devoid of the forms of color and so forth is not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); nor is there a perceiver of it."
Nor is there any object of apprehension (*grāhya*) perceived by another, because no connection is observed.

(110) The phrase "released from the form of color and so forth" means that it is devoid of the aspects (*ākāra*) of color and so forth; thus, its being the apprehender (*grāhaka*) of those colors and so forth is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Nor is any object of apprehension perceived through direct perception; rather, it is only the aspect of color and so forth—whose nature is self-cognition (*svasaṃvid*), non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*), and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*)—that manifests as direct perception. The point is that the nature of the apprehended object and so forth is merely fabricated by the artifice of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). As it has been said:
There is nothing else to be experienced by the intellect, nor is there any other experience of it;
due to the absence of the distinction between the grasped and the grasper, it shines forth by itself.
Likewise: "Although the nature of cognition is undivided, it is perceived as such by those whose vision is distorted. (Pramāṇaviniścaya 1.38)
