It appears as if possessing a distinction between the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and the consciousness itself.

(Pramāṇavārttika Pramāṇasiddhi 354). Now, [it may be argued: the cognition of an object is a property (*dharma*), namely, the act of experiencing (*samvedana*); how could that exist without an experiencer? For properties are seen to depend upon a substratum (*dharmin*), just like cooking and so forth. Therefore, this act of experiencing must necessarily have a substratum as its agent—the experiencer. And that very [agent] is called the grasper (*grāhaka*). Since it has form and other [objects] as its domain, the grasped (*grāhya*) is also established.

To the objection that "the establishment of the apprehended and the apprehender follows from inference or presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), so how can they be denied?", he says: "Because no relation is perceived, nor by another. The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "The apprehender and the apprehended are seen as being devoid of forms such as color and the like."

This is the intended meaning: neither through inference, nor through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), nor through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) postulated by others, is there a direct apprehension of an imperceptible object on its own part, for that would entail its becoming perceptible. Nor is there apprehension from another [source] if it is unconnected; for it is impossible for both [inference and presumptive testimony] to occur from everything, as this would lead to the perception of everything. Indeed, those two cannot exist when the subject (*dharmin*) is an imperceptible grasper. Consequently, even their arising from that [subject] is impossible.

Nor can the grasper be inferred—like the eye and other faculties—from the impossibility of the cognition of form and so forth, because the cognition bearing the aspect of form and so forth arises solely from a preceding causal complex. Even so, if one were to admit another cause, there would be the unsurpassed consequence of an infinite regress. Therefore, there is no real distinction between the grasped, the grasper, and consciousness.

As for cooking and the like, in ultimate reality they are simply the forms of things arising in such and such ways, with distinctions imagined through mere exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*); even there, there is no real distinction between action and its factors (*kriyā-kāraka*) in the form of property (*dharma*) and substratum (*dharmin*).

111.0. Now, one might object: "Granted that there is no apprehension other than consciousness itself; however, that very consciousness, being internally cognized in the form of pleasure (*sātā*) and so forth, is experienced as grasping the forms of color and other objects located in external space. Therefore, how can non-duality be established? In response to this doubt, he says: "The operation," and so on.
"No operation whatsoever is observed in pleasure and the like for the grasping of these [objects]."
That which is perceived simultaneously,
like form (*rūpa*) and so forth, is itself not the grasper.
In the apprehension of that form and so forth, the function belongs to the experience of pleasure (*sāta*) and the rest.
This internal delimitation appears as if it were an external part;
for the appearance of division in cognition, which is itself undivided, is indeed a cognitive distortion.

(Pramāṇavārttika Pramāṇasiddhi 212) But surely, by virtue of being the producer of cognition, form and so forth are present first, and only later does the arising of the experience of pleasure and so on occur. How then can there be simultaneous perception? To this it is replied:

If, according to the Vaibhāṣika position, consciousness is held to be formless (*nirākāra*) and yet is considered the apprehender of an object possessing form by virtue of being obstructed from arising [without it], then—since mere cognition is common to all objects—there would be no specific determination of cognition such that "this is the cognition of blue" or "this is the cognition of yellow. Consequently, those seeking the causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) of dyeing and so forth would not invariably engage with blue and the like; therefore, there would be no awareness of the object at all.

Now, if according to the Sautrāntika system, consciousness possessing an aspect (*sākāravijñāna*) is held to be the apprehender of a preceding momentary object that produced it—by virtue of its arising from that [object]—then, since at the time of the cognition the producing momentary object no longer exists due to its momentariness, and because there is no perception of two aspects, only the aspect of the cognition itself is perceived. Thus, the form of the object does not differ from a flower in the sky; so how can there be an acceptance of the object?

111.2 If it is argued that, since perception according to the restriction of place, time, form, and causal efficiency is not possible in the absence of an object, the existence of an object that is eternally beyond the senses is established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), we say: no. Even in the absence of an external entity restricted by place and so forth, perception with restricted place and so forth will occur due to the restriction of mental impressions (*vāsanā*), as in dreams and the like. Why should we deceive ourselves with the postulation of a useless object? 111.3 It might be argued that even in dreams and the like, the cause is indeed an external object seen in another place. As it has been said:
In cognitions such as dreams, an external object is by no means denied;
rather, in every case, the external object serves as the objective support (ālambana), though its nature is altered by place and time.
(Ślokavārttika, Nirālambanavāda 107cd–108ab).

Thus, how can it be said that the restriction of place and so forth for consciousness occurring in the waking state is described by means of the analogy of dreams and the like? That is incorrect, because an objective support (*ālambana*) for dream-cognition and the like is untenable. For such cognition must be either of the nature of a direct perception (*grahaṇa*) or of the nature of a memory (*smaraṇa*). In this regard, it cannot first be a perception; for since a perception does not depend on a prior perception, there would be no fixed restriction regarding its grasping the object of a prior observation, just as in the case of any other [independent] observation.

Furthermore, its nature as recollection is untenable because it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), because its object is present, and because it appears with vivid clarity (*sphuṭābhā*). Therefore, we do not understand how it can have as its object things seen in another location and so forth.

Granted, let that be the cause [of the dream]. However, it is impossible to justify that the restriction to a specific place and so forth is caused by that [external object]. For if the external object were present in the very same place and so forth as in the waking state, it would appear there even in a dream; yet, even in the absence of an object, causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) is indeed perceived in dreams. Just as in the waking state, pleasures and the like caused by a woman, as well as their dependent causal effects such as emission, are directly experienced, exactly the same occurs in the state of dreaming.

Therefore, just as in dreams and similar states, spatial restriction and other such phenomena occur even in the absence of external objects, why are these same phenomena in the waking state not subject to the same [explanation]? As it has been said:
"For someone, something specific serves as the awakener of internal latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
therefore, the determination of cognitions depends on this, not on dependence upon external objects."
Thus [it is said in Pramāṇavārttika Pramāṇasiddhi 336].

Since that cognition lacks an external cause, we do not understand how it could be appropriate to describe the fault of the absence of simultaneous perception when color-form (*rūpa*) and pleasure (*sātā*) exist in a temporal sequence of prior and posterior.

But surely, even when they are perceived simultaneously, pleasure (*sātā*) and so forth—which are determined as the apprehenders of form and the rest—are indeed the apprehending subjects (*grāhin*), whereas the object, such as form, is the apprehended object (*grāhya*) because it is common to all perceivers; this is understood from the preceding causal complex alone, since that [complex] has a universal as its object. Therefore, the cognition itself is what is perceived simultaneously with the unique forms and so forth, because it is known by itself to those situated in a suitable location who do not know [the object].

112.0 [30a7–30b1] One might object: "Is it not the case that the external object, such as a whole (*avayavin*) and so forth, is non-momentary and singular? Since it persists through prior and subsequent times, its commonality (*sādhāraṇatva*) is also known through inference; therefore, this [argument] is not incoherent. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And what is seen," and so forth. That which is seen as white and so forth at one time is not seen as such at other times, because they are mutually contradictory.
In these two cases, as with pleasure (*sātā*) and so forth, it would be eternal.
112.1 [30b1-4] If that which is white and so forth—namely, the form of white and the like—were [eternal], the consequence of its being perceived at all times would be unavoidable.
112.2 And it was stated by the Master in the *Ātmasādhanāvatāra* for the purpose of refuting external objects:

If it is asked, "How can cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), which appears in the form of the apprehended object (*grāhya*) and so forth, be of the nature of mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*)," we say: no, because the object of cognition is not established as being the apprehended object and so forth. For apart from the appearance of forms (*rūpa*) and the like, nothing else—neither an apprehended object nor an apprehending subject—is perceived. Nor can that whose nature is not being cognized be the object of the conventional usage of "existence," for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, there is no cognition of that [subject] through a cognition connected to it, because a connection with anything whose essence is entirely imperceptible cannot be established.

If it is argued that pleasure (*sātā*) and so forth, which appear internally, possess the nature of the grasper (*grāhaka*), whereas blue and so forth, whose characteristic is to be perceived as external to that [internal appearance], possess the nature of the grasped (*grāhya*), we say no; for the operation of pleasure and so forth upon blue and so forth is unestablished. Furthermore, that whose operation is not perceived cannot be called a "grasper"; if that were the case, an external insentient object would be a grasper. Thus it has been said:
“Subhūti, it is not the case that one dharma knows another dharma” (*Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, p.
xxx), and so on at length. As for what was stated:

"Even so, forms are cognized by two types of consciousness," and so forth; this [statement] is not a fault, as it is made with reference merely to the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of those forms, similar in some respects to the teaching of a "person" (*pudgala*) and so on. (Ātmasādhanāvatāra 52b3–53a4)
112.3 [30b4] Thus far, the refutation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establish the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) has been shown.

113.0 [30b4] Now, demonstrating the state of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) because external objects do not exist due to subverting means of valid cognition, he says: "And it is not one," and so forth.
It is not one, such as form (*rūpa*), etc.
Because it is not perceived through distinctions such as beginning and end,
nor even as individual atoms,
it does not possess multiple forms, just like that [space]. 113

113.1 This is the intended meaning. An external object (*artha*)—which, as will be seen in verse 115d, is described by others as being of many kinds through the distinctions of qualities (*guṇa*), substances (*dravya*), and so forth—is what is at issue.

Among these, substance (*dravya*) is the substratum (*āśraya*) of qualities (*guṇa*) and attributes (*dharma*); since those [qualities] are uprooted along with their very foundation by the negation of that [substance], no separate refutation is stated for them. Furthermore, since there can be no inherence (*samavāya*) in the absence of that which is inherent (*samavāyin*), its refutation is likewise not mentioned. And substance is of nine kinds: earth, water, fire, air, space, time, direction, self, and mind.
In this regard, the self (ātman) must be refuted immediately thereafter.

However, space (ākāśa) is accepted as having sound as its quality. Since that [space] is one, all sounds would occupy the same location; consequently, there would be no distinct perception of sounds. Furthermore, a sound perceived at a distant location would be heard just like one nearby. Moreover, it is not the case that there is no other [space], for if [space] were singular, the notions of "east," "west," and so forth would be untenable, as both direction (dik) and time (kāla) would be one.

It might be argued that this distinction in cognition is due to the difference between the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Is the priority and posteriority of these adjuncts intrinsic (*svataḥ*) or extrinsic (*parataḥ*)? In the first case, since the cognition of them is established by that very [intrinsic nature], these two [adjuncts] are purposeless. In the second case, if it is by space and time alone, then because these two are one, this does not cohere. If it is from something else, then their uselessness remains as before.

Furthermore, since these—space, direction, and time—are eternal, how could they produce their own effects only at certain times, whether in the presence of auxiliary conditions or in their absence, given that no difference in their intrinsic nature has been acquired? For instance:
"Whether their capacity or incapacity is established by their very nature, who is able to alter it, since they are eternal and thus incurable?"

By this, the mind (*manas*) is also refuted. For those who maintain that the mind exists, the mind is to be inferred from the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions. However, cognitions are indeed experienced simultaneously during such events as watching a dancer; and this would never be possible if a [unitary] mind existed.
Therefore, space and the other [elements] do not exist at all.

Earth and the other elements remain. These too are conceived as twofold, by way of the distinction between the composite whole (*avayavin*) and the atom (*paramāṇu*). Even there, neither the composite whole exists nor do the atoms exist, because in both cases there are subverting arguments (*bādhaka*).

He explains that very refutation in due order: "One" [partless whole] does not exist at all—neither the form of a composite (*avayavin*) such as a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth produced by atoms in sequence, nor well-known objects like jars and the like. This is because they are perceived as being devoid of a single gross form, precisely due to the presence of mutually contradictory properties such as the distinctions of beginning, end, middle, and so on, belonging to color and other qualities. By this, he has stated the reason consisting in the non-perception of an object associated with a single cognition. Indeed, only the parts appear arranged in such and such a way; moreover, no other partless entity possessing those parts ever appears.

(Dharmakīrti, untraced/lost) We shall proceed. Now, when one [atom] is negated, that which possesses a manifold nature remains. And that manifold nature has been postulated in various ways by many: for instance, by the Vaibhāṣikas as being directly within the range of perception; by the Vaiśeṣikas, however, as the constituents that initiate a composite whole (*avayavin*); and by the Sautrāntikas, as atoms that are eternally beyond perception, resembling *piśācas*, and which, when seen, are inclined to project their own form [into consciousness]. In this regard, he says—"even atom by atom," etc.—in order to refute the atoms postulated by the Vaibhāṣikas.

And just as a single gross object does not exist, so too a plurality of them does not exist. He states the reason: "Because even in the form of atoms they are not perceived. This means that the nature of atoms, when considered individually and distinct from one another, is not apprehended. (114.0) Now, he addresses the argument that atoms must be inferred because the existence of gross objects cannot otherwise be accounted for: "If the atom were partless," and so forth. *If the atom were partless...*
Because there is an absence of a retinue of multiple atoms,
there could not be any accumulation of forms such as the circle of the earth here. || 114 ||

114.1 This is the intended meaning: First of all, an atom with parts (sāvayava) should not be perceived as such, because it would follow that it is manifold—just like a gross object—due to its conjunction with six [atoms] situated in opposing directions via their parts, resulting in a connection with contradictory properties (viruddhadharma-saṃsarga). If it were partless (niravayava), then even in that case, this same fault would apply; for even in the mere state of facing one another, despite the absence of actual proximity, this very defect persists.
Consequently, since it would follow that the mass has the form of a mere atom, there could be no accumulation here in the form of the earth-mandala and so forth. As it has been said:
The form of an atom situated in the middle [of a cluster] is conjoined with [other atoms], located in a distant place, arranged without interval, and facing toward a single atom.
If that very same atom is conceived as being oriented toward another atom,
then the accumulation of mountains and the like would not be possible under such circumstances.
(Tattvasaṃgraha 1989–1990).

Therefore, one must necessarily admit a distinction between those two natures. And just as there is a distinction between these two, so too there is a distinction between the natures of those atoms adjacent to the lower, upper, southern, and northern [sides]; thus, by force of logic, the atom necessarily results in having six parts. As it has been said:
Through simultaneous conjunction with six [atoms], the atom would have six parts; because the six occupy the same location, the aggregate would be no larger than a single atom.
(Viṃśikā 12). Thus,
since the non-establishment of one does not entail the establishment of many, atoms do not exist.
And the Mīmāṃsakas do not necessarily accept atoms [as real entities]. (Ślokavārttika 5.4.183ab)
Thus, the whole (avayavin) would not be refuted merely by the refutation of the atom; therefore, its critique is not futile.

114.5 Let it be, then, that the world has the nature of mere consciousness (*vijñānamātra*). Yet, as before, that too—whether it be one or many—is not tenable in terms of its form; thus, like a lotus in the sky, it cannot be the object of conventional discourse regarding existence. Since there is no other alternative for a real entity besides being either one or many, it must exist as one or many. But since it cannot be established in that way, we do not understand how this can be an object of conventional discourse regarding existence. Now, if it is impossible to deny that it possesses the nature of being both one and many...

For that refutation based on [the cognition's] being external to consciousness does not apply such that it would exist by virtue of its [consciousness's] having that [external] nature. The claim that the sublation based on corporeality applies only to the conscious self which is incorporeal is also insubstantial; for if consciousness possesses the form of blue and so forth, it too is corporeal. For this very extension in space is what constitutes corporeality; thus, we do not understand how there could be a designation of "corporeality" for this [consciousness] if it were external.

114.6 It might be thought: let this fault apply to those for whom consciousness possesses an aspect (*sākāra-vijñāna*). But for those whose position is that [consciousness] is aspectless (*nirākāra*) and that pleasure and so forth are real in their own nature (*tāttvika*), how can this [argument of] being devoid of unity and plurality be consistent? To this it is replied: Here, consciousness is of the nature of luminosity (*prakāśātman*), and there is no manifestation of blue and so forth distinct from that which is being manifested. Even in a dream, no manifestation of these [objects] apart from that is found. And if it is argued that it is not logical for blue and so forth—which are being manifested—to be unreal like pleasure and so forth, because of the existence of subverting evidence (*bādhaka*), then we ask: what is this subverting evidence?

114.7 If it is argued that pleasure and so forth cannot be obstructed because pleasure and the like are formless (*amūrta*), and thus their absence [as spatial entities] follows, this is not the case; for even that [pleasure], as it manifests through the extension of space, is capable of being denied. Indeed, when one is exhausted, pleasure arises and is experienced as pervading as many limbs as enter into the water.

Nor can it be that which is experienced as having no spatial extension, for that would entail the same state for the body as well; and if it did have spatial extension, then like the body, it too would possess material form (*mūrtatva*). Therefore, whether this consciousness is possessed of form or devoid of form, it does not escape the refutation regarding the absence of external objects; thus, it should be understood that the Teacher has not applied a separate refutation for it.

114.8 Thus it is established: even this consciousness does not deserve to be treated as existent. If that is so, since both the knower and the known are non-existent, reality would be of a non-existent nature. No; consciousness may exist conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), because conventional reality cannot be denied. If it is argued that because existence is negated, non-existence follows by necessity, we say no; for non-existence is preceded by existence, and if that [existence] is not established, this [non-existence] is likewise not established. As it has been said:
Non-existence is preceded by existence; existence is preceded by non-existence. Therefore, one should not say "it does not exist," nor should one imagine that it exists.
(Laṅkāvatārasūtra 3.83).

Nor is it of a dual nature consisting of both existence and non-existence, because existence and non-existence are contradictory. Nor is it something other than existence and non-existence, having a nature that is neither, for it is illogical for there to be a negation of what is excluded from both. One might then conclude that there is no reality whatsoever. But is this not itself the very reality, namely, that which is called "the absence of reality"? Thus it is established: consciousness appears as free from the four extremes.
Thus, the reality for those who know reality is not even reality from the perspective of ultimate truth.
Thus it is said by Jñānapāda: [114.9]—
"Let it be then that the world has the nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*) and is devoid of intrinsic essence (*anasvarātmaka*)," and so forth; [to this we reply:
no, because of contradiction.

If it is asked, "But if all things are entirely devoid of self-nature (nirātmaka), from where does this experienced diversity of causal efficiency (arthakriyābheda) arise?", it has been explained that this is due solely to preceding and preceding conceptual constructions (kalpanā) regarding an unexamined singular essence, since nothing other than that is perceived.

If it is argued that, therefore, all things must exist by way of their very being (*bhāva*), because the nature of a real entity (*vastutva*) is defined by causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), we say: no. For there is no contradiction in accepting existence as mere appearance. It is precisely through the exclusion of the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-viveka*) according to the sequence already stated that selflessness (*nairātmya*) is established; it is not established by denying even mere appearance. As it has been said: "Subhūti, form is not one thing and emptiness another; rather, form itself is empty of the characteristic of form" (*Prajñāpāramitā*, untraced).
Thus is the detailed exposition. For this very reason, because all conventional entities appear with distinctions of prior and posterior, one should not suspect their permanence.
As for what was said, “O Sons of the Conqueror, that which is ‘representation-only’ is the triple world” (*Daśabhūmikasūtra*, p.

49), that was for the purpose of dispelling the determination of external objects by those who are attached to absolute existence. Since, when that [external object] exists, it is possible to easily eliminate even the determination of mind-only. He says that very thing:
Relying upon mind-only, the external nature of objects should be known;
then, abiding in the focal point of suchness, one should transcend mind-only.

Thus, by this much, the existence of a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) has been demonstrated. (Laṅkāvatārasūtra 10.256; Ātmasādhanāvatāra 53a4–53b5). 114.7 [32a7] This concludes the demonstration that there exists a valid cognition which refutes [the opponent's position].

115.0 [32a7–32b1] And therefore, because there is an absence of subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) and because of the presence of subverting evidence, [the author], concluding that this world has a nature constructed solely from conceptual construction (*kalpanā-mātra-nirmita-svabhāva*) due to the selflessness (*nairātmya*) of all things such as the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), says: "That [world], because it is devoid of a grasper, etc."—
it has the form of a conceptual construction of independent forms and so forth.
The entire reality, including the moving and the non-moving, is like a city of Gandharvas.

(115) By the force of the arguments just stated, because it is devoid of a grasper and so forth, it is like a city of Gandharvas; and because it lacks any ultimately real cause and consists of a continuum of conceptual constructions, the reality of the stationary and the moving is of the nature of conceptual constructions regarding independent forms and so forth.

116.0 [33a7–33b1] Now, if reality (*tattva*) is thus indeed pure, how can there be cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), and in its absence, how could there be purification (*vyavadāna*)? In response to this doubt, he says: "Self," and so forth.
This cyclic existence is a continuum of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-santāna*) arising from the superimposition (*āropa*) of self and what belongs to the self;
purification is the opposite of that.
But it should be understood as consisting of its own nature alone.

In that very mind, which is devoid of the four alternatives, cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is the form of a continuous stream of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) based on the superimposition (*āropa*) of a self (*ātman*) and so forth. Purity, however, is liberation (*mokṣa*), and it should be understood as consisting of its own nature of selflessness (*nairātmya*), which is the opposite of the superimposition of a self and so forth. For this very reason it has been said: "One should strive for purity from conceptual construction. (Source: Locana; location untraced).

For indeed, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which determines an external object, is ordinary and conforms to [the nature of] entities because it is erroneous. Being restricted to its own nature alone, it is non-erroneous; and because it is non-conceptual, it has the form of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and is completely pure. As it has been said:
"Even conceptual construction is accepted as [perception] with respect to self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*), but not with respect to the object, because [with respect to the object] it is conceptual.
(Pramāṇasamuccaya 1.7ab)
Thus, even passion and the other afflictions, while superimposing [conceptual constructs], ultimately abide in the true nature of the mind as it is perceived. As it is said in the *Śrī-Paramādya*:
"Passion, hatred, and delusion—these three have become poison."
These [qualities] become poison when practiced in an improper manner,
but they attain the state of nectar when practiced for the sake of immortality.
(Paramādya 220bX).
Therefore, yogins must strive to turn conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) away from the fault of determining external objects and to establish it within its own nature (*svarūpa*).

Thus, even conceptual construction is indeed non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) in its own nature; therefore, all phenomena (*dharma*) are pure by their very essence (*svabhāva-śuddha*). Regarding this, he says: "And there is no one... and so forth.

And there is no distinction whatsoever by way of the true nature (*dharmatā*) among those things whose intrinsic nature is peace and existence, because the absence of forms such as the "apprehended object" and so forth is always established everywhere. (117)

117.1 [33b4-6] "Something" refers to the distinction or differentiation—such as "this is nirvāṇa, this is saṃsāra," "this is the stained state, this is the stainless state," "this is to be abandoned, this is to be adopted"—which is not at all tenable from the perspective of *dharmatā* in terms of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*). He states the proof for this: "the object of apprehension," and so forth. For this very reason, the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna also said:
"Nirvāṇa and existence—these two do not exist.
The thorough knowledge of existence itself is called 'nirvāṇa.'"
(Verse 6 of the *Yuktiṣaṣṭikā*) There is not the slightest distinction of saṃsāra from nirvāṇa;
there is not the slightest distinction of nirvāṇa from saṃsāra.
Thus it is said in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (25.19). Furthermore, the Blessed One has also said:

"Subhūti, that which is the suchness (*tathatā*) of ordinary beings and that which is the suchness of the Tathāgata are one and the same. This is the beginning of the detailed exposition. [118.0] Now, if in reality there is no distinction between those whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists of peace and existence (as stated in 117ab), then how is it said that "there is an absence of the forms of the apprehended object and so forth everywhere" (as stated in 117cd)? For the word "all" (*sarva*), it is said, has as its domain multiple objects, and it would not be appropriate to employ it when there is an absence of distinction. Anticipating this objection, he says: "And all is not," and so forth.
Everything is not even something at all, because it is a conceptual construction whose intrinsic nature is that appearance;
nor could there be anything other than the mind such as "I," namely a self and so forth. (118)

118.1 [33b7–34a1] However, conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), there is indeed a distinction between those things whose intrinsic nature is peace (*śama*) and existence (*bhava*). Therefore, that which has the nature of appearing as a conventional object is conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa*); nothing other than that exists, for everything is merely a name. The word "everything" (*sarva*) has as its object a distinction superimposed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Thus, in every such case, the meaning is that the negation of an ultimate distinction (*tāttvikabheda*) is being established. In this way, even the moving and the non-moving are not other than the conceptual construction that has the nature of appearing as them.

118.2 [34a1–34b1] If it is argued: "But surely, if the view of a self (*ātmadarśana*) were to possess true reality, then because there would be no absence of self (*nairātmya*), existence (*bhava*) would exist; how then could there be no distinction between those whose nature is existence and those whose nature is peace (*śama*)?"—this is incorrect. Because a self is not established, and because a logical mark (*liṅga*) based on intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is impossible. Furthermore, no other positive probative mark is possible by which an inference of this [self] might occur. And by whatever other mark you propose, it must be pervaded by the probandum (*sādhya*).

Since neither the probandum nor the self is established anywhere, and because pervasion cannot be ascertained, it is impossible to determine that anything is pervaded by it; thus, no logical mark (liṅga) for this [self] is tenable.

[Objection: Granted, let visual and other sensory cognitions, or inference, not be the means of proving [the self]; however, a mental cognition in the form of the "I-notion" (ahaṃpratyaya) is possible, and the action of going, which conforms to corporeal substances, is established for the self.

118.4 Nor is it appropriate to treat this as a figurative usage—like the notion of a "lion" applied to a boy—because there is no failure [of the primary sense]. And when there is no failure, it is not reasonable to postulate a figurative application, for that would entail the disappearance of primary linguistic usage.

118.5 Therefore, it is established that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that proves the existence of a self (*ātman*). Consequently, its fitness for being treated as existent has utterly vanished. On the contrary, because there exists a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), its non-existence alone is logical. For if a self were to exist, it would have to be either of the nature of consciousness (*bodha-rūpa*) or of the nature of non-consciousness (*abodha-rūpa*). Regarding the first position, the consequence that the eyes and other sense organs are useless is unavoidable; for there can be no utility for the eyes and so forth if the self is eternal and identical with the perception of form and other objects. Furthermore, the non-perception of a self that is of the nature of non-consciousness subverts its very existence.

118.6 For instance, when there is a non-perception of something that has reached the conditions for perceptibility at a certain place, its absence there must be asserted; as, for example, the absence of horns on a horse's head. And yet, the self—which has reached the conditions for perceptibility—is not perceived in the body and so forth.
118.7 But surely, the view that the body and such are the locus of the self is precisely what those who advocate for the self do not accept.
As it is said: "To whom does the self belong in the body? (untraced).

Thus, there is nothing undesirable in the negation of such a thing. True; we too do not negate that which is to be contained (*ādheya*) here, but rather [its] connection (*saṃsarga*). For in this way, negation is everywhere performed through non-perception, and because even the negation of a jar or the like consists in its being connected. Furthermore, it is not the contained alone that is the connector; otherwise, there would be no connection with the external self, which is not contained [within the body], and thus even the state of having a self (*sātmakatva*) would not belong to the body and so forth.

And here, the body and so forth are not taken as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of that which is to be negated; rather, it is non-perception (*anupalambha*) and the conventional usage of negation (*niṣedhavyavahāra*) [that are the loci]. Thus, there is no fault.

Now, this non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is certainly not the mere absence of apprehension, for that cannot function as a means of proof. Nor is it clearly experienced as having the nature of apprehending another object associated with the same cognition. Therefore, only the body and so forth are associated with the self within a single cognition; and since no other entity distinct from those is experienced as being the object of the "I-notion" (*ahaṃpratyaya*), the apprehension of those [body, etc. is itself the apprehension of that [self].

Now, if the referent of the "I" (*asmadartha*) were not distinct from the body and so forth, the cognition "my body" would not occur; yet this cognition does exist. Therefore, the referent of the "I," being perceived as distinct from the body and so forth, places itself within the category of the cognition of distinction from the body of the seer—that is, it establishes itself as "my body" and so on. Enough of this prolixity. Consequently, it remains established that non-perception does not tolerate a self (*ātman*) that is the substratum of the self.

118.8 [34b6-7] Therefore, it is established that its non-existence alone is logical. 118.9 [34b7–35a3] Now, one might object: "How can the innate view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which is established for all the world, be refuted? Anticipating this, he says: "And not from the mind," and so forth. The intended meaning is as follows: Since, according to the sequence already described, there is an absence of all entities such as the knower and the known, there could not possibly exist anything other than the mind—as previously described—that could serve as the object of the "I-conceit" (*ahaṃkāra*) in the form of a stable grasper or the like. For this reason, the mind itself, as previously stated, is the object of the "I-conceit."

Therefore, because the self (*ātman*) does not exist in any way whatsoever, the perception of a self by another—just like the cognition of hair and so forth—is devoid of reality. Consequently, it is not the case that because existence (*bhava*) exists in the absence of selflessness (*nairātmya*), there is no negation of the distinction between those things whose nature consists of existence and peace (*śama*).
(See 117b) Establishing non-difference exactly as stated, he says: "That which is form," and so forth. That form which is apprehended...
What indeed is its own form? It is the non-differentiation of all entities due to the cognition that they are not distinct from that mind.

(119) And whatever form or object is apprehended by that mind is not established as external, because it follows immediately upon the mind. Therefore, what could its own form be? Since there is no existence other than the form perceived by the mind, its own form is precisely that which has been apprehended by the mind.

And then follows the investigation: since difference is not established, that mind which conceives of non-difference—that mental cognition of non-difference, which is the act of thinking—by virtue of that cause, all entities, being apprehended by a mind [perceiving] them as non-distinct, possess only a single, undivided intrinsic nature. Thus, their very non-difference is logically established.

Alternatively: That which is the conventional form apprehended by the foolish, its own true, ultimate nature is precisely that same own nature as it is apprehended by the wise who are free from error. Since this is so, therefore, because all things—whose intrinsic nature consists of both peace and existence—are non-different insofar as they have emptiness as their single form, there is no differentiation among all phenomena due to the realization of this understanding.
Thus it has been said:
"A single entity is the intrinsic nature of all entities."
All phenomena have the nature of a single phenomenon.
He by whom one phenomenon is seen in its true reality has, by that very fact, seen all phenomena in their true reality.
Thus [it is said in a source] whose location has not been traced.
It was also stated by the venerable Nāgārjuna:
"Reality is not apprehended apart from conventional reality."
Conventional reality is said to be emptiness, for emptiness itself is indeed conventional reality.
"Thus [it is said]: 'All, yet not anything at all' (ab = Bodhicittavivaraṇa 68ab; cd = Loc. class. untraced). Explaining this, he says: 'It appears,' and so forth."
Whatever object appears and whatever else is the locus of conceptual construction—
due to the absence of separation from each of those.

And therefore, for us, everything is not distinct from one another. (120) That which appears—that is, that object consisting of form (*rūpa*) and so forth which manifests as the apprehended (*grāhya*), and whatever other thing consists of the nature of the apprehender (*grāhaka*), being the object of the ego-grasping (*ahaṃkāra*), the locus and support of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*)—there is a separation, a state of being distinct, and a diversity between each such apprehended and apprehender. Because of the absence of that [diversity], for us, everything is not divided from one another. And therefore, for us, "everything" is nothing at all; because in ultimate reality it has the nature of mere emptiness (*śūnyatāmātra*).
The point is that multiplicity, however, is merely conceptual.
For this very reason, the Master Dignāga stated:
"The knowledge of ordinary persons which is naturally pure..."
It has been stated that by the word "Buddha," the Bodhisattva is likewise [designated as] a Victor (Jina).
(Prajñāpāramitāpiṇḍārthasaṃgraha 37).

For this very reason, even in the *Paramādya*, it is said that all sentient beings are the *tathāgatagarbha* because they have the Great Bodhisattva Samantabhadra as their universal self. (Adhyardhaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā 137ax).
Thus it has been said.

Therefore, because in reality there is equality between being a Buddha and not being a Buddha, there is no distinction among sentient beings from the Buddhas; they differ only conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*). And thus, one should understand that what was stated—that the entire world has been made fully awakened—is logical, because the world is pure by its very nature (*svabhāvaśuddhatvāt*). Nevertheless, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) must be purified through the practice of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because of the fault of superimposing distinctions such as "Buddha" and so forth based on the power of imagination (*kalpanāvaśāt*).

In this very way, it should be understood that the contemplation of one's own mantra—which has brought about the realization of the entire interior of the world as the Fully Awakened One—and the contemplation of the maṇḍala-circle of the nature of the universe within its bindu, are entirely logical; for in the absence of any object of knowledge and so forth, one's own self-manifestation arises in that manner. Thus, everything is well-established.

121.0 Now, applying the aforementioned *dharmatā* to the present context, and demonstrating through *dharmatā* that there is indeed no difference between the deities and the maṇḍala, he speaks of the mind in the form of the maṇḍala-circle of Yamāntaka and the others—despite all things having the nature of universal purity—as being determined by the purification of faith and so forth according to the inclinations of those to be trained, beginning with the words "Faith... and so on:
"Through the purification of faith and vigor, as well as through the purification of mindfulness and meditative concentration..."
Through the purification of wisdom (*prajñā*) in the form of the guardians of the six gates, the mind appears as all objects.

(121) In this context, by means of the terms "faith" (*śraddhā*) and so forth, that very same [wisdom] must be spoken of—as before—by way of its partial aspects, with reference to their conceptualized distinctions. Then, through the purification of those [aspects], there is the knowledge that the four forms of the guardians of the six gates, such as Yamāri and the others, as well as form and the other [sensory objects], are merely conceptual constructs; this is wisdom (*prajñā*). The superimposition of deities such as Rūpavajrā upon them is their purification. Through that [purification], the mind appears as all objects—that is, it possesses the aspect of all objects.
Having reflected thus, one should cultivate one’s own mind— this is the connection.
Furthermore, he qualifies that very same mind with the words beginning “signless” (*animitta*),
because of the purity of delight in the signless (*animittarativisuddheḥ*).
That is the intrinsic nature of the entire host of goddesses;
it is the purity of the evolving consciousness that consists of the conceptualization of the self for the sake of sentient beings. 122

122.1 [35b6–36a2] "Delight in the signless" (*animittarati*) refers to non-attachment through the discernment of delusion and so forth. Alternatively, it is the delight whose nature is great bliss (*mahāsukha*) because it is devoid of signs that exist as real entities; through its purification, the mind takes the form of the entire assembly of goddesses such as Locanā and others, appearing in the shape of a mandala circle. "Sentient being" (*sattva*) refers to the pentad of the eyes and so forth, because they are the cause for the conventional usage of "sentient being. "Object" (*artha*) refers to the objects of the senses, such as visible forms. "Self" (*ātman*) is the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which has the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) as its nature.

Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is consciousness associated with words. The active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are the five cognitions, such as that of the eye and so forth. Their purification is the cessation of stained suchness (*tathatā*), because they possess the stainless nature of the mirror-like wisdom and the others, and because they are the form of all Buddhas.
This [mind] is established as the Lord of the Wheel (*cakreśa*) through its union with the purity of suchness (*tathatāviśuddhi*).

Therefore, in due order, the very minds that are the mirror-like wisdom and so forth—being stainless and pure—are of the nature of those [wisdoms], and thus that mind is the form of all Buddhas, such as Vairocana and the others. The particle *ca* is used for conjunction.
123.2 This is the meaning: the purity of sentient beings consists in the form of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).

And that mirror-like wisdom is immovable. The three wisdoms beginning with the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) are dependent upon it and are mobile. Because it is free from the distortions of ego-grasping and the like, it is without "mine-ness" (*amama*), and it pervades all places and all times.

It is unconfused regarding all objects of knowledge because of its perpetual freedom from obscurations; yet it does not face toward them because it is formless (*anākāra*). It is like a mine of all-knowledge because it is the cause of all modes of omniscience, such as the knowledge of equality (*samatājñāna*), and because it is the source of the *saṃbhogakāya* and other manifestations. As it is said in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*:
"The mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) is immovable; the threefold wisdom is supported by it."
And also that which is called the equality [wisdom] and the wisdom of accomplishing activities.
The mirror-like wisdom is without "mine-ness," undivided, ever-present,
unconfused regarding all objects of knowledge, yet never directed toward them.
Because it is the cause of all gnosis, it is like a great mine of knowledge;
and because its arising is dependent upon the gnosis of the Sambhogakāya Buddhahood.
(Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 9.67–69).

Because it is luminous due to the purity of suchness (*tathatā-nairmalya*) when all adventitious obstructions and stains have been removed, that is the mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*), since the reflections of the world arise therein. As it is said in the *Ātmasādhanāvatāra*:
"Because it is luminous when adventitious stains have departed" (Ātmasādhanāvatāra 57a5).

Thus, there is the state of possessing the ten powers (*daśabala*), because by means of the gateway of making [all things] suchness (*tathatā*), one discerns the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of phenomena; and therefore, it has the ten powers as its essential nature (*svabhāva*).

And those powers are: the power of knowing what is possible and impossible, the power of knowing the ripening [of karma], the power of knowing inclinations, the power of knowing death and rebirth, the power of knowing the practice that leads everywhere, the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties, the power of knowing the attainment of meditative concentrations, the power of divine vision, the power of recollecting former abodes, and the power of the destruction of the outflows. This is stated in the *Mahāyānalakṣaṇasamuccaya*:

Since one enters into the intrinsic nature of phenomena by way of making them suchness (*tathatā*), therefrom arises the mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*) cultivated through power. Thus it is said in the *Mahāyānalakṣaṇasamuccaya* (305a3–4;

149c28–150a3). Because its nature is that [of suchness], that mind has the form of Vairocana; and because of the purity of objects, it has the nature of the stainless gnosis of equality (*samatājñāna*). And that...

The knowledge of equality (*samatājñāna*) that a bodhisattva has attained at the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) is held to be the knowledge of equality that culminates in non-abiding nirvana (*apratiṣṭhitanirvāṇa*) for one who has attained awakening, due to the purification of cultivation. It is accompanied by great loving-kindness and great compassion at all times, and manifests the form of a Buddha to sentient beings according to their respective inclinations; for some sentient beings see the Tathāgata as blue in color, while others see him as yellow in color, and so forth.
This is stated in the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*:
The wisdom of equality toward sentient beings is considered to arise from the purity of cultivation;
it is held that the wisdom of equality is that which is entered into non-abiding tranquility.
And it is held to be accompanied at all times by great loving-kindness and compassion,
manifesting the form of the Buddha to sentient beings according to their inclinations.
(Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 9.70–71).

Because its nature consists of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] that flow spontaneously without effort, and because no distinction is perceived among the infinite continuums of sentient beings—despite their being divided into categories such as "inferior" and so forth—it is held to be the *samatājñāna* (knowledge of equality). This is stated in the *Ātmasādhanāvatāra*:

"Because it has compassion and so forth as its essence, which are without objective support, and because there is no conceptualization of difference within the various mental continuums, it is the knowledge of equality. (Ātmasādhanāvatāra 57a5–6).

Thus, through the excellence of the realization of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and by being free from hesitation in all respects, there is the knowledge of equality characterized by the four forms of fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*). And those fearlessnesses are: fearlessness regarding the ascent to the Dharma, fearlessness regarding the teaching of the Dharma, and fearlessness regarding the introduction to the path of deliverance. As it is said in the *Mahāyānalakṣaṇasamuccaya*:
"Through the limit of reality and the excellence of its realization, there is therefore the knowledge of equality characterized by fearlessness" (*Mahāyānalakṣaṇasamuccaya* 305a4, 150a3-4).
And because it has this nature, that mind is the form of Ratnasambhava.

And by virtue of the purity of the self, it has the nature of the knowledge of stainless discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). This knowledge of discernment always directly perceives the expansion of all objects of knowledge in all their aspects; it is like a mine of all *dhāraṇīs* and *samādhis*; it displays supernatural powers that are beyond the reach of Hari, Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, and others, as well as all *śrāvakas*, *pratyekabuddhas*, and *bodhisattvas*; it cuts through all doubts of everyone; and it rains down the great nectar of the Dharma according to the inclinations [of beings]. As it is said in the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*:
The wisdom of discernment is always unimpeded regarding all objects of knowledge, and it is truly like a treasury of dhāraṇīs and samādhis.
It displays all manifestations within all circles of assemblies, cuts through all doubts, and rains down the great Dharma.
(Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 9.72–73).
It is also stated in the *Ātmasādhanāvatāra*:
"The knowledge of individual investigation arises from being non-erroneous regarding all objects of knowledge" (*Ātmasādhanāvatāra* 57a6).

Thus, because it purifies subtle conceptualization through the signless (*animitta*), the knowledge of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) has the nature of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisamvid*). And the analytical knowledges are: the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisamvid*), the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisamvid*), the analytical knowledge of etymology (*nirukti-pratisamvid*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisamvid*). As it is said in the *Mahāyānalakṣaṇasamuccaya*:

"Therefore, the knowledge of discernment, which has the nature of the analytical knowledges, [arises] from the purification of subtle conceptualization by means of the signless" (*Mahāyānalakṣaṇasamuccaya* 305a4, 150a4-5).
And because its essence is this, that mind has the form of Amitābha.

And because of the purification of conceptual construction, it has the nature of the knowledge that carries out activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*). This knowledge that carries out activities, however, effects the welfare of all sentient beings through emanations in all world-systems that are of various kinds, immeasurable, and inconceivable. Furthermore, that emanation of a Buddha is to be understood as always and in every way inconceivable, by way of the diversity of its functions, its number, and its fields.
As it is said in the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*:
The knowledge of accomplishing what is to be done, through emanations in all realms that are diverse,
immeasurable, and inconceivable, effects the welfare of all sentient beings.

The inconceivable emanation of the Buddha is to be understood at all times through its various functions, its distinctions, its numbers, and its fields; and it should be known in every respect as such.
Thus [it is said in] the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* (9.74–75).
And it is stated in the *Ātmasādhanāvatāra*:
"By virtue of being the cause for the gateway to the welfare of the entire world, it consists of the gnosis that accomplishes what is to be done" (*Ātmasādhanāvatāra* 57a6).

Thus, because it is determined to be the basis for the realization of the essence of all phenomena by means of the *dharmadhātu*, the [wisdom] that takes the form of great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and great compassion (*karuṇā*) serves as the cause for bringing about the separation of the entire world from suffering and its causes, and for establishing them in benefit and happiness. As it is said in the *Mahāyānalakṣaṇasamuccaya*:

"By means of the *dharmadhātu*, there is the state of being the basis for the realization of the essence of all phenomena; therefore, the wisdom of performing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) takes the form of great loving-kindness and compassion. (Mahāyānalakṣaṇasamuccaya 305a4-5, 150a5-6).

And this fourfold gnosis arises from *dhāraṇā* (retention) and the other [perfections]. Among these, from *dhāraṇā* there arises the mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*) regarding the teachings (*dharma*) that have been heard. From an even mind toward all sentient beings—through great loving-kindness and great compassion and through the equality of self—there is the full realization of the gnosis of equality (*samatājñāna*). The gnosis of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) has the correct illumination of the Dharma as its cause. The gnosis of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) has the performance of the tasks of all sentient beings as its cause. Thus it is said: "From retention, from an even mind, and from the correct illumination of the Dharma..."
And from the performance of duties, indeed, arises the manifestation of the four gnoses.
(Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 9.76).
Because its nature is the accomplishment of what is to be done, that mind is also the form of Amoghasiddhi.

And because it is the purification of the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), it is the form of the knowledge of the stainless and perfectly pure dharmadhātu. However, the knowledge of the perfectly pure dharmadhātu does not exist for Śrāvakas and others, as they suffer a loss of the vision of the knowledge of liberation. Furthermore, the threefold action of body, speech, and mind is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge; it is the knowledge of the three times that is unattached and unimpeded.
And because it has this nature, that mind has the form of Akṣobhya.

(123.3) The purification of suchness (*tathatā-viśuddhi*) is characterized by the omniscience in all its aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is the stainless suchness resulting from the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) of the path; it has the form of the inconceivable object of cognition as its antidote; it has the nature of being established and fixed as a subverter [of obstacles]; and it is like the appearance of birth in the form of a flower. Through its connection with that, by virtue of having that nature, this very mind is established as the Lord of the Mandala (*cakreśa*). (123.4) And that revolution of the basis of the path is differentiated according to the distinctions of the application to specific bases and so forth.

In that regard, the distinction is fourfold, consisting of the distinctions of the field, vision, teaching, and the attainment of mastery. Among these, the distinction of the field is the purification of the field, such as being composed of cotton-soft jewels and so forth. The distinction of vision is the direct perception of all objects of knowledge through the state of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). The distinction of teaching is the immeasurable teaching through various doors—profound, sublime, and diverse.

The distinction of the attainment of mastery is the specific attainment of qualities such as the unimpeded superknowledges (*abhijñā*), which serve as the basis for accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings.

The basis (*āśraya*) is fourfold, distinguished by way of the object (*ālambana*), the application (*prayoga*), the benefit (*anuśaṃsā*), and thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*). In this context, the "object" consists of the teaching of the *tantras* and so forth, because [the realization] arises depending upon that as its objective support; it also includes conviction in that, certainty regarding that, and the fulfillment of the accumulations (*sambhāra*). From the perspective of "application": there is the inconceivable distancing [of faults] characterized by the modes of signlessness, immeasurability, incalculability, and mastery; the bestowal of unsurpassed bliss; the purification of the afflictive and cognitive obscurations (*kleśajñeyāvaraṇa*) and the entry into the knowledge of all aspects of the knowable (*sarvākārajñeya*) attained subsequent to that; the complete purification of the Buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra*); and the ripening of sentient beings and the conferral of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

In relying upon and stabilizing these, there is a fourfold application and practice: the initially conceptualized, the one who has mastery over some knowledge, the one who has attained mastery over knowledge, and the one who has mastery over perfect knowledge. It is distinguished by that.
The object is fourfold; it is also distinguished by those divisions because there is no absence of means [to reach it].
The purpose, however, is only one.

The purpose is threefold, distinguished by the differences of aspiration, objective support, and application. That is to say: through the aspiration for perfect enlightenment in proximity to it for the sake of sentient beings; through the objective support of the welfare of sentient beings by means of teaching; and through the application of abiding in the various types of meditative concentration.
Its specific nature consists in its having great bliss as its intrinsic nature.

The distinction of qualities (*guṇabheda*), however, consists in: its excellence by virtue of being for the sake of others; the turning back of the *ālayavijñāna*, which is the cause of affliction (*saṃkleśa*); the cessation of afflictions; its duration until the end of *saṃsāra* because of the continued activity of the Buddhas; its dual nature due to the manifestation of both perfect enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*) and final nirvana (*parinirvāṇa*); its non-duality because it does not abide in either *saṃsāra* or *nirvāṇa* and is devoid of both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); its equality with the Śrāvakas and others through the commonality of liberation from afflictions; and [its distinction] by means of the Buddha-qualities such as the powers (*bala*) and the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*).
It is "distinguished" because of its incomparability, and it is "all-pervading" because it encompasses the instruction of all vehicles. As it has been said:
"Engagement, emergence, non-engagement, the basis, cessation, recurrence, and then that which is both dual and non-dual—this [path] is equal, distinguished, and all-pervading."
The transformation of the Tathāgatas is thus intended.
(Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 9.14) Thus,
because of the absence of error regarding form and so forth.
It is perfectly established as having the nature of the immaculate aggregates and so forth;
because of the cessation of stinginess and other such faults, it consists of the pure dharmas of the stages and perfections. 124

124.1 Due to the absence—that is, the non-existence through analytical investigation—of the delusion regarding form and so forth, which consists in the superimposition of oneness and so on, there are the aggregates, bases, and elements that are stainless and free from conceptual construction. Their existence is the ultimate nature (*pāramārthika-svabhāva*). That mind, established as the Lord of the Mandala (*cakreśa*), is perfected in that form. Because it is pure, qualities such as stinginess—the failure to relinquish—and the like are "white" (*śukla*) phenomena, being devoid of the stains of affliction (*saṃkleśa*). That mind consists of those; it consists of the white phenomena of the perfections (*pāramitā*) and the stages (*bhūmi*). [It is characterized by] the non-conceptual arising of self and others...
And by virtue of being its basis, the mind consists of wisdom and means through its profound and vast nature, proceeding in due order. (125)

125.1 [36b2-3] It is non-conceptual, effortless, and flows by its own nature; therefore, that mind which consists of wisdom and skillful means—by virtue of being the basis for the arising of the mundane and supramundane fruits for oneself and others, through the sequence of practice, and by way of being profound and vast—is the mind.

125.2 By this it is said: The nature of wisdom (*prajñā*) is profound because it is characterized by effortless flow arising from the abandonment of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and so forth, and because it is unfathomable due to its non-abiding in existence or non-existence. Its nature as method (*upāya*) is sublime because it is compassion (*dayā*) by nature, serving as the cause for the natural arising of both mundane and supramundane excellence. This mind, consisting of the support and the supported, has the form of the wheel of reality (*saccakra*). Furthermore, this state of being wisdom and method should be understood here as the form of the *vidyāpuruṣa* (the personification of knowledge), whose very nature is that. As it has been said:
"That which is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) is wisdom (*prajñā*), while the characteristic of existence is the means (*upāya*).
(Guhyasamājatantra 18.33cd).
Thus, it is precisely this mind, appearing in the form of the maṇḍala circle, that is the truth of the path to manifest enlightenment (*sambodhi*). And it has been said:
"The mind of awakening (bodhicitta) is defined as the inseparability of emptiness and compassion" (Guhyasamājatantra 18.38cd).

126.0 [36b6] Now, with the words "and not anything at all," etc. (cf. 117a), that absence of difference—or rather, the non-difference—between the intrinsic natures of existence and quiescence which was previously mentioned, is also not ultimately real; thus he says: "But from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*).
"From the perspective of ultimate reality, however, nothing is asserted as non-different from another, nor is anything non-different."
Because other apprehensions have ceased and because it is perceived as such, there is no variegatedness.
In reality, however, no entity whatsoever is non-different from another; thus, it is devoid of difference, for there is no perception of it as "non-different," which would constitute non-difference.

126.2 Thus, it is established by valid cognition that this conventional reality (*sāṃvṛta-tattva*), which is devoid of all objective form and is mere representation (*pratītimātra*), is the truth. And this being so, the meaning is that everything such as difference and non-difference, which is established by those engaged in worldly discourse, is merely the fabrication of the artisan of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Having thus reflected within one's own heart upon that which resides in the center of the mark situated in the stainless moon—
One should contemplate one's own mind as radiant, in the form of the drop (*bindu*) of the three mantras. 127

The word *iti* is used here in the sense of "thus. Having thus reflected upon and considered the meaning just explained within one's own heart—that is, within the heart of the *jñānasattva*—there is a stainless moon; situated in the center of the symbol (*cihna*) located therein is the mantra, the syllable *maṃ*. That very syllable, through its rays of light, brings about the inclusion of the world within the nature of the Victors (*jinatva*). Because it possesses rays and has the form of a drop (*bindu*), it is a "drop" (*bindu*). One should contemplate one's own mind as having that as its essential form (*svarūpa*) and nature (*svabhāva*)—that is, as having the form of the perfected drop—and as radiant. One should contemplate the garland of rays of that mind.
Having awakened the supreme body of the Vajra of Speech and Body,
one should again meditate upon the stream of the nectar of gnosis established right there. 128

128.1 [37a6–37b2] The connection is as follows: one should meditate on the garland of rays of that mind—which has the form of a drop (*bindu*) and the form of the syllable *Aṃ*—as being settled right here once again. Having done what? He says: "having awakened. That is to say, having illuminated the body of the Vajra of Speech and Body through the sequence beginning with the *Cihna-garbha* by means of the garland of rays expanded from that very [mind], which is supreme because it is non-different from the Vajra-body of the Tathāgata and so forth. And by this stream of rays, one should instantly resolve upon one's own lord (*svādhipa*), who, as before, takes the form of the three samādhis.
129.0 Now he describes the withdrawal preceded by the radiation that reaches the limits of space— beginning with the words "the internal body" (*antastanu*) and so forth:
"Then, having illuminated the entire internal body with that [light] on all sides, [with rays] infinite..."
"Then, filling the universe with arrays of light-rays emerging from every pore...

(129). The word "then" (*atha*) refers to the period immediately following the completion of the initial yoga, the mandala-kings, and so forth, within the drop (*bindu*). Having illuminated the internal body of Mañjuvajra by means of that garland of rays which has entered it, according to the sequence beginning with the "symbol in the womb" (*cihnagarbha*), one should meditate—connecting this with what precedes—that one fills the entire universe on all sides with infinite arrays of light-rays emerging from every pore, while that garland of rays remains sequentially established in that very same place (as seen in 128c and 128cd). This is the meaning.
"Visualizing the wheel even within the *bindu*, one should repeatedly perform such emanation and reabsorption as long as one desires.
(129.2) By this much, the third meditative absorption (*samādhi*), known as the "Supreme King of Actions" (*karmarājāgri*) consisting of the *bindu*-yoga, has been explained.
Immediately following the conclusion of the *bindu*-yoga, he states the procedure for the cultivation of the subtle yoga (*sūkṣmayoga*), beginning with the words "the subtle," and so forth. (130.0)
One should meditate on one's own subtle mark, or else on the radiant [point] situated at the tip of the nose,
within which the circle of sages is contained.
"By means of compassion, one whose true wisdom is mastered within... (130.1).

One should meditate upon one's own insignia, a sword, which is subtle and the size of a barley grain; or else, as for "steadfastness," one should meditate on it placed at the tip of the nose. "By means of compassion" (*kṛpayā*) means by means of skillful means (*upāya*).

"One whose true wisdom is mastered within" (*āntasatprajñaḥ*) refers to one by whom true wisdom (*satprajñā*) has been grasped or internalized; the meaning is that he is the embodiment of wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāyamūrti*).
Having perceived the sign of stability,
there is an emanation of rays issued forth by the Lords of Sages,
accompanied by various kinds of symbols.
The wise one should practice this again and again.
Regarding the signs of stability:
first is the appearance of a mirage, and the second is the appearance of smoke.
The third has the appearance of a firefly; the fourth blazes like a lamp;
the fifth, however, is constant light, resembling a cloudless sky.
(Guhyasamājatantra 18.150cd–151) Thus it is said.

Having perceived such a sign of stability (*sthairyanimitta*) of that subtle yoga (*sūkṣmayoga*), the wise one should repeatedly perform an emanation (*spharaṇa*) by means of those rays which have issued from that subtle sign (*tad iti sūkṣmacihna*), and by means of the Lords of Sages (*munīndra*) who have emerged from them, as well as by various signs, the excellent weapons, and the great clouds of Bodhisattvas.
By this much, the subtle yoga has been explained.

131.3 Regarding both the yoga of the drop (*bindu*) and the subtle yoga (*sūkṣmayoga*), the service (*sevā*), near-attainment (*upasādhana*), attainment (*sādhana*), and great attainment (*mahāsādhana*) of Mañjuvajra, his consort, and the deities of the maṇḍala should be understood—just as before—to have results, such as the natural outflow (*niḥsyanda*) and so forth, which are respectively weak, middling, and intense.

As for what has been stated by some—that for both *binduyoga* and *sūkṣmayoga*, there are four members each that are the results of the superior outflow (*adhimātra-niḥsyanda*) and so forth—that is not tenable. Since the Lord’s [yogas] have mild members and their fruits, and those of wisdom have middling ones, it is therefore appropriate to say they are the results of the mild outflow and so forth, and not the results of the superior outflow and so forth.

131.5 [38b1-5] Now, regarding the third meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because it is capable of exhausting all opposing factors (*vipakṣa*), it is said that even for the Blessed One there is no wheel of spokes (as noted in 130c). This is because other members, which possess outflows (*saniḥsyanda*) and are intended for specific purposes such as the gradual diminution of opposing factors, must necessarily be admitted. Consequently, by implication, here too there must be some distinction based on degrees such as "weak" (*mṛdu*) and so forth, in relation to one another.

Furthermore: "Through the resolutions (*adhimokṣa*) regarding the outflows and so forth, the drops (*bindu*), the subtle, and those born from the three secrets are to be meditated upon according to the distinctions of weak and so forth; likewise, the yogas are to be practiced like the services (*sevā*) and so on."

As it has been stated by Bhadrapāda in the *Guhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi* (113), even that has been refuted by those who speak thus, being far greater than the great; so, enough with excessive deliberation. Thus, this remains established: that even for the subtle drop (*bindu*), the limbs of practice such as service (*sevā*) and their results, such as its outflow (*niḥsyanda*), are distinguished by the divisions of "mild" (*mṛdu*) and so forth. And all of this is to be meditated upon through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) by means of another appearance by the yogin while still situated within the previous maṇḍala.
132.0 [38b7] To explain the recitation (*japa*), he says: "The recitation," and so forth.
With the mind focused upon the recitation, [one should perform it] within one's own mind, which is the Lord of Mind, the self-nature of all phenomena.
Having visualized his own mantra as a multicolored ray of light, the wise practitioner should perform the recitation.

(132) The meaning is as follows: with a mind focused through the firm conviction (*adhimokṣa*) of pure ego-identity (*viśuddhāhaṃkāra*) upon the Lord of One’s Own Mind—the King of Mind who is the nature of all phenomena, whose essence is the universe, and who takes the form of the mandala-circle; that is to say, one whose self is the mind in the form of the mandala-circle. The practitioner of mantra should perform the recitation while visualizing his own mantra—the syllable *Aṃ* residing in the heart of the Knowledge Being (*jñānasattva*)—as a multicolored ray of light, because it is interwoven with the syllables *Oṃ* and so forth located within the symbols in the hearts of one's own Body-Vajra and the others.
133.0 [39a2] How so? He says: "Restrained by breath-control" (*prāṇāyāma*), and so forth. [Having clearly recited... the King of Mantras.
One should perform the radiation (*spharaṇa*) of the body and so forth both gradually and simultaneously.

(133) By means of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), through the processes of propulsion and attraction, one should clearly utter [the mantra], well-restrained and free from rapidity and the like. Although the radiation and the utterance are simultaneous, the use of the absolutive suffix (*ktvā*) is intended to show that the commencement of the utterance occurs prior [to the radiation]. Thus, one should radiate while uttering, but not utter while radiating. And it is said in the *Śrīsamāja*:
"Uttering [the mantra], one should emanate the vajras; at the conclusion, one should indicate the withdrawal," so it is said in the *Guhyasamājatantra* (13.13ab).

133.2 Having thus uttered [the seed-syllables], one should perform the radiation (*spharaṇa*) of the body and so forth, either sequentially or simultaneously. From those syllables of the body and so forth, respectively, or simultaneously, one should meditate on the sequential radiation of Kāyavajra and the others, each accompanied by ten goddesses and a Tathāgata; indeed, the radiation of the body and so forth must be performed precisely as accompanied by the ten goddesses and the Tathāgatas.
However, from the seed-syllable of the Jñānasattva, one should radiate only the goddesses and the Tathāgatas, and not the Jñānasattva itself; thus one should radiate from both.
[The space of the belly is the body and so forth...]
Having filled [the space] with rays of light,

and having emanated [the deities] through various arrays of worship as before [... || 134 Then, having filled the interior of the sky— the belly of the firmament— with the light shining from the mouths of the rays, "as before" means according to the procedure previously stated in the second samādhi, beginning with "by the light of one's own seed-syllable within the heart of the lotus," [one visualizes] Vicitrarūpavajrā and the others.
[Having seen the vast multitude of lords of sages subdued by the great bliss of union with true wisdom— ]
*[One should cause them to enter into one's own self at the end.

|| 135 || (39b1-4) By this it is said: having withdrawn the subtle yoga, and having emitted from the *oṃ* syllables and so forth situated in the center of the wheel and other symbols the goddesses and Tathāgatas such as Kāyavajra, either sequentially or simultaneously at the time of recitation, one should perform the recitation (*jāpa*) while causing their re-absorption along with worship. This is the mantra-recitation.
(39b4) In order to explain the nourishment (*āpyāyana*), he says:
With the movement of his mind somewhat diminished by the fatigue of investigating the reality of his own heart,
[he was refreshed] by the musical performances of true knowledge.

"Having been awakened, one should worship the wheel. (136) "In one's own heart" means the syllable *maṃ* situated within the emblem located in the heart of the Jñānasattva; that very syllable is the reality (*tattva*) because it consists of the meditative absorptions such as the Initial Union (*ādiyoga*). "Contemplation" (*nirūpaṇa*) is meditation (*dhyāna*). One who is "afflicted by weariness" (*parikheda*) is one whose mental activity or movement has become diminished and contracted due to the fatigue resulting from that [meditation]. Being thus exhausted, having been awakened—that is, stimulated—by the songs of the assembly of vidyās such as Locanā and the others, as before, one should worship the wheel.
(137) He speaks of the nourishment (*āpyāyana*):
One should duly draw forth the stream of one's own mind with the goad of the radiance of the prāṇa and apāna breaths,
in order to dispel weariness.
One should cause it to descend into the Body-Vajra and so forth.

"True mind" is the *bodhicitta*. The stream of water of that nature consists of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, the inhalation and exhalation; that itself is the light, and that itself is the hook by which it is drawn.
Alternatively, it is joined with the light accompanied by the winds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).

137.3 To dispel fatigue, one should contemplate the [syllable *praṇava*] falling upon the body and so forth for the sake of calming exhaustion—[the *praṇava*] which has become liquefied through the touch of the rays from its own seed-syllable. One should visualize it as it descends.

"According to rule" means: having moved a span's distance above the crown of the head, one should contemplate that within a moon-disk of the same measure, there is the *praṇava* (the syllable OṂ) surrounded by the five substances presided over by their respective seed-syllables. This is unified with the Tathāgatas drawn in by the rays of those seed-syllables. Through the stimulation of the rays from the seed-syllable of the Jñānasattva, and by the touch of the *praṇava* which has been liquefied, one should imagine everything becoming nectar.
