Then, in the form of a stream of the water of bodhicitta, one should satisfy the body and so forth through the circulation through all the channels; this is the meaning. Having rested for a moment in this manner, the wise practitioner should proceed according to the previously mentioned procedure.
"One should perform the recitation of the excellent mantra incessantly, yet remain unattached even to the mantra.

(138) Having rested for a moment according to the procedure just mentioned, "by the previously stated method"— that is, by the method of meditating on one's own mantra with variegated rays— one who is skilled in that should perform the recitation of the excellent mantra incessantly, remaining unattached even to the mantra.
139.0 [40a1-2] Now he states the dismissal (*visarjana*): "Having performed," and so forth.
The mantra-practitioner, having performed the praise, worship, and other rites, becomes filled with reverence at the time of dismissal.
Having established the wheel beginning with the *praṇava*, one should meditate upon the imagined body and so forth. || 139 ||

139.1 [40a2-3] At the conclusion of the meditation on the wheel and so forth, the mantra-practitioner, filled with agitation and reverence, having performed the praise, worship, and other rites as before, should meditate—that is, fully contemplate—with the vision of suchness, that the external wheel has been placed within the wheel of the gnosis-being (*jñānasattva*) by means of the three-syllable mantra beginning with the *praṇava* (OM). He is one for whom the wheel has been placed within by the *praṇava* and so forth. His body and other attributes, which depend upon conceptual construction, have been properly constructed; because he is in the presence of the "Foremost King of Rites" (*karmarājāgri*), the subtle yoga and so forth, up to the withdrawal of the wheel, are included therein. Thus should he meditate and thoroughly contemplate. With such a vision of reality.
Relying on the realm of sentient beings who have been liberated [from suffering],
one should, out of compassion, bring forth the aspirational prayers for the sake of the welfare of the world. || 140 ||

140.1 Having thus focused upon and realized the realm of sentient beings as being liberated by such a vision of reality (*tattvadṛg*)—which takes the form of the mandala of deities (*devatācakra*) and so forth—one should bring to mind the previous aspirational prayers, thinking: "Out of compassion, for the sake of the welfare of the world, may I always and in every way act for the benefit of the world," and so on.
Then, having arisen, one who is a pure being (*śuddhasattva*), maintaining the form of one's own deity within the mind, [should proceed].

Contemplating the objects of the senses as they were before, while establishing the arrangement of all sensory domains, he should—having arisen from that meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and maintaining the ego-identification (*ahaṃkāra*) with his own deity—thereby, being a pure being (*śuddhasattva*) because his ordinary form is empty by virtue of having the form of the deity, accomplish all his duties while contemplating the objects. This is the connection [of the verse]. To the question, "Of what kind are the objects? he says: "as before," meaning they are like an illusion (*māyopama*) due to the absence of the grasped (*grāhya*), the grasper (*grāhaka*), and so forth.
141.2 For this very reason, there is the systematic arrangement of all objects such as form and so forth,
through the purification of their respective intrinsic natures, corresponding respectively to those that have become the vajras of the body and so on.

But by way of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they are glorious and mutually inseparable from the form of Vajradhara. Furthermore, he specifies that through the complete purification of their own intrinsic natures, they have respectively become the vajras of body and so forth. For instance: through the purification of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) or the sense-field of form (*rūpāyatana*), there is Kāyavajra; through the purification of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*) or the sense-field of odor (*gandha*), there is Ratnasambhava; through the purification of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*) or the sense-field of taste (*rasa*), there is Amitābha; and through the purification of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) or the sense-field of touch (*sparśa*), there is Amogheśa.
Through the purification of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) or the sense-field of sound (*śabdāyatana*), one becomes the Mind-Vajra (*Cittavajra*).

Such purification, however, should be understood as being in accordance with the diverse inclinations (*adhimukti*) of sentient beings; in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), the Buddhas are to be understood as having the very nature of universal purity. Thus, meditating upon the objects—which have become the nature of the Body-Vajra and so forth—as the *dharmatā*, that is, in their true reality as non-different from one another, and as the forms of the deities of Vajradhara whose essence is suchness (*tathatā*), one should accomplish the totality [of the mandala]. (See 141d).
*Sampādayet samastam*.
Free from conceptualizing things erroneously,
his supreme worship of the entire circle of sages is constant. 143

143.1 Therefore, one who is liberated from—that is, has abandoned—the ordinary ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) consisting of erroneous conceptualizations in the form of the apprehended object and so forth, may accomplish and perform every duty, whether it be the wandering for the sake of expounding the true Dharma or the enjoyment of sensual pleasures.

143.2 And thus, for the yogin endowed with the divine ego-sense according to the aforementioned rule, the accomplishment of all duties is at all times this supreme worship of the circle of Sages (*municakra*), because that yogin remains perpetually in a state of meditative absorption (*samāhita*).
143.3 Thus far, the morning twilight ritual (*prātaḥsandhyā*) has been explained.
144.0 Now he describes the procedure for eating, beginning with "the moon at the heart":
"At the time of eating, having visualized the Lord of the Mandala upon the moon at one's own heart by means of his own seed-syllables..."
One should meditate on the nature of perfected bodhicitta as having a luminous radiance.

At the time of eating, one should take up and contemplate the circle of deities—the lords of the mandala—along with their respective seed-syllables such as *vuṃ*, within the moon at the heart of the *samayasattva*. Then, according to the previous procedure for tasting nectar, one's own food, which is of the nature of perfected bodhicitta and possesses a luminous radiance through the syllable *oṃ*, [should be visualized].
One's own food, purified by the equality of all things and consecrated with the three principles (*tattva*),
[is offered] to the deities of the body and so forth.
One should perform the act of satiation with that.

(145) One should meditate on it as purified by the equality of all things, consecrated as desired with the three principles—the syllables Oṃ, Āḥ, and Hūṃ. Through that, there is the satiation of the deities such as Kāyavajra;
one whose tongue is the vajra placed with the syllable Hūṃ.
One should act thus. Therefore, the mantra-practitioner should eat with the firm conviction (*adhimokṣa*) that he is nourishing the entire circle of sages residing within his heart.
Since the yogi’s meal has the nature of a fire-oblation (*homa*), the author states the procedure for the oblation in connection with that context, beginning with the word "unneya" (to be inferred).
This external procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*) is to be inferred; however, the mental [oblation] is performed by the mind alone,
through the burning of the fuel that consists of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth.
But he who abides in the samādhi of Vajrasattva, firm in intellect and performing [the rite], is proclaimed as unsurpassed in the blazing of gnosis.

"The knower of mantras should perform the homa" (Guhyasamājatantra 16.32cd–33a),

and so forth; by means of this very procedure prescribed for the homa in the sixteenth chapter, the external ritual of homa— consisting of oblations such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*)— is to be inferred, and it is to be applied and extended through this same method of excellence.

146.2 [41a2-3] However, this mental procedure for the fire offering (*homavidhi*), which consists in the nature of the yogin’s meal, should be understood as being performed by the mind alone through the very resolve (*adhimukti*) of that ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). But "in the blazing of gnosis" means that, moreover, there is a supreme fire offering in the fire of the gnosis of the equality of all phenomena; it is known as such because the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth are themselves the fuel, and they are consumed therein. Thus, the three types of fire offerings have been described: the external, the mental, and the supreme. In this way, with all desired objects, one's own self in the form of one's chosen deity...
One should worship either oneself or another;

this is considered by the Sugatas to be the correct commitment (*samaya*). (147) In this way—that is, according to the sequence described—one should worship with all desired objects such as form and so forth, whether it be oneself, one’s own [belongings], or another in the form of one’s chosen deity. Furthermore, although self and other are distinguished merely through conceptual imputation, in reality they consist of the aforementioned forms of self-cognition and take the form of the described deities; thus, the worship of the pure forms and so forth is the "commitment" (*samaya*) rightly intended by the Sugatas, because it is not to be transgressed. As it has been said:
While enjoying all objects of desire as one pleases,
one should worship both oneself and others through the yoga of one's own presiding deity.
When practiced with difficult observances and arduous hardships, it does not succeed;
but when practiced while enjoying all sensual pleasures, it succeeds quickly.
(Guhyasamājatantra 7.2–3).

[Question: But how can the enjoyment of all desired objects and so forth by the self itself—taking the form of worship—be the cause of the highest goods for the Śrāvakas and others, who [regard] form and so forth as [impure]? (Ātmasādhanāvatāra 59a2–3)
If it is argued that, in that case, even an image or the like—which is the very form of the intended deity and distinct from one's own self—could not be worthy of worship, we say:

no. For although it was stated that the enjoyment [of such objects] by Śrāvakas and others is prohibited, that too is untenable; for a prohibitive statement that functions in a general sense is sublated by a specific injunction. Indeed, a contradiction between an injunction and a prohibitive statement occurs only when they share the same object, not when they have different objects. (Ātmasādhanāvatāra 59a3–5)

For instance, for a śrāvaka who is attached to external objects, unskilled in means, and ignorant of the reality of things, it is good for a monk to have restraint with the eye; it is good to have restraint with the ear;
it is good to have restraint with the nose; it is good to have restraint with the tongue.
Restraint of the body is good; restraint of the mind is good. A monk who is restrained in every way is liberated from all suffering.

Regarding such scriptural statements as those from the *Mahāsāṅghika-prātimokṣasūtra* (p. xx), which generally prohibit the enjoyment of sensual pleasures: for yogins who have realized the reality of things, whose vision is most subtle, who possess firm divine pride (*devatāhaṃkāra*), and who are skilled in means, one should, having discerned form, offer it to the deities in its threefold aspect.
By serving with the enjoyment of all desires, one attains accomplishment swiftly.
Having attained the stability of body, speech, and mind, one attains enlightenment;
otherwise, one will certainly die prematurely and be cooked in hell.

(Guhyasamājatantra 7.5) Through difficult and intense observances, the body withers and becomes afflicted by suffering. From suffering the mind is distracted, and through distraction, accomplishment is otherwise.
There is nothing whatsoever that should not be performed by means of a mind endowed with wisdom and skillful means.
Always being free from doubt, enjoy the fivefold objects of desire.

By means of these [verses] beginning with *Guhyendutilaka* 271a, joy arises for one who is gladdened; for one whose mind is joyful, the body becomes pliant; one whose body is pliant experiences happiness; for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated; and one whose mind is concentrated understands things as they truly are. (Śrāvakabhūmi, p. xx)

If it is argued that because there is a difference in scope—since [the latter] is contradicted by specific scriptural injunctions such as those mentioned above which prescribe the enjoyment of desires—and because the nature of what is to be done is not different, it is impossible for them to have different objects, we say: no. This is like the production of a *ḍittha* (a name for a person), or like the forceful extraction of earth submerged in water even while it bears the designation "water. However, for Bodhisattvas, whatever action is impelled by virtuous mental orientations such as compassion is within the scope of permission, because that is the defining characteristic of the Bodhisattva path.
"There is no offense for one whose mind is virtuous, out of affection and compassion" (Bodhisattvasamvaraviṃśikā 20cd). Likewise—
"Even that which is prohibited is permitted for the compassionate one who perceives the welfare [of others].
And it is further said:
Through the resolve of Bodhisattvas,
whether it be auspicious or inauspicious,
everything attains the state of goodness.
For their minds are under control.
(Catuḥśataka 5.5).

This is because the abstention from taking life and so forth is established for those lacking skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*), whereas for one skilled in means, such actions are permitted. As it is said in the *Trayastriṃśa* and the *Vairocanābhisambodhi*:

In this regard, a bodhisattva completely and in every way abstains from taking life, even to the point that he sees other beings harming the Three Jewels. Likewise, he abstains from taking what is not given, even to the point that he sees other beings being miserly. Similarly, regarding the wives of others or those belonging to another, he does not even give rise to a mind of covetousness, much less proceed to embrace them or engage in the union of the two sexual organs. (From the *Vairocanābhisambodhi*, source untraced)

"Except in such cases where [an action] ought not to be done"—thus, the detailed classification of all the trainings (*śikṣā*) should be consulted. For bodily and vocal actions motivated by an intention for gain and so forth are unwholesome (*akuśala*) because they yield undesirable results, but they are not unwholesome by their own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), since their intrinsic character (*svabhāva*) is neutral (*avyākṛta*). However, that which is impelled by the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) to benefit others is of the nature of the Bodhisattva training because it brings about the unsurpassed fruit. And a Bodhisattva who maintains his own conduct in this manner would not be blameworthy. As it is said in the *Āryākṣayamatinirdeśa*:
"Without feeling disgust toward any skillful means" (*Avijugupsamānā sarvopāyakauśaleṣu*).

For even when the enjoyment of objects and so forth is equal, the distinction between what is blameworthy and what is blameless is established by virtue of one's resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*); for the enjoyment of objects is defiled for one whose attachment is defiled, whereas it is undefiled for one whose intention is undefiled—thus everything is well-established. (Ātmasādhanāvatāra 59a5–60a5)

147.9 For this very reason, he will say: "In such a case... and so forth (see 149a), as well as: "When the mind is free from all impurities, how could there be black karma? (see 151cd). Furthermore, this honoring of oneself and others with all desired objects is the *samaya* (vow/pledge), because it is not to be transgressed. 147.10 And this has been stated specifically with reference to those yogins who possess a skillful and firm divine pride (*devatāhaṃkāra*). Otherwise, however, there would be a fall into the miserable states of existence (*apāya*). As it has been said:
"The wise person, having thoroughly examined and carefully reflected, should effect the entry."
Otherwise, his entering the fire does not equal even a sixteenth part [of this merit].
He who, having understood the reality through diligent effort, cultivates resolute conviction, attains success; otherwise, he falls into the great hells.
Thus [it is said in a source not traced].

Now, with four *āryā* verses, he explains in detail and with supporting arguments this very same point that was previously stated in the passage beginning with "And he who, having arisen, is a pure being" (*yaś cotthāya śuddhasattva*).
Reflecting upon the benefit for the world in accordance with its needs, as well as the complete worship of the Sugatas,
he performed various actions of body and so forth.

One should always perform it with a concentrated mind. (148) Constantly weighing the benefit for the world—namely, the mundane and supramundane purposes of beings—in accordance with each respective action of body and so forth; and constantly weighing the appropriate worship of the Sugata, such as external offerings of flowers and the like; one who is always concentrated, whose self is purified through the divine identity (*devatāhaṃkāra*) both externally and internally, should perform those various actions of body and so forth, such as circumambulation and the rest. And while the mind is in such a state...
Whatever action consists of body and speech,
that has been declared by all the perfectly awakened ones to be the form of mudrās and mantras. (149)

149.1 When the mind is thus filled with the divine ego-sense (*devatāhaṃkāra*) and is resolved in this way, it has been declared by all the Perfect Buddhas that whatever action of body or speech exists takes the very form of mudrās and mantras.
150.0 To address the doubt as to how bodily and other actions, which appear otherwise, can come to have the form of mudrās and so forth, he says: "But in one and the same thing" (*ekatraiva tu*).
That is, in one and the same object.
Since there are many specific karmas that produce suffering, happiness, and liberation, and which possess forms brought about by various volitions. (150)

150.1 [41b6–42a3] For those who know the reality of detachment and attachment toward objects such as the body of a woman, there arise—respectively—the various conceptual constructions (*saṃkalpa*) that [perceive her] as a corpse, a woman, or an illusion. These [constructions], having been accumulated and produced as their own nature, become specific karmic actions through successive performance and so forth, which give rise to suffering, pleasure, or liberation. Thus, regarding all objects, one should see that according to whatever conceptual construction arises, so too will specific appearances (*pratibhāsa*) result from its repeated practice. This is what is meant by the words "many" (*bahavaḥ*).
And likewise, it has been stated even in the system of external objects (*bahirarthanaya*):
Even though the external object is without distinction, pleasure and pain arise due to the distinction in mental cultivation; therefore, pleasure and the like do not have the form of the object.
Likewise: "In the case of a wandering ascetic, a lustful man, and a dog, with respect to the body of a single woman... (Pramāṇaviniścaya 1.23).
There are three conceptual constructions: [the body as] a corpse, a woman, or food.
(Bodhicittavivaraṇa 20).

However, in the absence of external objects, there is no fault, for mere cognition—being under one's own control—becomes exactly as it is habituated. "Yad" means because this is established by experience in the form of wholesome and unwholesome [states].
It was stated that the body and so forth [arise] through the power of volition;
thus, when the mind is free from all impurities, how could there be black karma? 151

151.1 Therefore, it has been taught by the Sugatas that bodily and other actions take the form of wholesome or unwholesome due to the power of volition (*cetanā*), but not in reality. Consequently, it is entirely logical that bodily and other actions assume the form of seals (*mudrā*) and so forth through the power of conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*), because they are purified by the purification of conceptualization. As it has been said:
"By whatever state of being the minds of men are joined, they attain the nature of that very thing, just like a multiform gem."* *This verse is cited from the *Bodhicittavivaraṇa* (verse 38).*
Thus [it is said in a source] whose location is untraced.

By the principle just mentioned, since the mind consists entirely of purity and all defilements have been eliminated, how could black karma possibly arise? There is no possibility for such an occurrence in one whose mind is virtuous.
The meaning is that, according to the sequence stated in such passages as *Bodhisattvasamvaraviṃśikā* 20c, [the violation] could not possibly occur at all.
Now, he states the procedure for restoring one who has broken the commitments (*samaya*), beginning with the words "the commitment" (*samaya*) and so forth.
When the samaya is impaired, one should correctly place the universal heart-vajra upon the moon held in the heart;
[this is] the illustrious Samayavajrayogin.

Having meditated upon the world as pure by nature (*prakṛtiviśuddha*), [the connection is as follows]: regarding the commitment (*samaya*) such as that which is to be guarded, when it is impaired, one should receive initiation (*abhiṣeka*) for the sake of destroying that fault (see 153b). To the question "How? he says: "according to rule" (*yathāvat*), meaning according to the sequence of the oral instructions. In the center of a lotus with petals of all colors, upon a moon disc, is a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*); situated upon that moon is the glorious Samayavajra, who is Amoghasiddhi. His "yoga" refers to the meditation on the initial yoga and so forth; he who possesses this is the "glorious Samayavajra-yogin."

One who has placed the universal heart-mantra upon the moon at the heart, together with the seed-syllable of the universal vajra—that is the "universal vajra" (viśvavajra); he is thus "one by whom the universal vajra is placed upon the moon at the heart. The meaning is: the universal vajra empowered by the syllable *khaṃ* produced from the syllable *khaṃ* emanated from the moon at the heart. Having meditated that the entire world is pure by nature (*prakṛtiviśuddha*), one should receive consecration in the center of a lotus with universal petals according to the previous sequence.
This very sequence should be meditated upon specifically even in the external ritual of bathing.

(153) "According to the previous sequence" means that one should receive the consecration and cultivate it within oneself according to the order stated beginning with "to the Best of Sages" (verse 61a). However, regarding faults such as disrespect toward the guru, it should be understood that after performing the rite in this manner, one should provide a meal accompanied by a dakṣiṇā and attend to other duties. Pointing out that this same sequence of consecration is to be meditated upon even in the external ritual of bathing, he says: "Even in the external," and so forth. "Specifically" means according to one's own deity.

154.0 [42b4] Now he describes the yoga to be practiced during the intervals between the junctions (*saṃdhyāntara*): "Also during the intervals between the junctions. Having likewise performed the recitation (*japa*) preceded by worship and other rites during the intervals between the junctions, with the wheel situated within the heart.
"Endowed with compassion and wisdom, one should sleep.

(154) 154.1 The word "also" (*api*) indicates that he did not merely perform the recitation preceded by worship and other rites earlier [in the morning], but also during the intervals between the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*). This is the meaning: for there are two kinds of practitioners of yoga—the distracted (*vyagra*) and the one-pointed (*ekāgra*).

154.2 In that regard, a busy practitioner, even during the midday or other junctions, should sit upon a comfortable seat and visualize the insignia and so forth of his own deity. Having expanded the mandala by means of the three syllables and received initiation, he should likewise perform recitation preceded by offerings and so forth as before. Upon dismissal, being filled with devotion, he should perform the offering, praise, and tasting of nectar (*amṛtāsvāda*). Then, with the wheel having entered his heart by means of the three syllables, he should carry out the subsequent procedure as previously described; this is the remainder [of the instruction].

At midnight, having released the *jñānacakra* with the three-syllable mantra ending in *muḥ*, and having caused the external wheel to enter the internal wheel, one who is endowed with compassion and wisdom should sleep oneself.

(154.3) The one-pointed yogi, likewise, having performed the recitation preceded by worship and so forth according to the sequence beginning with the initial yoga (*ādiyoga*), and desiring to dismiss [the deities], should perform worship, praise, and the tasting of nectar (*amṛtāsvāda*). Then, with the wheel situated within the heart by means of the three syllables, he should carry out the subsequent practice as before. At midnight, however, he should sleep in the same manner. (155.0) Regarding the object of meditation at the time of rising from sleep, he says:
At the time of rising,
the glorious Sage, urged by the musical concert of the goddesses,
should rise.
*Japādikaṃ pūrvavidhinaiva* (The recitation and so forth are according to the previous rule).

At the time of rising, during the morning twilight (*prātaḥsandhyā*), impelled by the concert of goddesses such as Māmakī, the glorious sage—possessing only the seed-syllable situated in the moon of the heart, appearing in his ordinary form, and not engaging in irrelevant matters such as delighting in speech—being a yogin conceived from the beginning, should perform the recitation and so forth. "According to the previous rule" means that one should accomplish the recitation and so forth either by the previously mentioned rule of the initial yoga (*ādiyoga*) and so on, or by the rule stated as "or else" (*athavā*) and so forth.

But one who possesses some mastery over knowledge, impelled by the songs of the goddesses, should rise in the morning and, assuming the form of Mañjuvajra, utter the mantra: *oṃ dharmadhātusvabhāvātmako ’ham*. Thereafter, having visualized everything else as before, he should perform the recitation and other rites according to the same rules for the twilight period and the previously established procedure.

Furthermore, one who has attained mastery over knowledge and is made beautiful by even more firm practice, being free from the conceptualization of rules regarding the junctions of time (*saṃdhyā*) and so forth, should constantly rely upon yoga, contemplating at every moment the wheel that consists of emanation and reabsorption, which resides within the atoms of all things and is perfectly accomplished in all its aspects; for in his case, the rules regarding the junctions of time and so forth are merely conceptual constructs.

But one who has mastery over right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), through extremely firm practice, meditates upon the self as all-pervading, liberated from moment-to-moment perception, consisting of the wheel of the three truths that functions effortlessly, and having the form of supreme bliss; such a person accomplishes the welfare of the worlds, because for one who has arrived at this state, the reliance on yoga at every moment is no longer a mere mental construction. Indicating the procedure for the means of accomplishment (*siddhi-sādhana*), he says: "In accomplishment" (*siddhau*).
This refers to one who has obtained the causal signs (*nimitta*) for accomplishment.
Having performed the worship of the three principles within one's own mind,
situated in the previously described wheel,
one should accomplish the desired siddhi. 156

Whether for a minor accomplishment (*kṣudrasiddhi*) or a great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*), having obtained the respective signs—having attained the auspicious signs such as dreams of deities as described in the fifteenth chapter and elsewhere—and having performed the worship of the three principles (*tritattvapūjā*), which is the worship consisting of the meditation on the Body-Vajra and so forth as previously stated, one should, while abiding in the wheel situated within one’s own mind (one’s own consciousness), accomplish the desired accomplishment (*siddhi*) of the sword and so forth according to the method taught in the eleventh chapter and elsewhere.

156.2 Therefore, it should be understood that by this, the fulfillment of the accumulations (*sambhāra*) through the attainment of the signs of the accomplishment of one's desired goal is established by means of the worship of reality (*tattva-pūjā*) and so forth.

157.0 [43b2-3] He states the procedure for warding off obstacles (*vighna*) if they should arise at the time of drawing the maṇḍala or performing the means of accomplishment (*siddhi-sādhana*), beginning with the words "the obstacle" (*vighnam*):
"The obstacle in the wheel called Amṛta... (*vighnam amṛtākhyacakre*).
Having received the consecration, one destroys [the obstacles] without effort;
moreover, he who remains situated in its center shall possess that wheel. 157

157.1 [43b3-4] One who has received initiation into the wheel of Amṛtakuṇḍalin, which is called Amṛta, destroys obstacles without effort because the yoga of the deity has become naturalized within him. To the question, "What is that wheel called Amṛta? he says: "But the wheel... That wheel of the deities of the maṇḍala would belong to him who should stand in the center of that maṇḍala-wheel; such is the general rule.

Therefore, because he stands in the center and acts as the presiding lord (*adhipati*), that wheel belongs to Vighnāntaka alone. The meaning is that, having become the enemy of the presiding obstacles therein, one should receive the consecration according to the ritual rules for the purpose of dispelling those obstacles.

(158.0) [43b6-7] Now, wishing to conclude the subject matter of this section, and demonstrating that the mind—whose form is the inconceivable wheel of deities—is the antidote to the suffering of existence, he says: "Ordinary," and so forth.
[This refers to] the activity of ordinary conceptualization.
Furthermore, there is indeed no suffering of existence whatsoever;
this [state] is perceived directly by the mind as being its opposite. (158)

158.1 [43b7–44a1] Ordinary conceptualization (*prākṛtavikalpa*) is the construction of "self" (*ātman*), "belonging to self" (*ātmīya*), and so forth; its activity (*vṛtti*) is its arising as a continuum. There is nothing else that constitutes the suffering of existence (*bhavaduḥkha*) apart from that—it is simply this [conceptualization] itself that is the suffering of existence. And it is precisely that which is directly opposed to such ordinary conceptualization—the mind (*cetas*) in the form of the maṇḍala-circle, possessing a profound and sublime nature—that is realized, because it is directly opposed to the [process of] affirmation and negation. 159.0 [44a1-2] Demonstrating this very opposition, he says: "profound," and so forth. [In the phrase] "in the profound and sublime self..."
In that [consciousness], no conceptual construction appears;
nor has anything other than pure awareness been established before us. (159)

159.1 Because that nature of the suffering of existence—the ordinary conceptual construction—does not appear, does not manifest, within that mind which consists of the truth of the path, having the form of the maṇḍala-circle and the essence of profound and vast wisdom and skillful means; this is the meaning of "experience itself is the valid authority" (*pramāṇa*).

If it is argued that "the state of being a manifestation will nevertheless persist," he says in response: "because of consciousness" (*saṃvitti*). This means that it has been established previously—by such statements as "there is nothing else, such as a self (*ātman*), apart from consciousness which is of the nature of the conventional" (cf. 110a)—that there exists no other entity whatsoever. The meaning is that it has been demonstrated that the entire universe is mere cognition, free from the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).

159.3 Therefore, since there is no self (*ātman*) or other entity apart from consciousness, and since it is impossible for consciousness to exist without being cognized, it is established that within a mind characterized by a profound and noble form, there can never be the occurrence of its opposite—namely, ordinary conceptualization (*vikalpa*). 160.0 [44a5-6] Now, one might raise the following objection: "Even if a mind with a profound and noble form is seen to be the antithesis of ordinary conceptualization, nevertheless, it will not completely eliminate it, just as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the like do not entirely eliminate hatred (*dveṣa*) and so forth. To this, he says: "And that which is opposed... and so on.
For that which is opposed by something...
Even if it occurs but once, that [insight], having its effort directed toward that [object],
through the intensification of the practice of vision, becomes the absolute suppressor of its own opposite. (160)

Furthermore, whatever entity is even once contradictory with something else, all of that—when it has reached its culmination through the increase of repeated practice by means of a view ascertained by valid cognition—is capable of absolutely obstructing its own opposite, such as compassion, just as the cruelty of a Vedic *śrotriya* or a *kāpālika* obstructs compassion and the like. Therefore, it is logical that this mind, characterized by a profound and noble form, is indeed the absolute overturner of ordinary conceptualization.

However, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the other [immeasurables] that have sentient beings as their object do not completely eliminate hatred and the like, even while suppressing them for a time, because both [the immeasurables and the afflictions] are rooted in the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). It is therefore rightly said that the mere temporary postponement of hatred and the like by means of loving-kindness and the others is like the [temporary] suppression of phlegm and the like by fire and so forth.
As it has been said:
"Because they share a single source in the grasping at a self, and because of their relationship as cause and effect... (Verse 160)
Although attachment and aversion are distinct, they do not mutually exclude one another;
because they are not in opposition to delusion, loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] do not completely suppress the defects.
And all impurities have that as their root, and that [root] is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
(Pramāṇavārttika Pramāṇa 213cd–215ab).

161.0 [44b1-2] One might object: "Is it not the case that the path consisting precisely of the practice of generosity and so forth is superior, as it opposes the suffering of existence? Why then is there this mental focus on the form of the maṇḍala-circle? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "From the ordinary and innate forms," and so on.
Even generosity and the rest, though endowed with selflessness, [are inferior] compared to the ordinary and innate forms.
It is not contradictory because, even when that exists, it does not undergo cessation.

(161) For an ordinary worldling (*prākṛta-pṛthagjana*), their own inherent forms (*nijāni rūpāṇi*)—when giving and so forth arise from those causes—are not in contradiction with the suffering of existence (*bhavaduḥkha*). This is likewise true for one who is endowed with selflessness (*nairātmya*). For even when this giving and so forth exist, that suffering of existence, which consists of the inherent forms of the ordinary person, does not undergo cessation. This is the meaning.

Giving and so forth, when performed with either the view of apprehension (*upalambha*) or the view of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), do not contradict the functioning of ordinary conceptualization (verse 161.2). Alternatively, giving and so forth do not conflict with the nature of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); yet, even though they are endowed with selflessness (*nairātmya*), they do not become [selfless] themselves. There is no direct contradiction with selflessness itself, because by logical necessity it is of the very nature of selflessness. This is because [giving and so forth] are absent in its absence; and even though the activity of giving and so forth consists in non-apprehension, it is restricted to specific objects to be given and so on.

If it is argued that [the goal] might be achieved through aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), that is not so, because even that is not direct. Consequently, the system of the perfections (*pāramitānaya*), consisting of the perfections such as generosity and the rest, is not the direct cause of perfect enlightenment; thus, it is neither concise nor free from difficulty. Therefore, those who desire to accomplish the welfare of the entire world—quickly, always, and in every way—should practice this very truth of the path (*mārgasatya*). They should be endowed with superior wisdom, skilled in means, seeing no contradiction in the afflictions (*kleśa*), and being clever in directing their efforts toward the non-differentiation of the goal through the internalization of reasoning. For it is said: 161.4 Thus:

To begin with, even a continuous stream of wholesome deeds such as giving—which arises from compassion and is conditioned by the perception of a recipient and so forth—is not capable, in the slightest degree, of bringing about the non-conceptual state for oneself or others; this is because a contrary mental determination is the cause for the arising of conceptualizations that correspond to it. Thus it is said: “Without wisdom, these five perfections are eyeless;
lacking a guide, they cannot aspire toward enlightenment.”

(Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā 7.1cd). However, the ascertainment of the selflessness of all things, although itself conceptual in nature, constitutes precisely the cessation of all conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*) through its very nature as the ascertainment of its own object. Furthermore, whatever has once been observed to contradict something else will, through extreme habituation, entirely eliminate that which is its opposite—just as fire [eliminates] cold and so forth; otherwise, due to the suspicion of error, practical activity (*vyavahāra*) would be impossible everywhere. And it is said in this regard: "If one examines phenomena as being without self..."
Having examined them, if one should cultivate them,
that is the cause for attaining the fruit of nirvāṇa;
any other cause does not lead to liberation.
(Samādhirāja p. xx).

Furthermore, the practice of selflessness (*nairātmya*), when devoid of a specific excellence of means (*upāya*), is incapable of producing the omniscient gnosis (*sarvajñajñāna*) which is free from the stain of all conceptual construction and benefits the entire world. Therefore, one must strive for the manifestation of an extraordinary excellence of means. For omniscient gnosis is characterized by the benefit of the entire world without exception, and such benefit arises from unsurpassed magnanimity; its cause is precisely the practice of means, because the practice of selflessness has as its fruit only the abandonment of mere conceptual construction. As it is said:
Through both its vastness and its profundity, there is ripening and non-conceptuality;
because these two are taught herein, this is the unsurpassed means.
(Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 1.13).

Thus, let it be that the functioning of the volition toward generosity and so forth by one who is free from error constitutes the means (*upāya*), because when there is the dedication toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), that [volition] becomes a cause for perfect awakening (*sambodhi*). And so it has been said:

Generosity, ethical discipline, patience, as well as vigor, meditative concentrations, and wisdom—these should be dedicated toward supreme enlightenment. Yet, one should not grasp at these aggregates of enlightenment as being signless; this is how it should be taught to those who are beginners.

(Prajñāpāramitāsaṃcayagāthā 131/15.3) Thus it is said. This is not so; for the intellect resulting from the cultivation of dissimilar causes is the cause for attaining the state of a Perfectly Awakened One. As it says: "How, O son of good family, will you realize unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, since you undertake all these difficult feats while remaining ignorant of the reality of all the Tathāgatas? (Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha 1,23,18)
Thus, one should cultivate magnanimity (*audārya*) as being non-different from its own intrinsic nature, just like selflessness (*nairātmya*).

If it is asked: "But how can a magnanimity that does not exist, even when cultivated, be capable of bringing about the attainment of the desired fruit?"—it is not so; for even that which is unreal becomes the cause of a perfectly clear manifestation through the practice of cultivation, just like the "earth-totality" (*pṛthivī-kṛtsna*) and other such meditations.

If it is argued that its unreality consists in the fact that it functions as an act of mental engagement (*adhimukti-manaskāra*) through the superimposition of that [Buddha’s] form upon one's own self, which is devoid of the form of a Buddha’s body, then in that case, even the mental engagement with reality (*tattva-manaskāra*) would not be real, because it does not function in accordance with reality. For reality has the sole characteristic of being non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), yet that mental engagement is not such; for in the stage of a beginner, it functions in a conceptual form.

Let it be granted that the mental engagement has a nature constructed by conceptualization, yet it is not a mental engagement whose object is the Sugata’s form—endowed with excellence—as it appears in that [non-conceptual] light.

If it is asked: "If no other form whatsoever is superimposed upon its own nature, which is not noble, how can this [mental attention] be its antidote? [The answer is: because the mental attention that manifests the form of a Sugata arises by its very nature as something non-ordinary, and because, through the power of cultivation, it becomes the cause for the arising of a continuous and perfectly clear cognition of the same kind; furthermore, at the time when the noble cognition arises, no other cognition having an ordinary form as its object is experienced there, nor is such a thing even unperceived.
It can be determined that this primordial nature indeed exists, for it has been largely established that its essence consists of mere manifestation (*pratītimātra*).
Therefore, one should realize oneself as Samantabhadra, whose conceptual constructions have been eliminated and whose splendor radiates everywhere.
By cultivating [this] alone, one possesses enlightenment.
As it is said:
"By means of which ritual procedure for mudrās, [one attains the goal] in tens of millions of incalculable eons."
The state of all-buddhahood, which was previously unattainable, is attained right here in this very life.
Therefore, I shall perform the visualization,
as far as [the text specifies]. (Sarvabuddhasamāyogaḍākinījālaśaṃvara 1.18–19a)
Therefore, through union with one's own presiding deity, one should contemplate the Self alone.
(*Sarvabuddhasamāyogaḍākinījālaśaṃvara* 1.24cd).

It is with reference precisely to such a mental engagement (*manaskāra*) that the Blessed Ones—who possess the excellence of perfected gnosis—describe the equality even of a practitioner of reality who is not yet perfected; for, due to their resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) in the nature of perfect Buddhahood, those perfected yogins do not perceive any difference [between themselves and the Buddhas]. For if they were to perceive such a difference, there would be no mental engagement with the mind that has the Sugata as its essence, because the Blessed Ones have abandoned all determination of difference. Furthermore, a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that determines the essential nature of the Blessed Ones—who appear in various forms—to be something different from that [nature] could not yield a faultless result.

Having established that infinite form of the Jina within himself as if it were his own mind, one whose body is pure and whose supreme intellect is equal to all Buddhas shall become the means for accomplishing the desires of all beings without exception.

And one should contemplate oneself as being embraced by the lady Prajñā— that which is garlanded with the faces of countless shimmering rays, the supreme means because it is the locus of infinite accomplishment for the benefit of self and others, and which, being inseparable from the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*), is free from the fear of conceptualization. It is perfectly endowed with the excellence of the savor of supreme passion, and is the constant means for that [attainment].
The wise one should meditate upon his own nature.
Thereafter—
relying upon non-duality through the emanations produced by wisdom and skillful means—
One should worship one's own body with objects that consist of the spheres of appearance and stability.

Bringing his own nature, which consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), into manifestation according to the sequence described, he should bring into manifestation as many emanations (*nirmāṇa*) as are necessary for the perfection of mastery over them. It must be understood that these [emanations] are non-different in form from his own essential nature, because they possess the single characteristic of consisting of wisdom and means—given their fitness for arising with an unerring nature—and because they have the nature of an undivided continuum (*santati*).
For a continuum is indeed a succession of conceptualizations produced by preceding volitions (*saṃkalpa*); and what is called an "emanation" is nothing other than that very volition.

If it is asked, "How can there be unity given that there is a manifold nature due to differences in color and so forth? [the response is: In that case, there would be no unity anywhere at all, because even the body of a single deity possesses a manifold nature and thus consists of multiple entities, and because a partless [entity] is not perceived. Rather, each individual arising in the minds of yogins must be contemplated as having the nature of all the deities of the maṇḍala, by way of being a form in which all opposing factors have been eliminated; for each respective meditative absorption (*samādhi*) indicates the non-perception of its corresponding opposite.
Thus, it is established that this alone is the uncommon cause of perfect enlightenment.

Alternatively, regarding those ordinary abodes of the primordial nature (*prakṛtibhavana*), which are therefore innate forms of the mind characterized by natural luminosity, emptiness, and so forth—even while engaged in generosity and the like, it is not in contradiction with a mind in the form of the circle of deities; the meaning is that it is not in contradiction because it is endowed with selflessness (*nairātmya*).

161.6 This is the intended meaning. For when one is endowed with selflessness (*nairātmya*), there is the nature of being merely conceptual construction; and since that [nature] is dependent on mere desire, it consists of the forms of goddesses such as Rūpavajrā and so forth. Thus, because it is of that very essence, how could there be any contradiction? Therefore, it is said to be "shown by the conventions of complete purification. 161.7 [45a2-3] This very point is clarified: because even when the mind takes the form of the circle of the mandala (*maṇḍalacakra*)—which is the nature of the union of wisdom and means—that vow of generosity, ethical discipline, and so forth does not cease. 162.0 [45a3] With the words "thus" (*iti*) and so forth, he now concludes.
Having understood this, who indeed would not meditate upon the glorious Samantabhadra, one's own true nature, whose mind is instantly perfected through wisdom by the compassionate one? 162

162.1 Having understood the meaning just explained, [the author] indicates that [the goal] is to be accomplished without effort by means of the sudden, concise realization through the knowledge of wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāyajñāna*), using a description as if it were already established. The meaning is that it can be accomplished quickly and without exertion.

Who that is compassionate and desires the welfare of beings would not meditate upon him whose own form is his own manifestation to all, who is *Śrīmān* (the Glorious One) by virtue of being the substratum for the complete attainment of his own welfare, and who is *Samantabhadra* (Universally Auspicious) by virtue of being the locus for the attainment of the welfare of others—since from him there arises, as appropriate, complete (*samantam*) and auspicious (*bhadram*) well-being for those to be trained? The word *vai* expresses intolerance; it is not tolerated that some wise person should not meditate upon him.
(163.0) [45a6] Now, the Master, wishing to avoid any appearance of self-conceit, says: "O stainless one," and so forth.
What opportunity is there for one such as I to compose this work, when all darkness has been dispelled by the rays of the stainless intellect? Nevertheless,
whatever little [I have] adopted from the opinion of my elders, that is placed at the beginning.
Since this effort loosens the bond of existence, it is for that reason undertaken.
Only those of stainless intellect—those great ones by whom the darkness of all delusion has been dispelled—are capable of and able to compose this *sādhana* of Mañjuvajra.

But what opportunity is there here for one such as I? Nevertheless, whatever opinion of the venerable teachers has been received and grasped—that indeed, when practiced by way of performing the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), first of all, at the very beginning, loosens the tight bonds of worldly existence—because of that, this effort in composing the means of accomplishment is undertaken; the implication is that it is not out of pride in knowledge. (164.0) Now, he speaks regarding the dedication of the merit arising from the composition of the means of accomplishment: "Thus," etc.
"Thus, that which has arisen from the composition..."
Whatever in the world is auspicious and stainless, let him always meditate upon that as being supported by the wisdom of the Buddha and inclined toward it. 164

164.1 By means of that stainless merit produced from the composition of this proof, may the minds of all beings in the world come to be endowed with the aforementioned Buddha-knowledge; being inclined toward it and flowing toward it, may they always meditate upon this circle of deities.
Closing Verse:
To the glorious Mañjughoṣa, the unsurpassed ocean of the jewel of great compassion—

By whatever merit I have gained through this extensive exposition of the complete sādhana— the very tongue of wisdom that knows the unfolding of all ritual manuals— may all people attain uninterrupted delight in the one who possesses every form and has conquered Māra.
Colophon: The commentary on the *Caturaṅgasādhana*, titled *Sāramañjarī*, is completed. This work is the composition of the venerable master Ācārya Śrī Samantabhadra.
End. Scribal colophon of the diplomatic transcript:
Those phenomena that arise from a cause, their cause the Tathāgata has explained, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa. May there be no fault.
